en: Commentary on the First Fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-ratna-sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Upper Tianzhu Monastery;
the meaning expounded by the Chinese Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu.
The First Chapter: The Heart of All Buddha-Speech.
"All" refers universally to the ten directions and the three periods of time. "Buddha" means awakening. The Buddha has taught immeasurable dharmas.
It clarifies only the meaning of the single mind; therefore, it is said that "the Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence.
If one is deluded regarding the mind and pursues the words, the words become mere dregs. If one seeks the mind apart from the words, the mind is like the hair of a tortoise.

Now, by harmonizing the mind with the words and sealing the mind with the words, it is titled the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Words and the Mind. Furthermore, this single sutra exists in three translations; this [version] is named the Song [Dynasty]...
The first translation is the earliest; its text consists of four fascicles and contains a single chapter title. It was originally translated during the Northern Wei dynasty by Bodhiruci;
its text consists of ten fascicles and contains eighteen chapters. Next is the translation by Śikṣānanda of the Tang dynasty;
its text consists of seven fascicles and contains ten chapter titles. One must consult all three translations together before one can truly understand this sutra.

Regarding the essential principles and underlying intent: the introductory section (*nidāna*) of the current translation is extremely brief, and the dissemination section (*parīndanā*) has not been transmitted.
Therefore, I have also cited two other translations to complete the three-part structure: first, the Introductory Section (brief in this translation, detailed in the two others);

second, the Main Body of the Teaching (this translation consists of one chapter, the Wei translation is divided into fifteen chapters, and the Tang translation is divided into seven chapters); and third, the Dissemination Section.
(These two translations both contain two chapters; this version lacks them).

The first part, the introduction, is divided into two sections: 1. The general introduction; 2. The specific introduction. (In the Wei translation, this is titled "Chapter One: All Buddhas. In the Tang translation, it is titled "Chapter One:
King Rāvaṇa’s Exhortation"). Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the designation of the time and place where the Dharma was heard.
Second, the citation of the companions who heard and retained [the teaching]. △ Now, the first [part]:
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the summit of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the Southern Sea, adorned with various precious flowers (as the Wei translation says:
"The Bhagavān dwelt on the summit of Mount Malaya by the edge of the great ocean, at the city of Laṅkā").

In its center is that mountain, composed of various precious substances, with diverse jewels interspersed therein. Its brilliance blazes and flares like hundreds of thousands of suns, illuminating the golden mountain.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable flower gardens and fragrant trees, all consisting of precious incense forests.

When a gentle breeze strikes them, shaking the branches and moving the leaves, hundreds of thousands of wondrous fragrances are simultaneously diffused, and hundreds of thousands of exquisite sounds are simultaneously produced. Amidst these layered cliffs...
It is winding and curved, with such places existing everywhere. There are countless grottoes and sanctuaries for immortals, fashioned from various jewels;

they are transparent both inside and out, such that even the radiance of the sun and moon cannot shine upon them. These are all sites where the sages and holy worthies of antiquity contemplated the Dharma as it truly is and attained the Way.
(The Tang translation states: "The Buddha dwelt in the city of Laṅkā on Mount Malaya, by the shore of the great ocean.")

The Commentary states: This refers to the fourth of the five matters that serve as evidence for faith. "Thus" (*evam*) indicates the Dharma that was heard. "I heard" (*śrutam mayā*) clarifies the person who was able to retain it.
"At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) clarifies the harmony between hearing and retention. "The Buddha" (*bhagavān*) clarifies that at that time, he heard it from the Buddha.
"On the shores of the South Sea," etc., clarifies the location where it was heard and retained. According to the two [dynasties] of Wei and Tang...
The translation also states: "Atop the summit of Mount Laṅkā. This refers to the "summit of Mount Laṅkā" (楞伽山頂); it is an abbreviated or metaphorical expression.

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the "ocean" is the realm of the eight consciousnesses; the "mountain" is the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena); the "city" is the Great Parinirvāṇa;
and the "various precious flowers" are the wondrous jewels of innate wisdom and the wondrous flowers of meritorious virtue. From the *Dharma*...

The nature-born [beings] further adorn the *dharmatā*. That the Buddha abides therein is precisely the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedyāryajñāna*), which does not depart from the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the manifestation of one's own mind.
△ Second, citing companions who hear and uphold [the teaching].
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas who had come from various diverse buddha-fields,
these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possessed the sovereign power of immeasurable samādhis and sported with supernatural transformations.
With the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati as their leader, all the Buddhas poured water upon their heads from their own hands, [empowering them] with the manifestation of their own minds.

He thoroughly understands the meaning of the spheres of experience (*viṣaya*). For various sentient beings with their diverse mentalities and physical forms, he universally manifests through immeasurable gates of liberation according to their respective types.
He has reached ultimate penetration regarding the five dharmas, the three natures (*svabhāva*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*). [The Wei translation states:
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas, all of whom had come from various Buddha-lands in other directions, they gathered together. This is...
The Bodhisattvas, endowed with the power of immeasurable sovereign samādhis and supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), travel and transform through the world with vigorous ease.
They are skilled in knowing the five dharmas, self-nature, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness, having attained ultimate penetration.

With the Mahāsattva Mahāmati as their leader, all the Buddhas pour water upon their crowns from their own hands, conferring upon them the rank of Buddhahood. They are well-versed in the fact that their own minds constitute the objective realm.

Its meaning is as follows: for various sentient beings with various mentalities and physical forms, he universally manifests according to their various minds and various diverse thoughts, through immeasurable gates of liberation, in accordance with those who are to be saved and what they ought to see. [The Tang translation says: "Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus."
Together with a great assembly of Bodhisattvas, all of whom were Mahāsattvas who had thoroughly mastered the five dharmas, the three natures, the various consciousnesses, and selflessness;
who well understood the meaning that objects are manifestations of one's own mind; who sported in immeasurable sovereign samādhis, supernatural powers, and various strengths;
who manifested diverse forms according to the minds of sentient beings to tame them through skillful means; and who were anointed by the hands of all Buddhas.
Their leaders all came to this assembly from various Buddha-lands; Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva was their chief).
The Commentary says: According to the present edition and the Wei translation, both the assembly of bhikṣus and the assembly of bodhisattvas came from other lands.
They have gathered. According to the Tang translation, it appears that the *bhikṣus* are the regular retinue, while the Bodhisattvas have come from other lands.

Regarding the *bhikṣus* of the regular retinue, there are two types: those who are transformational (*nirmāṇa*) and those who are of actual practice (*yathābhūta*). As for the *bhikṣus* who have gathered here, the majority are likely transformational ones;
or perhaps those transformational ones, by means of their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), have brought along those of actual practice as well.
Those who come must be capable of hearing the Mahāyāna Dharma before they may attain this auspicious assembly.
The reason for listing the names with the bhikṣus at the forefront is that they represent the signs of transcending the world and possess a fixed monastic lineage.

The reason for praising the virtues solely of the bodhisattvas is to manifest the Mahāyāna and to show that they shall succeed to the Buddha’s work. The remaining points can be understood by comparing them with the two other translations. The introduction is concluded.
2. The Specific Introduction (exists in two translations; it is missing from the present sutra).
The Commentary states: According to the Wei and Tang editions, the Buddha first taught the Dharma for seven days within the palace of a dragon king.
Looking toward a mountain city on the southern shore of the sea, he smiled and spoke of the causes and conditions of past Buddhas. When that king heard this, [he was moved].

Having done so, they welcomed the Buddha into the city, where he manifested various supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). Regarding the two dharmas presented in the dialogue, those who seek them should look for them there.
The introductory section is concluded. (As for the "two dharmas," the Tathāgata said: "Even dharma should be relinquished, let alone non-dharma. Thereupon, [the interlocutor] asked:
"What is called dharma? What is called non-dharma? How can there be these two?")
II. The Main Body (*śarīra-bhāga*). This major section is divided into two parts: first, a general exposition of one hundred and eight statements; second, a detailed exposition of thirty-nine gates.

Regarding the first, the general exposition of one hundred and eight statements (in the Wei translation, this is titled "Chapter Two: Questions and Answers"; in the Tang translation, it is titled "Chapter Two:
Collection of All Dharmas"), the text is divided into three sections: first, the recitation of verses in praise of the Buddha; second, the request [for instruction]; [third, the response].

The Buddha granted his permission. Part Three consists of the formal exchange of questions and answers, which has two sections: first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler describing the ritual setting;
second, Mahāmati’s verses of praise. △ Now, the first section.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, together with the Bodhisattva Maitreya, traveling through all the buddha-fields, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha in verse.
(The Wei translation states: "At that time, the Noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, together with all the Mahāmati Bodhisattvas...")
"...travelling together to all Buddha-lands," and so forth.
The Commentary states: *Mati* is also called *mati*; this is translated as "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

This is because, in order to reach the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the self-manifesting measure of one's own mind, one must rely upon the great wisdom of noble self-realization (*pratyātma-ārya-jñāna*). Wisdom is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); all...
The Dharma leads to wisdom. By realizing that all Buddha-fields are merely manifestations of one’s own mind, one is able to traverse them all;
yet both the traverser and the traversed depend upon the fundamental awakening of Buddha-nature. Therefore, it is said that they "rely on the Buddha's spiritual power."
Knowing that all phenomena are empty, yet not realizing [nirvana] therein, he is said to "rise from his seat," manifesting the skillful means for delivering sentient beings.
Because these skillful means do not depart from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), he is said to "place his right knee on the ground."
The provisional and the ultimate are non-dual; because this accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is said that he "joined his palms in reverence.

Because the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) reveals the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), it is said that he "praised the Buddha with verses. II. Mahāmati’s Verses of Praise. This has two parts:
first, the actual praise of the Buddha’s virtues; second, the exhortation to practice contemplation. △ Now, the first part.
The world is free from arising and ceasing, just like flowers in the sky. Wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet it gives rise to great compassion.
(The Wei translation says: "The Buddha’s wisdom and great compassion observe that the world is free from arising and ceasing, just like flowers in the sky;
existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended. The following three verses follow this pattern. [The Tang translation of the current edition is largely the same].)
The Commentary says: This praises the Buddha’s ultimate and thorough penetration of the five dharmas. Worldly names and signs are established solely from deluded conceptualization;
their nature is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), free from arising and ceasing. To realize that these are neither existent nor non-existent is called "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*).
Because this wisdom does not apprehend existence or non-existence, it is not the compassion born of the two conditions of birth and dharma; thus, it is called "Great."

Out of compassion, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Therefore, the wisdom that does not abide in the two extremes is called the wisdom that does not apprehend existence or non-existence.

All phenomena are like illusions and are far removed from mind and consciousness; while this wisdom does not apprehend existence or non-existence, it nevertheless gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
The Commentary states: This praises the Buddha’s ultimate penetration of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). All phenomena are like illusions arising through conditions;

the mind and consciousness grasp them and thereby produce deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*). When one is far removed from the deluded thoughts of the mind and consciousness, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is revealed.
Distant from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, the world is ever like a dream. Wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, yet it gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
The Commentary states: This praises the Buddha’s ultimate penetration of the eight consciousnesses.

Since the eight consciousnesses act as mutual causes and effects, continuing in a revolving succession, they are neither annihilated nor eternal. They manifest the world, all of which is like a dream.
Knowing that persons and phenomena lack self, and that afflictions and their latent tendencies are eternally pure and signless, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
The Commentary states: This praises the Buddha’s ultimate penetration of the two kinds of selflessness. "Afflictions" refers to the various delusions, both conceptual and innate;

their nature is that of affliction, which disturbs and confuses the practitioner—this is precisely the grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*). "Latent tendencies" (or *anuśaya*)... [text fragment ends]
*Jñeya*. This is translated as "that which is known" (*jñeya*) and also as "object-sphere" (*viṣaya*). It refers to the various phenomena (*dharma*) within and without the three realms.
If wisdom is obstructed, it cannot clearly know these things; therefore it is said: "That which is known is not itself the obstruction; rather, the obstruction is what obstructs that which is known."

This is precisely the grasping at a self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Now, knowing that afflictions are eternally pure and signless is the ultimate realization of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*);
knowing that suchness (*tathatā*) is eternally pure and signless is the ultimate realization of the selflessness of phenomena.
There is no nirvāṇa in anything; there is no Buddha in nirvāṇa, nor is there nirvāṇa in the Buddha.

Far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened, one is free from both existence and non-existence—abandoning both of these. (The Wei translation says: "The Buddha neither enters nor ceases; nirvāṇa likewise does not abide.
One leaves behind the dharmas of awakening and that which is awakened, abandoning both existence and non-existence. The Tang translation says: "The Buddha does not abide in nirvāṇa...")
The Buddha is non-abiding; he is far removed from the subject and object of awakening, whether existent or non-existent. The Dharma-body is like an illusion or a dream—how could it be praised?
To know that there is no intrinsic nature and no arising is truly to praise the Buddha. The Buddha has no characteristics of sense-faculties or objects;
not seeing is called seeing the Buddha. How, then, could one ever praise or disparage the Muni?

The Commentary states: Although this praise of the Buddha indicates that he has ultimately and thoroughly realized the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and selflessness, in reality there are no two characteristics—the subject that realizes and the object that is realized.
"All" refers precisely to the five dharmas, the self-natures, the various consciousnesses, and selflessness. All phenomena have, from the very beginning, been eternally characterized by quiescence.
Since there is no further cessation, it is said that "all things have no nirvāṇa.
There is no Buddha who enters nirvāṇa, nor is there any Buddha capable of entering nirvāṇa. This is because the Buddha is the wisdom that realizes, while nirvāṇa is the principle that is realized;
since wisdom and principle are non-dual, in reality there is neither subject nor object. Therefore, it is said: "Far removed from the realization and that which is realized."
Furthermore, if one were to definitively state that the Buddha and Nirvāṇa exist, then there would be subject and object, falling into the error of reification (*samāropa*).
If one were to definitively state that the Buddha and Nirvāṇa do not exist, then it would become nihilism, falling into the error of denial (*apavāda*). Therefore, it is said:
"Whether as existent or as non-existent, both of these are completely abandoned. This concludes the initial section on the formal praise of the Buddha's virtues. △ Second, the conclusion.
Exhortation to Practice Contemplation:
The Tathāgata’s contemplation of tranquility is that which is far removed from arising; this is called non-appropriation. In this life and in future lives, one is pure.
(The Wei translation says: "If one contemplates the Buddha in this way—tranquil and free from arising and ceasing—that person, in this and future lives, will be free from defilement and untainted.")
To grasp. ○ The Tang translation says: "If one sees the Muni as tranquil and detached from arising, that person, in this and future lives, will be free from attachment and have nothing to grasp."
The Commentary says: This exhorts the practitioner to observe the World-Honored One, the Muni, by means of this principle of tranquility.
Thus, one remains far removed from the two kinds of birth-and-death; this is called "not grasping at any phenomena.
In this way, both the present life and future lives will be entirely pure. The first section, the verse of praise to the Buddha, is concluded. II. Requesting the Buddha.
The second part consists of two sections: first, the formal request; second, the Buddha’s permission for him to ask freely. Regarding the first:
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāmati had praised the Buddha with verses, he stated his own name: "My name is Mahāmati; I have attained mastery in the Mahāyāna.
Now, by means of one hundred and eight points of meaning, I respectfully consult the Most Honored One" (the Wei translation says: "I respectfully consult the Unsurpassed One").
[The Honored One].
△ Second, the Buddha grants permission to inquire.
The Sage, Knower of the World, having heard those spoken verses, surveyed the entire assembly and addressed the sons of the Buddhas, saying:
"O you sons of the Buddhas, now all of you may ask whatever you desire; I shall explain for you the realm of self-realization.

Thus ends the second part, the request for the Buddha’s permission. III. The actual presentation of the questions and answers, which has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. △ Now, the first part: the question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having received the Buddha’s permission, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and asked in verse:
"How does one purify mindfulness? How does mindfulness increase? And how does one perceive delusion?"
How do delusions increase? (The Wei translation says: How are all perceptions purified? By what cause do perceptions arise?
By what cause does confusion arise? By what cause is there confusion? The Tang translation says: How do conceptualizations arise? How are conceptualizations purified?
How does confusion arise? How is confusion purified?)
The Commentary states: This is a general inquiry into the source of delusion and enlightenment. It asks: How does one purify deluded thoughts? How do delusions increase?
How does one perceive this ignorance and confusion? And how does ignorance and confusion increase?
"Why are there lands, transformations, and various non-Buddhists? (The Wei translation reads: "For what reason are there lands, transformed appearances, and various non-Buddhists?
The commentary states: This asks why there are buddha-lands, and why there are transformations such as the six realms of existence.
Characteristics. For what reason are there furthermore the teachings of the various non-Buddhists?
What is the sequence of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*)? Why is it named "non-appropriation"? Why is one named a "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*)? To what destination does liberation lead?
Who is bound and who is liberated? (The Wei translation says: What is called a Son of the Buddha? Quiescence and its sequence; where does liberation reach?
Who is bound and by what cause is one released? The Tang translation says: What is called a Son of the Buddha?
And the shadowless sequence; where does liberation reach? Who is bound and who can liberate?)
The Commentary states: "Non-reception" (wu shòu) is what the Wei translation calls "quiescence" (jìjìng) and the Tang translation calls "absence of shadow" (wúyǐng).

Because it does not receive any sensations whatsoever, it is named "right reception" (zhèngshòu) and also "non-reception. This is the fundamental wisdom (mūlaprajñā) that directly realizes suchness (tathatā).
Because its characteristics do not change and because it is free from conceptual discrimination, it is called "absence of shadow" and also "quiescence."
Although this realm of suchness has no sequential order, it is established with multiple names according to the sequence of abandoning the hindrances,
as is extensively explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
What is the sphere of dhyāna? How do the three vehicles come to be? We pray that you will explain this for us. (The Wei translation says: "In dhyāna, what dharmas are observed?
For what reason are there three vehicles? The Tang translation says: "What is the sphere of dhyāna? Why are there three vehicles? From what does dependent origination arise?
What is the agent and what is the acted upon? (The Wei translation says: "For what causes and conditions do phenomena arise? The second line is the same.)
The Tang translation says: "By what cause does that arise? What acts and what is capable of acting? How are the two different explanations?

What serves as their growth? The Wei translation says: "For what reason are the two different explanations? For what reason does that which is non-existent appear? The Tang translation says: "Who speaks of the two being different?"

What is the arising of all existences? What is the formless attainment (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—how do both constitute the attainment of cessation?
What is the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-nirodha*) [i.e., the attainment of non-perception]? By what cause does one awaken from that concentration? And how is the activity produced?
Entering and maintaining the body. (The Wei translation says: "How does a cause produce a fruit? How do the body go and stay? How does manifestation differentiate?
How are the various stages (*bhūmi*) produced? (The Wei translation says: "By what cause is that which is seen observed? By what cause are the various stages produced?
The Tang translation says: "How are all things seen? How does one enter the various stages? Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence (*tribhava*)? Where is the body? What is it called?
What is it? Where does one go after rebirth? What is a most excellent son? (The Wei translation says: Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence?
With what body does one go to what place? In what state does one abide? What is a son of the Buddhas? The Tang translation says: What is a son of the Buddha?)

Who is able to shatter the three realms of existence? Where is the body, and of what nature is it? Where does birth arise and where does it abide? By what cause are the supernormal powers, masteries, and samādhis attained?
What is the mind of samādhi? O Most Victorious One, please explain this to me. (The third line in the Wei translation reads:)

By what cause is the concentrated mind attained? [The rest is the same as in the Song edition. ○ In the Tang [translation] it says: How does one attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), mastery (*vaśitā*), and samādhi?

What are the characteristics of the mind in samādhi? I pray that the Buddha will explain this for me. What is called the "store" (*ālaya*)? What are the "mind" (*manas*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)?

What is arising and what is ceasing? What is it that, having been seen, returns? (The Wei translation asks: By what cause is there the *ālayavijñāna*? By what cause are there the *manas* and the [six] consciousnesses?
By what cause are various views produced? By what cause are those views severed? The Tang translation asks: What is called the *ālayavijñāna*?
What is called the mental consciousness? How do various views arise? How are various views abandoned? What is meant by "spiritual lineage" (*gotra*)? It is not...
The seeds and the mind-only. (Wei: What is nature and what is non-nature? What is the mind and the absence of dharmas?
Tang: What is nature and what is non-nature? Why is it called "mind-only"? How are the characteristics established, as well as the meaning of non-self?
Why are there no sentient beings? Why is there conventional discourse? (Wei: For what reason is the dharma-characteristic taught? What is called "non-self"?)

For what reason is there no sentient being? For what reason does conventional truth exist? [The Tang translation says: For what reason are characteristics established? How is non-self accomplished? Why is there no sentient being?
Why is it spoken of according to worldly convention? How is it that the views of annihilationism and eternalism do not arise?
[The Wei translation says: For what reason is eternity not seen? For what reason is annihilation not seen? [The Tang translation says: How is it that one attains...]
[Arising]. [The views of] permanence and annihilation). What is the Buddha and the non-Buddhists? Their characteristics do not contradict one another.
(Wei: "They act as two. What will be in future ages? The various different schools. (What is it? Wei: "By what cause? Tang:
"For what reason? What is emptiness and by what cause? What is momentary destruction? (Wei says: "What is called emptiness? By what cause is it mindfulness?")
Non-abiding. ○ [The Tang translation asks: What is meant by "emptiness of nature"? What is meant by "momentary extinction"?
What is meant by "birth from the womb"? Why is the world immovable? [The Wei translation asks: For what cause is there a womb? For what cause is the world immovable?
[The Tang translation asks: How does the womb arise? Why is the world immovable? Why is it like an illusion, a dream, and a city of the Gandharvas? Why is the world burning?
At that time, [the Buddha spoke of] the mirage and the moon in the water. (The Wei translation says: "Why are they like illusions and dreams?
Why are they said to be like a *gandharva* city, a mirage, and the moon in the water? World-Honored One, explain this to me. The Tang translation says:

"Why are all worlds like illusions and also like dreams, like a *gandharva* city, a mirage, and even the moon in the water? For what reason did you speak of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and awakening (*bodhi*)?

[Section] (The Wei translation asks: "What is called the awakening factor (*bodhyaṅga*)? By what cause are they the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*)? The Tang translation asks: "What are the factors of enlightenment?
From where do the factors of awakening arise? Why is the land in turmoil? Why does one form views of existence? (The Tang translation asks: "For what reason does one perceive all existences?
Why are there no arising or ceasing? The world is like flowers in the sky. How does one awaken to the world? What is it that is taught?
Free from syllables. (The Wei translation asks: For what reason is there no arising or ceasing? For what reason is it like flowers in the sky? For what reason does one awaken to the world?

For what reason is there no teaching by means of syllables? The Tang translation asks: How does one know worldly phenomena? How does one transcend words and letters? How is it like flowers in the sky?)
Neither arising nor ceasing—what is it that is free from false conceptualization? Why is there the analogy of space? (The Wei translation says: "Why is there non-discrimination?
For what reason is it like space? The Tang translation says: "How is it like space? How is it free from discrimination? How many kinds of suchness are there?
How many are the perfections of the mind? (The Wei translation says: "How many kinds of *tathatā* are there? What is called 'mind,' and how many [are there]?)
[The Buddha] said: "What are the various kinds of *tathatā* (true suchness)? How many are there? What are the causes by which the mind of the various *pāramitās* traverses the stages (*bhūmi*)?

Who reaches the state of non-apprehension? [The Wei translation says: "By what cause are the stages sequential? True suchness has no sequence. [The Tang translation says: "What is the sequence of the stages? How does one attain the shadowless?
"What are the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*)? How is the flame purified? [The Wei translation says: "What are the two kinds of selflessness? How is the flame purified?"

By what cause are the two kinds of selflessness [attained]? By what cause is the objective realm purified? (The Tang translation says: What are the two kinds of selflessness? How is that which is known purified? How many kinds of wisdom are there?

How many types of precepts and natures of sentient beings are there? (The Wei translation says: How many kinds of wisdom and how many precepts? By what cause are sentient beings born? The Tang translation says:
How many kinds of noble wisdom are there? The same applies to the precepts and sentient beings. Who gives rise to the various natures of jewels?
Maṇi-jewels, pearls, and the like—(the Wei version says: "Who creates the natures of all jewels, such as gold and maṇi-jewels?";
the Tang version says: "Maṇis and all such jewels—how do these all emerge? Who gives rise to all languages? The various natures of sentient beings—(the Wei version says:
"Who produces languages? The various differences among sentient beings?"; the Tang version says: "Who initiates languages? Sentient beings and...")

The Commentary states: From "For what reason? up to "transformed here," he asks universally about all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane.
The intent is to reveal that these are all illusory manifestations arising from delusion and awakening. If one investigates and analyzes each one individually, it is certain that no reality exists.

The nature [of all things] does not, in its entirety, transcend the direct manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). However, by reading the two translations side-by-side, their essential meaning will become clear of itself;

there is no need for further individual explanation. The first and second names and characteristics are appended at the end of this volume. The initial inquiry concludes. II. The Response is divided into two parts:
first, the introductory verse; second, the formal response. The first part is further divided into five sections: first, general praise and consent; second, acknowledging the question.

The Commentary states: According to the present translation, these one hundred and eight phrases amount to only one hundred and four; according to the two translations of the Wei and Tang dynasties, there are respectively one hundred and six phrases.
In each case, there are slight differences in what is omitted or included, and how they are combined or separated.

This is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) manifested within the measure of one’s own mind: following conditions without changing, and remaining unchanged while following conditions.

This concludes the first section, the general clarification of the one hundred and eight phrases. II. The detailed clarification of the thirty-nine gates, which consists of thirty-nine sections.
The first is the gate of the arising, abiding, and changing of the various consciousnesses (the Wei translation calls this the "Chapter on the Collection of All Buddha-Dharmas").
(3) The text is divided into two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. △ Now, the first part.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses?"

The Commentary states: Within the detailed exposition, the initial inquiry regarding the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the various consciousnesses is made because, from time immemorial, the Tathāgatagarbha mind has remained immutable while conforming to conditions;
thus, by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there are eight kinds of consciousness.

Based upon these, the five categories and one hundred dharmas—comprising the causes and effects of both defilement and purity—are established. It is through this that there arise the various dharma-gates of saṃsāric transmigration and the cessation of suffering.
This is because one can thereby discern the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two absences of self.

As for arising, abiding, and ceasing, these are the characteristics of conditioned, illusory phenomena. Nevertheless, various sūtras and śāstras may clarify four characteristics, three characteristics, or merely the two characteristics of arising and ceasing.
One should know that whether there are two, three, or four, they are all equal and identical; they are not [different].

There is increase and decrease. Why is this so? To begin with, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are birth (*jāti*), subsistence (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"However, because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise through the power of causes and conditions, they exist now where they previously did not, and having existed for a brief moment, they return to non-existence.

To represent the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), the four characteristics are provisionally established. 'Existence where there was previously none' is the state called birth; the state of birth remains for a brief pause."

This is then designated as "abiding. Abiding is differentiated according to its prior and subsequent states, and further established under different names. That which exists for a moment and then ceases is called "cessation" (*nirodha*) when it is no longer present.
Because the former three exist, they are all situated in the present; because the latter one is non-existent, it is situated in the past. Furthermore, it is said:
Arising indicates that a phenomenon previously non-existent now exists; cessation indicates that a phenomenon which existed subsequently becomes non-existent;

changeability indicates that this phenomenon is not immutable; and duration indicates that this phenomenon possesses temporary function. These four characteristics are provisionally established based upon the moment (*kṣaṇa*). They may also be provisionally established according to the stages of a single lifetime (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*):
the initial existence is called arising, and the subsequent non-existence is called cessation. Once arisen, the similarity [of successive moments] is...

The continuation [of the stream] is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). This very transformation of the continuum is called "alteration" (*anyathātva*). Therefore, all four characteristics are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
(Text) Now, according to this passage, there are two kinds of four characteristics: first, the four characteristics of a single moment (*kṣaṇika-catur-lakṣaṇa*);

second, the four characteristics of a single lifetime (*āyuṣka-catur-lakṣaṇa*). Within the context of a single lifetime, if we consider the physical body with its faculties, these are birth, old age, sickness, and death.

If we speak in terms of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), it consists of formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness. Next, to clarify the three characteristics, this sutra speaks of arising, subsistence, and cessation;
some say arising, change, and cessation. Because there is change yet no difference, it is conventionally termed "subsistence.
Because there is subsistence yet no remaining, it is conventionally termed "change. Just as old age and illness are both characteristics of change, they are also all [characteristics of subsistence].

This refers to the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). Next, to clarify the two characteristics: among the three—arising, abiding, and change—since they all equally belong to existence (*bhāva*), they are simply termed "arising.
Since cessation belongs to non-existence (*abhāva*), it is still termed "cessation. Furthermore, because abiding serves as the fulfillment of arising, it may be subsumed under arising.

Diversity is the gradual process of cessation; it may also be categorized as cessation itself. Indeed, sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental store-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), giving rise to the illusory manifestations of the eight consciousnesses.
Consequently, they falsely perceive the four marks, three marks, and two marks of conditioned existence, flowing back and forth; once born, these states immediately perish.
Once extinguished, they arise again; from kalpa to kalpa, they circulate without ceasing.

If one penetrates the non-substantiality of arising and extinction and realizes their true essence, which is the primary truth (*paramārtha*), then arising is fundamentally non-arising—what, then, is there to be extinguished?

The noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) will be perfectly accomplished in a single thought-moment. The very crux of delusion and enlightenment both depends upon this; therefore, it was asked about first. ○

In the second part of the response, there are two sections. First, the direct answer concerning arising, abiding, and ceasing; second, the clarification of the gates of the heterodox and the orthodox.
The first section also has two parts: first, the direct explanation of their characteristics; second, the detailed analysis of their causes. △ Now, the first [part].
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing. (The Wei translation says: 'Each consciousness has its own two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
These are not to be known through discursive thought. (The Wei translation says: 'Not that which can be known by those who employ discursive thought. The Tang translation says:)"
This is not something that can be known by those who rely on mere conjecture. All consciousnesses arise in two ways:

namely, arising as a continuous flow (*pravāha-utpāda*)—which constitutes the continuity of both [the cause and the effect]—and arising as a manifestation (*lakṣaṇa-utpāda*). They abide in two ways: namely, abiding as a continuous flow and abiding as a manifestation.

They cease in two ways: namely, ceasing as a continuous flow and ceasing as a manifestation. Mahāmati, all consciousnesses have three kinds of characteristics: namely, the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), and...
Characteristics. The characteristics of reality (the Wei translation states: consciousness is of three kinds: first, the characteristic of transformation; second, the characteristic of karma;
third, the characteristic of cognition).

The Commentary states: "The various consciousnesses" refers collectively to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings (*citta-rāja*), and it also includes the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), the form (*rūpa*) produced by transformation, and the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

"Each has two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing" means that each of the eight consciousnesses, along with their mental factors, possesses the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing in their state of active manifestation (*samudācāra*); these are termed "aspects" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Arising, abiding, and ceasing each possess their own characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing from seeds; these are termed the "flowing current" of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Since this flowing current of arising, abiding, and ceasing arises as active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) from seeds, it in turn perfumes those seeds through its manifestation.
It is like the wick and the flame, which mutually produce and consume one another, acting as cause and effect without a moment’s interval.
Because it is severed, both translations name it "continuity" (*saṃtati*). Regarding the "flowing forth" (*pravṛtti*) of the eighth consciousness:
by the power of the perfuming of the seven evolving consciousnesses, the seeds of maturation (*vipāka*) are caused to arise in succession. Regarding the "abiding in flow" (*sthiti*):
by the power of the *ādāna*-consciousness’s grasping and maintaining, the seeds of maturation are caused to remain unchanged for a long duration. Regarding the "extinction of flow" (*nirodha*):...
By the power of internal permeation through the wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), the seeds of maturation (*vipākavāsanā*) are caused to be relinquished forever and completely.

Regarding the arising of the characteristics of the eighth consciousness: because it is summoned and induced by the power of projecting karma (*ākṣepakakarman*), it initially undergoes the fruit of maturation within the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
Regarding the persistence of its characteristics: by the functional differentiation of the power of projecting karma, it is determined for the duration of a single lifetime.
Regarding "the cessation of characteristics": because the power of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is exhausted, it causes the death of the body and life-force that were being sustained.

Regarding "the arising of the flow of the first seven consciousnesses": because the eighth consciousness is capable of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*), it causes those active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) to be perfumed into seeds, whereby they flow and continue.
Regarding "the abiding of the flow": because the seed-consciousness is capable of sustaining [them], it causes...

That seed is neither lost nor destroyed; as for its "cessation through continuous flow," it is because the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) can oppose it, causing that seed never again to arise in succession.
Regarding the arising of the first seven consciousnesses: the seventh consciousness arises by relying on only three conditions;
therefore, it follows what is produced and bound by the eighth consciousness, and it constantly evolves in dependence upon the eighth.
It still takes the eighth consciousness as its object. The sixth consciousness requires five conditions to arise; therefore, it arises frequently and does not arise infrequently.
The first five consciousnesses require nine, eight, or seven conditions to arise; therefore, they arise infrequently and do not arise frequently.
Regarding the abiding of the characteristics of the first seven consciousnesses: the seventh and the eighth abide for the duration of a single lifetime together, whereas the first six [abide]...
It varies in length according to conditions; its duration has no fixed limit. Regarding the cessation of the characteristics of the first seven consciousnesses:

although the seventh consciousness shares the same nature of arising and ceasing as the eighth, when the eighth consciousness perceives the body and its elements (*kāyadhātu*), it ceases momentarily at the time of death.

However, when the seventh consciousness perceives the eighth, even though one dies, its characteristic does not cease, because the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) remains uninterrupted. Only upon entering...

When one contemplates the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), or when entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the marks of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) are temporarily extinguished.

When one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the marks of grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) are temporarily extinguished. Regarding the first six [consciousnesses], it is easy to understand that they cease as soon as their objective referents (*ālambana*) cease.
Next, concerning the statement that "the various consciousnesses have three kinds of marks," the *Zongjing lu* says: "The arising of the mind is called..."
"Transformation. Because they arise together in groups of eight, all possess arising and ceasing; therefore, they are called the "characteristic of transformation. Movement constitutes karma;
since all eight consciousnesses are mobile, they are all termed the "characteristic of karma. The true nature of these eight is entirely termed the "true characteristic.

(Text) One should know that the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the eight consciousnesses as they transform one another are all the "characteristic of transformation. The arising, abiding, and ceasing of the continuous flow of the eight consciousnesses are all the "characteristic of karma."

The two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are without substance and without intrinsic nature; they are like waves and currents, which are of one single moist nature—this is the true aspect (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the Wei translation’s "wisdom-aspect consciousness" (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna*): it is because only the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) can realize that delusion is itself reality.
II. Extensive Differentiation of Its Cause (three parts): 1. Direct Clarification; 2. Manifestation through Simile; 3. Exclusion of the Erroneous.
△ First: Mahāmati, briefly stated there are three kinds of consciousness; explained in detail, there are eight aspects. What are the three?

They are the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*). (The Wei translation says: "Mahāmati, there are eight kinds of consciousness; briefly stated, there are two kinds.")
What are these two? First is the consciousness that discerns; second is the consciousness that discriminates phenomena. (In the Tang translation, it says:
"O Mahāmati, consciousness is extensively explained as being eightfold, but briefly there are only two: namely, the manifesting consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena.")
The Commentary states: This should be understood according to the two translations as being correct.

For what is here called "manifesting consciousness" (*xiànshí*), which the Wei translation terms "discriminating consciousness" (*liǎobié shì*), refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness. This is because it can suddenly manifest the sense organs, the body, the environment, and all seeds, and it spontaneously discriminates these three types of objective realms.
As for what is here called "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*fēnbié shìshí*):
This refers collectively to the preceding seven consciousnesses. That is to say: the seventh consciousness falsely discriminates the provisional entities of self and dharmas;

the sixth mental consciousness discriminates all provisional and real entities; and the five sensory consciousnesses discriminate the real entities of the five sense-objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, the current translation adds "True Consciousness" (*tathatā-vijñāna*) to speak of three types; this is likely not the original Sanskrit formulation.

The purport of the text is as follows: If one wishes to provide an exegesis, it should be stated that the single *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, which is the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), manifests its entire substance as both the manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*) and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*vikaalpa-vastu-vijñāna*).

This is like taking the nature of moisture and manifesting it as both seawater and waves. If one correlates the true consciousness with the aforementioned aspect of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), and the manifesting consciousness with the aforementioned aspect of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), they are thus distinguished.
If the evolving consciousness were to face the preceding evolving aspect as a separate entity, then the Tathāgata would incur the fault of redundancy.
Mahāmati, it is just as a bright mirror holds various forms and images; the manifestation of the ālayavijñāna is likewise so. Mahāmati.

The manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates objects (*vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*): these two possess the characteristics of being perishable and imperishable, respectively.

They serve as causes for one another (the Wei translation states: "Those two kinds of consciousness have no distinct characteristics and mutually serve as causes for each other"; the Tang translation states: "These two consciousnesses have no difference in appearance and act as mutual causes").
The Commentary says: This passage precisely clarifies that the eighth consciousness is able to manifest all phenomena, and is therefore called the "manifesting consciousness" (*ādarśa-vijñāna*);

it also concurrently clarifies its mutual causality with the preceding seven consciousnesses. Now, just as all forms and images are sustained by a clear mirror and do not exist outside of the mirror, one should know that all seeds of the sense organs, the physical body, and the receptacle world are likewise sustained by the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and do not [exist apart from it].

It exists outside of the *ālayavijñāna*. However, while there is still an external objective reality corresponding to it outside of a bright mirror, there is no such corresponding objective reality outside of the *ālayavijñāna*.

This is because the *ālayavijñāna* fundamentally lacks form and substance, and possesses neither spatial dimensions nor boundaries, unlike a bright mirror which has form, substance, spatial dimensions, and boundaries. Therefore, one should know that it is merely a fragment.

This is a metaphor; it is not a complete analogy. Regarding the "characteristics of destruction and non-destruction," according to the Wei and Tang translations, they simply speak of "the characteristic of no distinction" and "the characteristic of no difference.
Now, that which is without difference and without distinction is what is called the "true" (*tathatā*);

thus, the absence of distinct characteristics is itself the characteristic of destruction, which is also what was referred to in the preceding text as the "true characteristic" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). That which is now further called the "characteristic of non-destruction" is...
The so-called "eight unimpaired characteristics" mentioned in the following text are also what were previously termed the "characteristic of transformation" and the "characteristic of activity.
Excluding the characteristic of reality (zhēnxiàng), there would be no distinct characteristics of the eight consciousnesses; just as there are no waves apart from the nature of moisture.
Excluding the eight consciousnesses, there is likewise no characteristic of reality; just as there is no nature of moisture apart from the waves. Therefore, it is said:
The characteristics of being subject to destruction and not subject to destruction are mutually dependent causes. Furthermore, in terms of the eight consciousnesses:

if there were no seeds maintained by the eighth consciousness, the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the first seven consciousnesses could not arise, nor could the eighth consciousness’s own manifestation exist independently.
Conversely, if there were no active manifestations of the first seven consciousnesses, they would be unable to perfuse the seeds maintained by the eighth consciousness.
Furthermore, the eighth consciousness itself cannot exist independently of its seeds; thus it is said that these two serve as causes for one another.

Generally, the eighth consciousness is the "perfumable" (the object of conditioning), while the preceding seven are the "perfumers" (the agents of conditioning). The preceding seven are what is produced, and the eighth is that which produces.
This is stated in terms of the eight [consciousnesses] as they appear in their undifferentiated characteristics. The "agent" is also the nature of the storehouse (ālaya); the agent is precisely...

The subject is not [independent], and the object is likewise the nature of the storehouse (*ālaya*). The object is precisely "not an object. This is stated in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), where there is no distinction between characteristics.

Outside of the ultimate there is no conventional (*saṃvṛti-satya*); outside of the conventional there is no ultimate. Outside of the subject there is no object; outside of the object there is no subject.
Yet, the ultimate and the conventional, the subject and the object, remain perfectly distinct and unconfused. Therefore, it is said that they are "mutually dependent causes" (*paratantra-hetu*).

Mahāmati, the inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*). Mahāmati, the grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization are the causes of the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*).
(The Wei translation says: "The consciousness of discernment has the inconceivable perfuming and transformation as its cause.
The Tang translation says: "The manifesting consciousness takes inconceivable perfuming and transformation as its cause. Mahāmati, [the former]... (The Wei translation says: "Discriminating...")

The consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vastu-vijñapti-vikalpa*) apprehends objects by taking as its cause the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

(In the Tang translation, it is called "the consciousness that discriminates phenomena," which takes the discrimination of objects and the habitual tendencies of beginningless proliferation as its causes.)
The Commentary states: This precisely clarifies the causes for the arising of the eight consciousnesses.
Now, the Tathāgatagarbha, the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), manifests its entire substance as the seven preceding evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

These seven evolving consciousnesses, in turn, perfuse the Tathāgatagarbha mind moment by moment, causing it to maintain the seeds of all phenomena; this is termed the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Therefore, it is so named.
The inconceivable permeation. Now, the Tathāgatagarbha, the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*), in its entirety constitutes the ālayavijñāna.
This ālayavijñāna, from moment to moment, manifests the sense organs, the body, and the objective world, as well as giving rise to various primary minds and mental factors in active operation;
these are termed the "ten thousand dharmas of the three realms. Therefore, it is called "inconceivable transformation. Apart from these two—permeation and transformation—[there is nothing else].
Regarding phenomena (*dharma*), no further manifest consciousness can be found; therefore, it is said to be the cause of the manifest consciousness.

Now, form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena are called external objects (*bāhyaviṣaya*). To falsely grasp the seeing-division (*darśanabhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as one's own internal self and phenomena is called an internal object (*adhyātmaviṣaya*).
The reason for grasping these objects is entirely due to seeds perfumed by beginningless false habitual tendencies.
This is due to the power of the son [of ignorance]. If there were no seeds of deluded thought, even if sensory objects were present, no discrimination would arise;

even if sensory objects were absent, even if seeds of delusion were present, no discrimination would likewise arise. It is because of the delusive objects manifested by one's own mind that [discrimination occurs].
It further serves as the condition for deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Because the seeds of delusion inherent within one's own mind serve as the cause for deluded conceptualization, there arise the first seven types of consciousness that differentiate objects. Beyond this, there is no other cause whatsoever.
Mahāmati, if the various unreal consciousnesses that veil that true consciousness are extinguished through their falsity, then all the sense-faculty consciousnesses are extinguished;

this is called the extinction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*). (The Wei translation says: "When the various seeds of false discrimination in the *ālayavijñāna* are extinguished, the various sense-faculties are also extinguished.
Mahāmati, this is called the extinction of characteristics. The Tang translation says: "The seeds of false discrimination in the *ālayavijñāna*...")
When the various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are extinguished, all sense-faculties and consciousnesses are extinguished;
this is called the extinction of characteristics (*nimitta*). The commentary states: This first explains the cause for the extinction of the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses.
The phrase "covering that true consciousness with various unreal and false [phenomena]" refers to the *ālayavijñāna* being perfumed by the false and maintaining the false.

Although these seeds are in their entirety the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), they are nevertheless able to obscure that true consciousness, just as waves arising from water entirely can obscure the essence of the clear, still water.
"The extinction of all false delusions" refers to the extinction of the causal aspect of the eighth [consciousness];

"the extinction of all sense-faculties and consciousnesses" refers to the extinction of the resultant aspect of the preceding seven [consciousnesses]. These are both spoken of in terms of active manifestation (*pravṛtti*); therefore, they are called "aspects" (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Extinction. However, this refers to extinction through the process of reversal (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), not to ordinary, momentary cessation.

Mahāmati, as for the extinction of the continuity (*saṃtati-nirodha*): when the causes of continuity are extinguished, then continuity is extinguished; when that from which it proceeds and its objects of perception are extinguished, then continuity is extinguished.
(The Wei translation states: "As for the extinction of continuity: when the causes of continuity are extinguished, then continuity is extinguished.")
With the cessation of causes comes the cessation of conditions; thus, the continuity [of existence] ceases. (The Tang translation states:

"The cessation of continuity means that the supporting cause and the objective condition have ceased, whereby the continuity itself ceases. Mahāmati, why is this so? Because these are its supports. (The Wei translation states:)
Mahāmati, "relying on the Dharma" and "relying on conditions": "relying" refers to the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination;

"conditions" refers to the false discrimination of the objects of the various consciousnesses, such as the views of one's own mind. (The Wei translation states: "Relying on the Dharma" means the perfuming of beginningless playful discourse and false discrimination;
"relying on conditions" means the differentiation of the objects of the views of one's own mental consciousness. The Tang translation states: [As above].

The causal basis refers to the habitual tendencies of beginningless conceptual proliferation and false imagination. The object of perception refers to the objects of discrimination perceived by one's own mind.
The Commentary says: This section explains the cause for the cessation of the continuous flow of the eight consciousnesses.

The continuous succession of all consciousnesses occurs solely because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) as seeds can produce manifest activities (*pravṛtti*), and manifest activities, in turn, perfume seeds.
The perfumed seeds are termed the "source" (*yonsu dong*, *anuśrita*); the manifest objects are termed the "object-condition" (*yonsu yeon*, *ālambana*). The source...
The object-condition (*ālambana*) is also termed a cause for the continuity [of seeds], because it is by depending on these two that the continuity of seeds exists.

In the text, the character "depending" (*yi*) specifically indicates the source from which [the continuity] proceeds; this is different from the character "depending" (*yi*) used in the sense of "that upon which something depends.
This is because the latter "depending" character refers generally to both the source from which [something proceeds] and the object-condition. First, the correct explanation:

"Mahāmati, it is like a lump of clay and its atoms; they are neither different nor not different. It is the same with gold and its ornaments.
Mahāmati, if the lump of clay were different from its atoms, it would not be produced by them; yet in reality, it is produced by them. Therefore..."
They are not different. If they were not different, then there would be no distinction between a lump of clay and its constituent atoms.

The commentary states: Here, the atoms are used as a metaphor for the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and the lump of clay is used as a metaphor for the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

Furthermore, the four subtle elements upon which the atoms and the lump depend are used as a metaphor for the true nature of the eight consciousnesses. Additionally, gold is used as a metaphor for the storehouse consciousness.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*). The ornaments are used as a metaphor for the *parikalpita-vijñapti-matram* (the consciousness that discriminates phenomena), while the four subtle elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the golden ornaments depend are also used as a metaphor for the true nature of the eight consciousnesses.
Generally speaking, all metaphors are established by conforming indirectly to what is known through worldly sentiment and cognition;
they use the easy to illustrate the difficult so as to enable understanding. However, the true Dharma is in reality not a metaphor.
This extends to all analogies. For instance, consider atoms, lumps of clay, gold ornaments, and the four subtle elements of form, odor, taste, and touch upon which they depend.
From the perspective of ultimate reasoning, these are all the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective images) manifested by one's own mind; they acquire their substance through the mind.
Outside the mind, there are no phenomena. Fundamentally, there are no distinct characteristics of the dependent and the supported, nor of the establishing agent and the established object.

This can be understood. However, according to worldly convention, the four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*) serve as the support (*āśraya*), while the lump of clay, atoms (*paramāṇu*), and golden ornaments all serve as the supported (*āśrita*).
This may be used as an analogy for the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) serving as the support and the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*) all serving as the supported.
Furthermore, according to worldly convention, the atoms and the gold serve as the "formers" (*nirmāpaka*), while the lump of clay and...

The ornaments are that which is accomplished; this can be compared to the manifesting consciousness (*nirmāṇa-vijñāna*) as the agent of accomplishment and the consciousness of discriminating phenomena (*vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*) as that which is accomplished.
Since they are both the basis and the accomplished, they are not definitively different. Since they are distinguished as agent and object, they are not definitively one.
Therefore, True Suchness (*tathatā*) and all consciousnesses are neither different nor non-different. The eight consciousnesses are mutually related in this way.
They are mutually related; they are neither different nor non-different. In this text, the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the four subtle elements (*catvāri-aṇūni*).
2. The Convergence of Dharmas:

"In this way, Mahāmati, if the evolving consciousnesses and the true nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) were different, the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause. If they were not different..."
When the evolving consciousnesses cease, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) would also have to cease; yet its own true nature does not actually cease.
Therefore, Mahāmati, it is not the cessation of the consciousness of its own true nature, but rather the cessation of its karmic aspect.
The Commentary states: "The evolving consciousnesses correspond to the preceding lump of clay and the ornaments; the storehouse consciousness corresponds to the preceding fine dust and the gold.
The two characters 'true' (zhen) and 'form' (xiang) precisely correspond to the four subtle elements indicated by the word 'that' (bi) in the preceding passage. This is according to the analogy."
One should then say: If the lump of clay and the four atoms were different, the atoms would not be its cause.
If they were not different, then when the lump of clay perishes, the atoms should also perish; yet, in reality, the four atoms do not perish.
This is because the clay is identical to the atoms; although both take the four atoms as their substance, both lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and while the lump of clay is subject to change...
It is destroyed. A subtle atom cannot be further destroyed; this may be compared to the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Although both take true consciousness as their substance and are both devoid of self-nature, the evolving consciousness is easily extinguished, whereas the storehouse consciousness does not undergo further extinction.

The concluding statement—that it is not the true characteristic of consciousness that perishes, but rather its karmic characteristic that perishes—is intended to clarify the various consciousnesses mentioned in the preceding text.

There are three kinds of characteristics. Only the evolving characteristic (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) and the karmic characteristic (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) can be extinguished, whereas the true characteristic (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be extinguished.
Now, all eight consciousnesses possess arising, abiding, and ceasing; these are all termed the evolving characteristic. All eight consciousnesses possess the flow of arising, abiding, and ceasing;
these are all termed the karmic characteristic. Once these two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are extinguished, that very state is itself [the unconditioned].
That which is born does not perish; this is what is called the true characteristic (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).

Thus, it is not only that the true characteristic of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is imperishable, but the true characteristic of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is likewise imperishable. Because they are true, their characteristics are non-distinct.

Therefore, within the state of the Tathāgata, there arise the mental states associated with the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-samprayukta-citta-varga*). These four are neither fixed as four nor fixed as one; they are designated according to the True.

Thus, since both the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) are non-existent, they cannot even be called "one. How then could they be called "four" or "eight"? From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), the characteristics are not destroyed and there are eight;
yet, whether one speaks of eight, four, or one, all are without obstruction. This concludes the second section: Manifestation by Analogy.
△ Third, the Section on Distinguishing the Non-True.
If the self-characteristic were to cease, then the ālayavijñāna would cease. Mahāmati, if the ālayavijñāna were to cease, it would not differ from the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists.
Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists maintain such a doctrine as that the cessation of the grasping of objects constitutes liberation.
The stream of consciousness also ceases. If the stream of consciousness were to cease, then this beginningless stream would have to be severed.

Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists speak of a cause for the arising of the stream; they do not say that it arises from the conjunction of eye-consciousness, form, and light, but rather that there is another distinct cause.
Mahāmati, as for that cause, they speak of it as the Primal Essence (*prakṛti*), the Person (*puruṣa*), the Lord (*īśvara*), Time (*kāla*), or atoms (*paramāṇu*).

The Commentary states: The minds of non-Buddhists are clouded and their wisdom is dark. They falsely reckon that if the manifestation of grasped objects ceases, then the seeds of the stream of consciousness will also cease.
Yet they do not know that the seeds of all phenomena have been transmitted through successive stages from beginningless time and never truly severed.
It is precisely because they do not know that the seeds inherent within their own minds constitute a single [stream]...

All phenomena have their own proximate causes, yet they arise only by depending upon a collection of various conditions; it is for this reason that people mistakenly calculate other causes, such as a superior and wondrous *puruṣa* (spiritual self).
When it is said that "eye-consciousness arises from the assembly of the eye, visible forms, and light," this is stated specifically with reference to eye-consciousness.
Although there is the seed as the direct cause, it still arises only through the gathering of nine conditions: the eye is the condition of the faculty;

consciousness is the eighth [consciousness]; the seventh and sixth [consciousnesses], along with attention and mental factors; the manifestation of the preceding moment of visual consciousness; and visible form.

That is to say, the objective sphere and emptiness are luminous; this refers to the light of the sun, moon, and lamps. The eye is the predominant, unique, and immediate support; the eighth consciousness is the fundamental support;
the seventh consciousness is the support for defilement and purity; and the sixth consciousness is the support for discrimination.

Attention (*manasikāra*) can induce seeds to arise in the present and can also induce the mind to engage with its object. These five conditions mentioned above are collectively termed "conditions of growth" (*puṣṭi-pratyaya*).
The manifestation of the preceding moment of visual consciousness serves as the "opening and guiding support" (*āśraya*), termed the "immediately antecedent condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The objective sphere—the immediate and remote aspects of the perceived form (*nimitta-bhāga*)—is termed the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Both emptiness and light also belong to the [condition of growth].

These are subsumed under superior conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). If it is ear-consciousness, it does not depend on the condition of light. As for nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, they do not even depend on the condition of space.
Therefore it is said: "Ear-consciousness arises from only eight [conditions]; nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness arise from seven.

*Śeṣvara* (the Supreme Lord) is also called *śeṣatva* (the Supreme Essence), which is the *pradhāna* (Primal Matter). *Puruṣa* is the *puruṣātman* (Spiritual Self), or the category of *mahāsattā* (Great Existence) in the Vaiśeṣika school. *Īśvara* (the Sovereign).

This refers to Maheśvara; the rest may be understood accordingly. The first section, the direct answer concerning arising, abiding, and ceasing, is concluded. Section Two: Clarifying the Gates of the Erroneous and the Correct.

2. Refutation based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). △ Now, first:
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). (The Wei translation says: "Non-Buddhists have seven kinds of self-nature. They are:

the self-nature of accumulation (*saṃgraha*), the self-nature of essence (*bhāva*), the self-nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the self-nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the self-nature of cause (*hetu*).
Nature (*svabhāva*). It is the nature of conditions; it is the nature of accomplishment. The Commentary states:
The harmonious conjunction of various conditions is termed "arising" (*samudaya*). That phenomena are each thus of themselves is termed "nature.

That each possesses its own form is termed "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). Earth, water, fire, and wind are termed the "great elements" (*mahābhūta*), for they are capable of producing [phenomena] directly.

That which is called the "cause" (hetu) is that which can remotely assist in the arising [of a result]. That which is called the "condition" (pratyaya) is that which assists in its arising. The production of a result through causes and conditions is called "accomplishment.

All of these are merely objects manifested by one's own mind; outside the mind, they have no inherent nature (svabhāva). Yet, non-Buddhists (tīrthika) falsely reckon that each possesses its own self-nature.
II. Refuting the Two [Views] Based on the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). A. Stating the Meaning. B. The Actual Refutation.
[This section] is refuted. △ Now, first [of the seven].
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). (The Wei translation says: "I have seven kinds of ultimate reality. That is to say:

the sphere of the mind (*citta-gocara*), (the Tang translation says: "the range of mental activity") the sphere of wisdom (*prajñā-gocara*)—both [versions] render this as *jñāna*—and the sphere of knowledge (*jñāna-gocara*). (The Wei...)

Cultivating wisdom. (In the Tang [translation], "seeing" is omitted. The realm of the two views. (Both versions render this as "the two views. Transcending the realm of the two views. (The Wei [translation] says: "passing beyond the two views.
Transcending the realm of the stage of the sons [of the Buddha]. (The Wei [translation] says: "passing beyond the stage of the Buddha's sons.

The realm of the Tathāgata’s own arrival. (The Wei [translation] says: "entering the internal practice of the Tathāgata stage. The Tang [translation] says: "that which is practiced by the Tathāgata; the holy realization personally attained by the Tathāgata.")
"...the sphere of wisdom.
The Commentary states: Regarding the seven kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one realizes that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Each and every one of these is the objective domain of the ultimate truth. Furthermore, this objective domain of the ultimate truth arises from the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and proceeds through cultivation; it permeates both cause and fruit, and may also be attained [as such].
In terms of their general meaning, there are seven kinds. However, each of these seven kinds refutes all seven kinds of self-nature;
it does not mean that one kind specifically refutes only one other kind. Regarding the "object-sphere of the initial mind":

this refers to the fact that the seven kinds of self-nature imagined by those non-Buddhists are all devoid of self-nature and are entirely object-spheres manifested by the mind alone. This is direct...
This reveals the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Whether awakened or not yet awakened, there are no objective realms external to the mind. Second, the sphere of wisdom (*prajñā*):
by relying on the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation—one comes to know that all things are solely mind. Third, the sphere of knowledge (*jñāna*):
by giving rise to untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one realizes that all things are solely mind. These two terms, "wisdom" and "knowledge," [are thus distinguished].

This encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate. During the Wei dynasty, wisdom (*jñāna*) was taken as the provisional and insight (*prajñā*) as the ultimate; now, however, insight is taken as the provisional and wisdom as the ultimate. Regarding the "sphere of the four and two views":
once one has realized that all is mind-only, one understands that various spheres are devoid of all marks and are, in fact, all phenomena.
Being devoid of all marks is called the "view of emptiness according to reality" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). This is the one...
All phenomena are called the "seeing of reality as it is, which is not empty.
Fifth, transcending the realm of the two views means thoroughly understanding that all realms are neither identical to nor different from [the nature], and are both dual and non-dual.
