The "analogy of stages" (*avasthā-sādharmya*) clarifies the following: the first, second, and third stages—characterized by generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration—are analogous to the mundane world.

From the fourth stage upward, they are analogous to the supramundane. The wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) on the fourth stage is analogized to the *srotāpanna*; the wisdom of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya*) on the fifth stage is analogized to the *arhat*;

the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) on the sixth stage is analogized to the *pratyekabuddha*; and the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta*) on the seventh stage [is analogized to the Buddha].

The "analogy to bodhisattvas" refers to those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, whose wisdom is effortless (*anābhoga*), and who clearly manifest the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) at the stage of Buddhahood.
This is merely an analogy using the shallow to clarify the profound; it does not mean that the fruit of bodhisattvas in the fifth or sixth stages is identical to that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Now, these śrāvakas, seeing the marks of the cessation of afflictions realized within their own bodies, falsely claim—

This is the same as the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*). It is because they do not understand the specific causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma that they continue to perfuse ignorance and afflictions, thereby falling into the inconceivable death of transformation (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*). According to the meaning of the Tang translation:

it means that they first sever the afflictions of conceptual discrimination within their own vehicle; having realized what is to be seen, they subsequently, at the fifth stage, the Stage of Thinning (*tanubhūmi*), [attain] the sixfold detachment...

In the stage of desire (*kāmadhātu*), through skillful cultivation, one severs the fetters of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) and thereby realizes the fruit of arhatship, which is equivalent to the stage of "having completed what was to be done" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*).
Yet, because one has not severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions, one still abides in inconceivable death.
One who truly utters the lion’s roar is one who has attained the noble wisdom that realizes the Four Noble Truths; therefore, they are fearless within the three realms, like a lion.
"Birth has been exhausted" refers to the knowledge of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). "The holy life has been established" refers to the knowledge of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

"What was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the knowledge of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). "There is no further existence" refers to the knowledge of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Cultivating the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is the cause of the Śrāvaka; attaining the realization of Parinirvāṇa is the fruit of the Śrāvaka.
II. Explanation of the Distinctive Natures (Prthag-gotra). This has two parts: first, the presentation of their views; second, the refutation. △ Now, the first:
"O Mahāmati, as for those of distinct and immediate [nature], they consist of the notions of self, person, sentient being, life-span, nourisher, and spirit.
Those beings form such conceptions and seek parinirvāṇa. (The Wei translation says: "Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who seek to realize nirvāṇa.")
And they speak thus: "One perceives and knows the self, the person, the sentient being, the life-span, the agent, the experiencer, and the man;

this is taken to be Nirvana. [The Tang translation says: "Furthermore, there are sentient beings who seek to realize Nirvana, claiming that the perception and knowledge of the self, the person, the sentient being, the nourisher, and the grasper—this is Nirvana.
Furthermore, other non-Buddhists say: "All things arise from a creator; one perceives all..."
[This concludes the section on] nature. It says: "This is parinirvāṇa" (The Wei translation says:
Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who, seeing that all phenomena exist in dependence upon causes, give rise to the thought of nirvāṇa. The Tang translation says:
Furthermore, some say that seeing all phenomena as existing because of an agent is [what they call] nirvāṇa).

The Commentary states: This clarifies that the two attachments to self and dharmas held by ordinary beings and non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize nirvana within that which is not the dharma of nirvana.
Although it is listed as the fifth in the enumeration of names, it is explained first here as the second for two reasons:

first, because it is precisely what is to be countered by the *pitaka* (Tripitaka) teachings; and second, because one wishes to join with the Three Pitakas in refuting and rejecting it. The text consists of two parts.
Section. First is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), which possesses sixteen types of views (*dṛṣṭi*). This sutra briefly enumerates six of them;

the Northern Wei version adds "the agent" and "the experiencer," while the Tang version adds "the appropriator. As extensively listed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, they ultimately do not exceed the single grasping at a self.
Indeed, within the Buddha-dharma, the eradication of this false grasping at a self is the primary objective.
This is the essential gateway for entering the Way. Therefore, when the masters of old received students, some would say: "Bring forth your mind and I shall settle it for you.
Others would say: "Who is it that drags this corpse here? Still others would say: "At the moment when you are thinking neither of good nor of evil, what is that which is your original face?
Or they would say: "Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Or they would say: [and so forth].
"From where does birth come? To where does death go? Some say: "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? Others ask:
"Before one's parents were born, what is one's original face? Still others ask: "When one has died and been cremated, what then? Or they ask:
"While one is fast asleep, in a state of no dreams and no thoughts, where is the master?"

All these [teachings] serve to strip away and shatter the grasping at a self, desiring to bring about the sudden realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Yet those of later generations, whose speech is mired in the literalism of words, conversely seek to find a single entity and take it to be the mind, the original face, that which is capable of recollecting, and even the master of the house. Is this not a fallacy?
The non-Buddhists [hold] to the grasping of a self (*ātman-grāha*).

Next is the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), which means that all phenomena are produced by a creator—whether by the primordial principle (*pradhāna*), or by a divine self (*puruṣa*), or by space (*ākāśa*), or by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), or by atoms (*paramāṇu*), or by the Lord God (*īśvara*), or it is said to be produced by time (*kāla*), or by direction (*diś*), or by sound (*śabda*); there is nothing that is not so produced.
That which is eternal possesses both arising and ceasing; that which can act as such an eternity, yet neither arises nor ceases, is called *nirvāṇa*.
This is similar to the heterodox teachings of the contemporary Lord of Heaven (*Īśvara*), who calculates that there is a Lord of Heaven without beginning and without end who can produce all things;
if one serves this Lord of Heaven, one can be born in heaven and eternally enjoy celestial bliss. This is of the same category. II. Conclusion and Rebuttal. Furthermore:
2. First, the direct refutation of the non-Buddhists; second, the incidental refutation of the Śrāvakas. △ Now, the first [part]:
they form such a realization that the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is not their lot; thus, they have no liberation (the Wei version says:
"Those various non-Buddhists have no nirvāṇa or liberation because they do not see the selflessness of phenomena"; the Tang version says: "They have no liberation because they have not yet...").
"Because they are able to see the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The Commentary states: "Non-Buddhists do not even perceive the non-self of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*);

yet, the text merely rebukes them for not seeing the non-self of phenomena because, having already given rise to the aspiration to realize *nirvāṇa*, they may at times encounter a Buddha and thus be led [to the truth]."
This is because the Tripiṭaka masters analyze phenomena with clumsy means of deliverance.
However, as long as these ordinary worldlings do not sever the two attachments to self and dharmas, the liberation realized by the Śrāvakas is beyond their reach.

Furthermore, according to the two translations, the fifth category—those of distinct lineages—is termed "without lineage" (*agotra*), which is explained within the context of the *icchantikas*. The present text follows this same interpretation.
The Śrāvaka-yāna is explained as being merely non-Buddhist (tīrthika) adherents attached to the Buddha-dharma. △ Second, a simultaneous censure of the Śrāvakas:
"Mahāmati, these various Śrāvaka-yānas possess the lineage of non-Buddhists who lack the realization of transcendence.

In order to overturn those evil views, they should practice and study [this]. (The Wei translation says: "This is called the Śrāvaka-yāna lineage of non-Buddhists; regarding that which is not liberation...")
One gives rise to the notion of renunciation while still dwelling [in saṃsāra]. You should turn away from this false view, for you must practice according to reality.

(The Tang translation says: "This is the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle and the non-Buddhists; while not yet having emerged [from saṃsāra], they give rise to the notion of renunciation. You should diligently cultivate and study.")
"Abandon this evil view. The Commentary states:
"Non-Buddhists do not transcend birth-and-death through segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*); Śrāvakas do not transcend birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jāti-maraṇa*).
Both falsely conceive of themselves as having emerged from birth-and-death; this is what the Bodhisattva must transform and abandon. These two interpretations are each distinct in their categories.
The section on the [Śrāvaka] lineage is concluded. △ Third, the explanation of the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna.

Mahāmati, regarding those of the uninterrupted lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna: if they hear it said that there are individual conditions for the uninterrupted [attainment], (the Wei translation says: ...).
That is to say, upon hearing the teaching on the Dharma realized by the Pratyekabuddhas—[the Tang translation states:

"that is to say, if one hears the teaching of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle"]—the hairs of his entire body stand on end, and he weeps with flowing tears, [due to] conditions that do not involve proximity [to others]. [The Wei translation states: "because he does not delight in clamor. The Tang translation states:]...

Free from the conditions of clamor and bustle, they remain unattached. (The Wei translation says: "Because they observe all dharmas of causes and conditions, they do not cling to any dharmas of causes and conditions.

The Tang translation says: "They have no defiled attachment. When they hear it said that there are various personal bodies and various supernormal powers—various transformations whether separated or combined—their minds enter accordingly. (The Wei translation says: "Hearing the teaching of their own...")
Regarding the various supernatural powers of the body—whether manifesting as diverse transformations of separation or union—their minds enter accordingly. (The Tang translation states:

"Sometimes they hear it said that various bodies are manifested, whether gathering or dispersing; through these supernatural transformations, their minds believe and accept them without any opposition.
If one knows that a person possesses the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle without interruption, one should teach the Pratyekabuddha vehicle in accordance with their disposition.
This is called the characteristic of the lineage of uninterrupted continuity for the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
The Commentary states: Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, because this exists, that exists; their characteristics are each distinct, yet they are all uninterrupted.

If one can distance oneself from clamor and distraction, observe the faults of the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) without grasping or attachment, then one will know that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) because they arise from conditions.
One will thus be able to give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such as appearing and disappearing or transforming at will.

This refers to the contemplative gate of realizing the essence of dharmas within the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*). Therefore, for those of the lineage of that vehicle, one should preach the Dharma in accordance with them so that [their delusions] may be destroyed.
The externalists and the śrāvakas who cling to the Dharma can be transformed and led into the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]. △ Fourth, explaining the lineage of the Tathāgata vehicle:
Mahāmati, that lineage of the uninterrupted Tathāgata vehicle is of four kinds. (In the Tang translation, it says: "The lineage of the Tathāgata vehicle...")

There are three kinds of realized dharmas: namely, the lineage of immediate succession regarding the dharma of intrinsic nature (the Wei translation says: first, realizing the true nature of dharmas);

the lineage of immediate succession regarding the dharma of the absence of intrinsic nature (the Wei translation says: second, the nature of realization that is free from real dharmas; the Tang translation says:
so-called dharmas of intrinsic nature and the absence of intrinsic nature); and the lineage of immediate succession regarding the noble self-awakened [wisdom] (the Wei translation says: ...).
Third, the nature of the noble wisdom personally realized within one's own body. (In the Tang translation: "The Dharma of the noble wisdom personally realized within one's own body.
Fourth, the lineage of the uninterrupted excellence of external lands. (In the Wei translation: "Fourth, the Dharma-nature realized through the sublime adornments of all external lands.
In the Tang translation: "The vast Dharma of all external Buddha-lands. Mahāmati, if one hears these four matters—even one—[one will attain realization].

When, at the time of a single teaching, or when teaching the inconceivable realm established by the manifestation of one's own mind as body and wealth, the mind is not startled or terrified—this is called the characteristic of the lineage of uninterrupted succession for the Tathāgata-yāna. (The Wei translation says:

"If, upon hearing each of these dharmas being taught, one realizes that it is only the Ālaya-consciousness perceiving external bodies, supports, and the vessel-world of the environment as inconceivable...")
Regarding the deliberation on the sphere of experience: one who is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid should be known as a person who has realized the nature of the Tathāgata-vehicle.
This is called the characteristic of a person who realizes the nature of the Tathāgata-vehicle. [The Chinese text states:

"If there are those who, upon hearing this exposition of each and every dharma, as well as the inconceivable realm of the ālayavijñāna established by the manifestations of one's own mind, body, and wealth, are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid..."
"One should know that this is the nature of the Tathāgata-vehicle.
The Commentary states: "The unconditioned lineage of the self-nature of phenomena" means that while following conditions, it does not change;
all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. This is the principle that all sentient beings have been originally enlightened. It is the dharma apart from self-nature.
Regarding those of the "uninterrupted lineage" (*anantara-gotra*): this refers to the Tathāgatagarbha mind, which does not change yet follows conditions;

it does not cling to its own nature, but manifests its entire substance as the myriad phenomena of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses. Yet these phenomena are all identical to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
All twelve classes of sentient beings are the seed of the Tathāgata. Both of these are the Dharmakāya of inherent virtue; therefore, the Tang translation combines them.

It is for the sake of oneness. Those who have attained the lineage of the uninterrupted noble self-awakening possess the three wisdoms within a single mind, which illumines the realm that is neither provisional nor real, yet both provisional and real; this is the virtue of *prajñā*.

As for those of the lineage of the uninterrupted excellence of external lands, the Buddha, through his wondrous clarity that is neither extinguished nor born, unites with the *tathāgatagarbha*, and thus the *tathāgatagarbha*...
Only this wondrous, enlightened clarity perfectly illuminates the Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it, one becomes many and many become one;
the small manifests the large, and the large manifests the small. Upon the tip of a single hair, a jeweled-kingland appears;
seated within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma-wheel. This is the virtue of liberation. To hear of these three virtues without being startled, terrified, or afraid—[and]...
If one hears that the inconceivable realms of the faculties, the physical body, the requisites of life, and the vessel-world are all manifestations of one's own mind-consciousness,
and yet remains neither startled nor terrified, then one knows that there is no difference between the three— mind, Buddha, and sentient beings— and is thus of the lineage of the Tathāgata-yāna.
△ Fifth, the explanation of the indeterminate nature.
Mahāmati, those of indeterminate lineage are those who, when these three types [of vehicles] are taught, enter according to what is taught and are established accordingly (the Wei translation says:
"If a person hears these three kinds of teachings and finds delight in any one of them, teach them in accordance with that;

the Tang translation says: "That is to say, when hearing these three kinds of teachings being expounded, they give rise to faith and understanding accordingly and practice and study in conformity with it").
The Commentary states: "The three kinds of dharmas are the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Tathāgata vehicle.
Now, those of the śrāvaka lineage of immediate succession take pleasure solely in hearing the śrāvaka dharma and do not delight in the Pratyekabuddha or Tathāgata dharmas.
Those of the pratyekabuddha lineage of immediate succession take pleasure solely in hearing the pratyekabuddha dharma; regarding the śrāvaka dharma, they [certainly...]"
Those who hold [the Lesser Vehicle] in contempt will certainly be unable to have faith in the Dharma of the Tathāgata.

Since those of the lineage of the uninterrupted vehicle (*anantarya-gotra*) are not startled or terrified by the inconceivable realm, they will certainly not aspire to seek the teachings of the two vehicles.

Now, since it is said that they produce faith and understanding immediately upon hearing [the teaching], we know that they do not belong to those three types of the uninterrupted lineage; they are merely termed "indeterminate" (*aniyata*).
Furthermore, the Dharma of the Śrāvakas corresponds to the Tripitaka Teaching; the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas corresponds to the Shared Teaching;
and the Dharma of the Tathāgata corresponds to the Perfect Teaching. Thus, this indeterminate lineage is capable of entering the Distinct, the Perfect, and the Distinct Teaching.
In other sutras, among the clarification of the nine vehicles, there are the Bodhisattva-Śrāvaka and the Bodhisattva-Pratyekabuddha. The Bodhisattva...

The Bodhisattva Sa. The Great Master Zhiyi classifies this as the Separate Teaching (biejiao); his intention is the same as this [interpretation]. The two explanations of the characteristics [of the teaching] are concluded. III. Harmonizing the Teachings has two parts:
first, harmonizing the Three Vehicles; second, harmonizing with the icchantika. Regarding the first, there are two sections: first, the long prose; second, the verses.
Regarding the first of these, there are two further sections: first, establishing the provisional through the ultimate; second, revealing the ultimate by opening the provisional. △ Now...
First. Mahāmati, this is the initial establishment of the stages of practice (*bhūmi-vyavasthāna*), which is for the purpose of entering the stage of non-existence (*abhāva-bhūmi*).
[The Wei translation says: "The teaching of the three vehicles is for the purpose of initiating the stages of cultivation. Thus is the establishment made.
The differentiation of natures is not the ultimate stage; it is established for the purpose of instituting the stage of ultimate quiescence regarding the grasper.

(The Tang translation states: "It is taught as 'lineage' (*gotra*) for those who are beginners on the path of cultivation, in order to cause them to enter the stage of imagelessness (*nirābhāsa-bhūmi*);
thus is this establishment made.)"
The Commentary says: First, as for those who are cultivating the stages (*bhūmi*), they have not yet realized the true and equal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Therefore, distinctions in spiritual lineage (*gotra*) are established so that they may feel shame for the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great, thereby abandoning the provisional to pursue the real. This is precisely intended to lead them into the stage of non-existence (*anupalambha-bhūmi*);
thus, while the three provisional means are bestowed, one must not cling to the provisional and thereby obscure the real. △ Second, the Opening [of the True Nature].
The provisional reveals the real.

As for that "self-awakened treasury," it refers to those who have purified the habitual tendencies of their own afflictions, perceived the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and attained the bliss of samādhi;
such śrāvakas shall attain the most supreme body of a Tathāgata. (The Wei translation states: "Those three types of persons are free from the heavy obstacle of afflictions.")
Through practice, because they attain purity, they perceive the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Because they attain the practice of the bliss of samādhi, and because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas ultimately realize the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. [The Tang translation states:

"Those Śrāvakas who abide in the bliss of samādhi, if they can realize and know the consciousness upon which they themselves depend, perceive the non-self of phenomena, and purify the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), will ultimately attain the body of a Tathāgata."
The Commentary states: "Self-awakened treasury" refers to the realization and knowledge of the inconceivable realm of the *ālayavijñāna* through the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
If even *śrāvakas* can attain the Buddha-body, how much more so for *pratyekabuddhas* and those of indeterminate nature?

Therefore, the Wei translation says, "those three kinds of people. Question: The function of opening up the provisional and revealing the real lies in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; yet this scripture is now...
[Included in] the summary. How can such an opening and revelation be possible? Answer: Those śrāvakas of dull faculties must wait until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for this opening and revelation.

Since this sūtra itself extensively expounds the essential points of the Mahāyāna for the sake of bodhisattvas, how could it be permissible to restrict it to a single path within one of the five distinct periods?
Would one wish to make the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma lack sovereignty? The initial long prose section concludes. △
Two verses in praise:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The fruit of srotāpanna, the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the non-returner (anāgāmin), and those who have attained arhatship—these are those whose minds are deluded. (The Wei translation says: 'Flowing against the current, they cultivate the unconditioned [asaṃskṛta].')"
Those who go and return, those who do not return, and the Arhats worthy of offerings—such as these have their minds deluded. (The Tang translation says:
"The fruit of Stream-entry, the Once-returner, the Non-returner, and the Arhat—all such noble ones have their minds entirely confused.
The Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle, as well as what I call the "non-vehicle"—(the Wei translation says: "I speak of the Three Vehicles, the One Vehicle, and the non-vehicle.")

The Tang translation says: "The three vehicles, the one vehicle, and that which is not a vehicle which I have established—for the sake of the foolish who possess little wisdom and for the sages who delight in tranquility.

This is the Dharma-gate of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), which is far removed from the two teachings [the Tang version reads 'two graspings'] and abides in non-existence [the Tang version reads 'non-objectivity']. What need is there to establish it?"
Establishing the three vehicles—(the Wei version says: establishing the three vehicles;

for dwelling in a place of tranquility)—the various dhyānas, the immeasurables, and so forth, the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the total cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*)—(the Wei version says: the non-conceptual attainment and the cessation-attainment; the Tang version says:

up to the cessation of sensation and perception)—there is also no mental construction (*citta-mātra*)—(the Wei version says: these are also all absent from within the mind; the Tang version says: it is *cittamātra* alone).
[It is] unobtainable). The commentary states:

*Srotāpanna* is also called *Srotāpan*. This is translated as "逆流" (*niúlíu*, "flowing against the current"). It means that by cultivating the untainted (*anāsrava*) path, one flows against the stream of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

It is also translated as "預流" (*yùliú*, "entering the stream") or "入流" (*rùliú*, "entering the stream"), meaning that for the first time, one enters the stream of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). 3.

That which is both a vehicle (*yāna*) and a non-vehicle is because the provisional is itself the real; this is taught for the sake of the sages who delight in tranquility. That which is both a single vehicle and a non-vehicle is because the real is itself the provisional;
this is taught for the sake of the foolish and those of limited wisdom. As for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is neither provisional nor real.
Since there are no objects external to the mind, how could there be three vehicles? If even the three vehicles do not exist, how much less so the four dhyānas and the four [formless absorptions]?

The immeasurable four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), as well as the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), etc.—how could there be any real dharmas external to the mind?
The first assembly concerning the three vehicles is concluded. II. The second assembly concerning the icchantikas has two parts: 1. The explicit explanation of the two types of icchantikas;
2. Questions and answers for reconciliation. The first part [of section I] also has two sections: 1. A general heading; 2. A detailed explanation. △ Now, the first [section]: the general heading.
"Mahāmati, those icchantikas are not truly icchantikas; for whom, then, would liberation from the world be turned away?

Mahāmati, there are two kinds of icchantikas: first, those who have abandoned all roots of goodness; and second, those who have made a vow regarding sentient beings since beginningless time [the Wei translation says:
'Which is the vehicle of no-nature? It refers to the icchantika. Mahāmati, the icchantika lacks the nature for nirvāṇa']. What [is this]?"
For this reason, they do not give rise to faith in liberation and do not enter nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, there are two kinds of icchantikas. What are these two? First, those who have burned away all roots of goodness;

second, those who, out of compassion for all sentient beings, make the vow to exhaust the entire realm of sentient beings. [The Tang translation says: "In this context, why is it that the icchantika... regarding liberation...
They do not give rise to desire or pleasure within liberation because they have abandoned all roots of goodness, yet they give rise to vows for the sake of sentient beings who have no beginning.

The Commentary states: According to the Wei translation, the two types of non-Buddhists explained in the preceding text are actually those among the Śrāvaka vehicle who have failed to grasp the essential meaning.
Now, we are correctly explaining those of no lineage (agotra). According to this present sutra, the preceding sutra...

The preceding sections have separately defined and explained the various spiritual lineages (*gotra*). Now, we shall properly reconcile the case of the *icchantika*. There must certainly exist bodhisattvas who are *icchantikas* for the purpose of transforming and delivering them;
such individuals can still attain Buddhahood. This differs from the provisional teaching which asserts that *icchantikas* lack the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Therefore it is said: "If those icchantikas who have severed their roots of goodness—even those icchantikas who have not yet resolved to attain great vows—did not exist, by what means could the world be transformed into liberation?
The remaining portions may be understood through comparison with the two other translations. Part Two: A detailed explanation, which is twofold.
First, the explanation of abandoning the roots of goodness; second, the explanation of generating the great vow.
△ Now, the first: What is meant by abandoning all roots of goodness? It refers to slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and uttering evil words, saying:
"This is not a teaching that accords with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or liberation. Because one abandons all roots of goodness, one does not enter parinirvāṇa.
The Commentary states: Although worldly evildoers may possess the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes, if they do not slander the Dharma, their roots of goodness are not yet severed;
they are still capable of practicing the two types of repentance—repentance for the perception of signs and the signless—and thus are not called icchantikas.
Now, since they have slandered the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, all supramundane roots of goodness are completely severed, even if they do not fully possess the five [heinous crimes].
Those who commit the ten evil deeds, even if they possess some slight worldly goodness, will inevitably remain forever within birth and death and will be unable to enter nirvana.
△ Second, the explanation of the arousal of the great vow.
Second, because Bodhisattvas possess the skillful means of their original vows, they do not enter parinirvāṇa until all sentient beings have entered parinirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, that parinirvāṇa is called the characteristic of the dharma of non-parinirvāṇa. This also leads to the state of an icchantika.
(The Wei translation says: "To feel compassion for sentient beings and make the vow to exhaust the realm of sentient beings—this is [the mark of] a Bodhisattva.")
"O Mahāmati, Bodhisattvas make a vow through skillful means: 'If all sentient beings do not enter nirvana, I likewise shall not enter nirvana.
For this reason, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not enter nirvana. These are called the two kinds of icchantikas."
There is no nature of *nirvāṇa*. For this reason, they resolutely adopt the conduct of an *icchantika*. [The Tang translation says:

"What is meant by 'arousing a vow for sentient beings who have no beginning'? It means that all Bodhisattvas, through the skillful means of their original vows, vow that all sentient beings shall enter *nirvāṇa*.
If even a single sentient being has not attained *nirvāṇa*, I shall never enter [it] myself. This, too, is abiding in the state of an *icchantika*.
[They] proceed [to such states]. This is the characteristic of those who lack the lineage for *nirvāṇa*. The Commentary says:
"Only when all sentient beings have been delivered does one enter *nirvāṇa*; because the realm of sentient beings can never be exhausted, one never enters *nirvāṇa* oneself.
For this reason, they are called Bodhisattva-icchantikas. First, the two types are correctly explained.
The section on *icchantikas* concludes. II. Question and Answer for Synthesis. Part One: The Question. Part Two: The Answer. △ Now, the first:
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, regarding this matter, what is meant by 'ultimately not entering parinirvāṇa'? (The Wei translation states:
"Of these two kinds of *icchantikas*, which one is the *icchantika* who never enters nirvāṇa?")
△ Second, the answer.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "A Bodhisattva-icchantika, having realized that all dharmas are originally in parinirvāṇa, ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa.
(The Wei translation says: "A Bodhisattva-icchantika never enters nirvāṇa. Why is this?")
Therefore, because they are able to know well that all dharmas are originally in *nirvāṇa*, they do not enter *nirvāṇa*;
yet, this is not the case for the *icchantikas* who have abandoned all roots of goodness.

Mahāmati, as for those *icchantikas* who have abandoned all roots of goodness, by the spiritual power of the Tathāgata, roots of goodness may arise in them at some time. (The Wei translation says: "Those who have abandoned all roots of goodness...")

If those with the icchantika-nature encounter Buddhas, spiritual friends, and the like, they may resolve their minds toward bodhi and give rise to various roots of goodness, thereby attaining nirvana.
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata does not abandon any sentient being. For this reason, the bodhisattva-icchantika does not enter parinirvāṇa.

The Commentary states: "All dharmas, from the very beginning, have always been characterized by quiescence and extinction, just as space is fundamentally devoid of flowers that do not require further destruction.
Therefore, the icchantika bodhisattva will ultimately never again enter nirvana.

The icchantika who has severed the roots of goodness merely severs cultivated goodness, yet their innate goodness is not severed; thus, they remain unaware and unknowing, receiving [the teachings of] Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Aroused by the influence of virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and others, one gives rise once more to roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and realizes the nature of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding these five distinct natures (*pañca-gotra*), if one relies on treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they definitely exist;

if one relies on sūtras such as the *Dharmarāja-sūtra*, they definitely do not exist. However, if one attains the meaning of this present sūtra and the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*), they do not exist.
Existence does not obstruct non-existence, and non-existence does not obstruct existence. Why is this so? The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is equal in both sentient beings and Buddhas;

fundamentally, there is no differentiation. Yet, due to beginningless habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), the myriad phenomena are not uniform. Consequently, we observe that the various capacities of sentient beings differ.
How could one unilaterally cling to non-existence? This is why Yogācāra-Vijñaptimātra clarifies its "existence."
Although the dispositions (*gotra*) of sentient beings differ from one another, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal, and the great vows of the Buddhas are likewise equal;
therefore, they ultimately cause all to attain Buddhahood. How could one persistently cling to existence?

This is why scriptures such as the *Dharmarāja-sūtra* clarify its non-existence. Because the provisional is established for the sake of the ultimate, non-existence does not obstruct existence; thus, the provisional is opened.
To manifest reality, there is the non-obstruction of non-existence. With respect to seeds that have existed from the beginningless past, the one mind necessarily possesses the ten realms;
how could it not possess the seeds of the Buddha-realm? With respect to seeds newly perfumed from the beginningless past, they grow and develop differently according to conditions;
how could there not be the distinction of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*)? Just as that which is produced from a single earth [must necessarily be so].
There are three types of grass and two types of trees; thus, there is no difference, yet this does not obstruct difference.
Just as these three types of grass and two types of trees ultimately return to the earth, there is difference, yet this does not obstruct non-difference.

This is the structural thread of the temporal teachings throughout this entire dispensation, and the ultimate aim of the Lotus Samādhi. The classification of the five sciences and their respective natures is complete. Six.

The third section: Explaining the characteristics of the three self-natures (*trisvabhāva*). This consists of three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Now, for the first part:
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should be well-versed in the three self-natures (the Wei translation says "the characteristics of the self-nature of the three dharmas";

the Tang translation says "the characteristics of the three self-natures"). What are the three self-natures? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)... (The Wei translation says...)

The characteristic of the conceptualization of names through false discrimination (Skt. *parikalpita-svabhāva*; Ch. 妄計自性; Tang: "the falsely imagined nature"; Wei: "the self-characteristic of the essence of causal phenomena"). The dependent origination nature (Skt. *paratantra-svabhāva*; Ch. 緣起自性; Wei:

"the self-characteristic of the essence of causal phenomena"; Tang: "the dependent nature"). The perfected nature (Skt. *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*; Ch. 成自性; Wei: "the characteristic of the essence of the ultimate truth"; Tang: "the perfectly accomplished nature").

The Commentary states: "The nature of the self-substance of deluded thought is termed the 'imagined nature' (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) in the *Vijñaptimātra* [school], and the 'discriminative nature' (*vikalpa-svabhāva*) in the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
It is called 'imagined' because it involves pervasive conceptualization; it is precisely the false dualistic clinging to a self and to phenomena."
For example, it is like perceiving a snake in a rope or a ghost in a tree stump; there is no actual object whatsoever.

Dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is termed "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), refers to the essence of mind and mental factors, as well as their objective and subjective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*), because they arise in dependence upon various conditions.
Perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is termed "consciousness-only," is the Great Vehicle’s *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

This is called "true reality" (*tathatā*). Because it is the perfect accomplishment of the true nature of all phenomena, revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, it is termed "perfected reality" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The second section [the explanation] is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); second, the explanation of the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
and third, the explanation of the perfected nature. Now, the first part.
“Mahāmati, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises from signs (*nimitta*). Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, how does the imagined nature arise from signs?

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “The imagined nature has two kinds of attachment to signs: the signs of the objective phenomena of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the signs of the manifestation of the activity of those phenomena.
These are what the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas [have taught].”
Establishment. (The Tang translation says: This refers to the manifestation of various categories of phenomena based on dependent origination;

because one gives rise to conceptual attachment, Mahāmati, that conceptual attachment to phenomena arises from two kinds of parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature). This is what all Tathāgatas have expounded. Namely:

the characteristic of attachment to names and marks (*nāma-nimitta-abhiniveśa-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of attachment to the characteristics of things (*vastu-nimitta-abhiniveśa-lakṣaṇa*). As for the characteristic of attachment to names and marks, it refers to the internal and external...

Attachment to dharmas (the Chinese translation states: this refers to attachment to internal and external dharmas). Attachment to the characteristics of phenomena (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) means that one is attached to the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of those very same internal and external [dharmas] (the Chinese translation states:
this means being attached to the specific and general characteristics within those internal and external dharmas).
These are called the two kinds of characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The Commentary states: "That which arises from the characteristics of the nature of false conceptualization" means that one gives rise to false conceptual discrimination based on the characteristics of dependent origination;
it is like the false conceptualization of a snake or a ghost arising from a rope or a tree stump.

"The characteristic of the phenomenal aspect of the nature of dependent origination" refers to "name" among the five dharmas. "The characteristic of the phenomenal aspect of the manifestation of activity" refers to [the remaining four] among the five dharmas.

This is the characteristic of the middle [nature]. To be attached to names and to engage in false conceptualization and discrimination regarding all internal and external phenomena is called the characteristic of attachment to names.

To be attached to characteristics and to engage in false conceptualization and discrimination regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) within internal and external phenomena is called the characteristic of attachment to things.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Next, as for the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*):"

Why? The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind and mental factors of universal construction (*parikalpa*).
This is what is meant. 2. Explanation of the Dependent Nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

That which arises based upon and conditioned by [factors] is called dependent origination (in the Tang translation: "arising from what is relied upon and what is taken as an object" is the nature of dependent origination).
The Commentary states: All phenomena of form and mind arise by depending on causes and relying upon conditions; therefore, they are called "dependent."

Regarding "arising," as for the bases of support: the manifestation of the eighth consciousness serves as the fundamental support; the manifestation of the seventh consciousness serves as the support for defilement and purification;
the manifestation of the sixth consciousness serves as the support for discrimination; and the seeds stored within the eighth consciousness serve as the seed-support.
For the first five consciousnesses, the five pure material sense-faculties (*rūpa-indriya*) serve as their specific and direct supports; for the sixth, it is the seventh [consciousness].
They serve as the unique mutual supports for one another. The seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] further act as supports for each other.

All mental factors (caitta-dharma) arise simultaneously by depending respectively upon the mind-kings (citta-rāja); therefore, they are called "supports" (āśraya). Regarding the "objects of cognition" (ālambana):

the eighth [consciousness] takes the three types of objective spheres (viṣaya) as its objects; the seventh [consciousness] takes the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth [consciousness] as its object; and the sixth [consciousness] takes one...
All dharmas serve as objects of perception (*ālambana*). The first five [consciousnesses] take the present five sense-objects as their objects of perception.
The objects of the mental factors (*caitta*) are the same as those of the mind-king (*cittarāja*); therefore, they are called "objects" (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) each rely upon their seeds as their supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*), and each takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind and mental factors as their predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Thus it is said: "whether as support or..."
It is dependently originated. △ Third, the explanation of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
How is the perfected nature established? It refers to that which is free from the delusions of names, signs, and the characteristics of things;

it is what is attained by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), as well as the sphere of activity reached by the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*). This is called the perfected nature, the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind. (The Wei translation says: "That is to say, all...")

The Buddha-Tathāgata is free from the characteristics of names, the characteristics of objects, and the characteristics of phenomena; it is the sphere of activity and the range of practice of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
This is called the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the *tathāgatagarbha* mind of all Buddhas. [The Tang translation states:

It refers to being free from all conceptualization regarding names, marks, and phenomena—the True Suchness (*tathatā*) that is the domain of self-realized noble wisdom. This is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*), the Tathāgata.
[The *Treasury of the Mind*].

The Commentary states: "If one is free from the two kinds of false conceptualization—namely, the conceptualization of names and signs (*nāma-nimitta*) and the conceptualization of things and signs (*vastu-nimitta*)—this is called 'correct wisdom' (*samyag-jñāna*).

The true nature of reality (*tathatā*), realized by this correct wisdom, is fundamentally unmoving and is thus termed 'suchness' (*tathatā*). There is no wisdom outside of this principle, and no principle outside of wisdom."
It is irrational. Rationality and non-duality are the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind. This concludes the two explanations. △ Third, the conclusion:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Names, marks, and conceptualization (the two being discrimination)—these are the two aspects of self-nature. Right knowledge and suchness—these constitute the perfected aspect."
The Commentary states: This [passage] subsumes the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) under five factors (*pañcadharma*). That is to say: first, name; second, appearance;

third, conceptualization—which constitutes the characteristics of the two natures of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*); fourth, correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*);

and fifth, suchness (*tathatā*)—which constitutes the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). However, regarding these three natures and five factors, the various sacred teachings provide inconsistent accounts of their mutual inclusion.

This is explained in detail in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Herein, names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) are taken as the object of false conceptualization, while awakening and thought (*buddhi-saṃjñā*) are taken as the subject of false conceptualization;

both are of the nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Names and characteristics exist in dependence upon awakening and thought, and awakening and thought arise conditioned by names and characteristics;
both are of the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are so called because they are free from inversion (*viparyāsa*).
This is for the purpose of establishing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Mahāmati, this is called the Sūtra on Examining the Characteristics of the Five Dharmas and the Three Natures. It is the sphere of activity reached by the right knowledge of self-realization;
you, all you Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, should practice and study it.

The Commentary states: "Correct wisdom (samyag-jñāna) and suchness (tathatā) constitute the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva); they may be called the sphere of activity reached by the noble wisdom of self-awakening (pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara).
Conceptual signs (nāmanimitta) and discriminative thought (vikalpa-saṃjñā), however, are the dependent origination of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).

How could these be the sphere of activity reached by the noble wisdom of self-awakening? One should know that there are two meanings here: first, outside the essence of correct wisdom and suchness..."

Because there are no other names, marks, or conceptualizations, one is able to realize that names, marks, and conceptualizations lack intrinsic nature; this is precisely right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*).
Second, sentient beings are submerged in names, marks, and conceptualizations, and for this reason they do not attain right knowledge and suchness.
Since the noble ones have already realized right knowledge and suchness, they are able to skillfully know the names of sentient beings.
The various distinctions within the dense forest of appearances, perceptions, and conceptualizations should be cleared away by administering medicine according to the disease;

that is to say, because one realizes the conventional through the realization of the ultimate, it is called "subsequently attained. This concludes the sixth section: the clarification of the characteristics of the three natures.
VII. Clarifying the Characteristics of the Two Kinds of Non-Self (Dvividha-nairātmya-lakṣaṇa). Part One: The Statement; Part Two: The Explanation. △ Now, the first:
Furthermore, Mahāmati, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully contemplate the two kinds of non-self characteristics. What are the two kinds of non-self characteristics?

They are the non-self of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) and the non-self of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya). [The Wei translation says: "The wisdom of the non-self of persons and the non-self of phenomena..."]
Wisdom. (In the Tang language: the mark of selflessness in persons; the mark of selflessness in phenomena). The Commentary states:
The two forms of selflessness are also called the two emptinesses, namely, the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena.

"Person" refers to a conventionally designated sentient being. "Selflessness" means that this conventionally designated sentient being lacks a real, sovereign essence or nature. "Phenomena" refers to...
The aggregates, bases, elements, and so forth, are all phenomena consisting of form and mind. "Selfless" means that these phenomena of form and mind also lack a real, sovereign essence or nature.
The Wei translation says "the wise," which refers to the subject who performs the contemplation; the Tang translation says "characteristics."
This is stated in terms of the objects of observation. The clinging to a person (*pudgala-grāha*) is restricted exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) extends to ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the three vehicles. The second section, the explanation, is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*); second, the explanation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). Now, the first part.

What is the selflessness of persons? It refers to the collection of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that is devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self," yet arises from ignorance, karma, and craving.
(The Tang translation states: "It refers to the aggregates, elements, and bases, which are devoid of self and what belongs to self, and are produced by ignorance, craving, and karma.

Consciousness arises through the grasping and attachment to the eye, forms, and so forth. (The Tang translation states: "The consciousnesses of the eye and so forth arise, grasping at forms and so forth, and thereby producing attachment.")
All sense-faculties, the self-mind-manifested vessel-world, and the body-treasury are established and displayed through the characteristics of one's own false imaginings (the Tang translation states:
"Furthermore, the bodies and the vessel-world perceived by one's own mind are all manifested by the *ālayavijñāna*"). They are like a flowing river.
Like a seed, like a lamp-flame, like a swift wind, and like a floating cloud, it perishes moment by moment in succession (the Tang translation says:
"momentary continuity, changing and decaying without ceasing"). It is as restless as a monkey; it delights in impure places like a fly;
it is insatiable like a wind or a fire (the Tang translation says: "like a fierce fire"); and it has the habitual tendencies of beginningless falsehood as its cause, like drawing water from a well.
The water-wheel; the wheel of existence within the realms of birth and death (the Tang translation says: flowing incessantly through all realms of existence like a water-drawing wheel).
Various bodily forms and colors, like images produced by magical arts, spells, or mechanical devices (the Tang translation says:
various physical bodies, postures, and movements are like a corpse that walks due to the power of incantations, or like a wooden man moved by a mechanism). Good.

The knowledge of those characteristics (translated in the Tang as "if one can skillfully know these characteristics therein") is called the wisdom of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya-jñāna*).
The commentary states: The contemplation of the selflessness of persons is, at first glance, the same as that of the *śrāvakas*; yet, upon close examination, there are differences.

The *śrāvakas* merely contemplate the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) as being without self or what belongs to a self (*anātman-anātmīya*), and as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure; they do not [further investigate].

Know that all these are manifestations of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). First, one should observe the aggregate of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) as a whole:

they arise from ignorance, karma, and craving, and are devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self. Next, one should specifically observe the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), such as the eye-consciousness, which arise from the grasping and attachment to sense organs and objects.
These organs and objects—both the primary body and the external environment—are all manifested from the storehouse consciousness; this is the case for everything.
It is consciousness-only. Consciousness is not autonomous; it has no sovereign ruler, no owner, and belongs to nothing. It is neither the self nor that which belongs to the self.
Furthermore, one contemplates this consciousness as being like a flowing river or a seed: it undergoes momentary transformation and decay without ceasing.

This is precisely the impermanence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It has no sovereign ruler, is not autonomous, belongs to nothing, and is likewise neither the self nor that which belongs to the self. Moreover—

Contemplate this consciousness: it is restless like a monkey; it is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), lacking a sovereign, being neither independent nor subject to another, and is neither the self nor what belongs to the self.
Furthermore, contemplate this consciousness: it delights in impure places like a fly.
Insatiability is like wind or fire; this is precisely the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) being without a sovereign, lacking autonomy, having no ownership, and being neither "I" nor "mine.
Furthermore, observing the various physical bodies within the wheel of birth and death, they are merely like figures moving when a mechanism is triggered;
this is precisely the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) being without a sovereign, lacking autonomy, and having no ownership.

It is neither self nor what belongs to a self. II. Explaining the Selflessness of Dharmas (Dharma-nairātmya). This has two parts: first, clarifying the contemplation; second, manifesting the benefit. △ Now, the first part. What is the wisdom of the selflessness of dharmas?

It refers to awakening to the fact that the self-nature of the false conceptualizations of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) is [empty]. (The Tang translation says: "That is to say,")

The aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are of an imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Just as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are devoid of "I" and "mine," so too are the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases bound by the ropes of karma and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) which arise from their accumulation;
[the Tang translation reads: "only through mutual accumulation, they are bound by the ropes of craving and karma"]. They arise through the successive reciprocal conditioning of one another.

There is no movement. (The Tang translation says: "They arise mutually as conditions; there is no creator. All phenomena are likewise: they are devoid of self-characteristics and common characteristics, being the marks of unreal conceptualization.
By the power of conceptualization, (the Tang translation says: "The aggregates and so forth are likewise: devoid of self and common characteristics, various marks appear through false discrimination.
This is the birth of ordinary worldlings, not that of the noble ones. (The Tang translation says: "It is the portion of the deluded. )

[They] are distinct from those of the noble ones (ārya), because [they] are free from mind, mentation, consciousness, and the five dharmas and their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). (The Tang translation reads:
"Thus observing all dharmas as being free from mind, mentation, consciousness, the five dharmas, and intrinsic natures. Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
"One should skillfully discern that all dharmas are without self" (in the Tang translation: "This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom of the selflessness of dharmas").

The Commentary states: The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are termed "dharmas. They are merely the appearances manifested by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Therefore...

There is no self. Since one has already realized that there is neither self nor what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*), how could there be any obtainable specific or general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
It is merely due to the power of the unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*) of ordinary beings that various specific and general characteristics appear as if they exist.
Therefore, the eightfold mind, intellect, and consciousness are all devoid of intrinsic nature; it is not only the three—name, characteristic, and conceptualization—that lack it.
The Dharma is fundamentally detached; thus, the two dharmas of correct wisdom and suchness are also fundamentally detached.

It is not only that the two natures of deluded thought and dependent origination are fundamentally detached, but even the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is fundamentally detached. It is like seeing a house spinning when one is intoxicated.
To speak of a house as "not turning" does not mean that the house is fundamentally called "not turning. It is like when, due to pressing on the eyes, one sees two moons;
to say that one moon is "real" does not mean that the moon is fundamentally called "one and real. It is like when, due to madness or terror, one loses the sense of one's head;
to say that the head is "not lost" does not mean that the head is fundamentally called "not lost. Therefore, if one penetrates the fact that names, signs, and false imaginings are fundamentally...

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is precisely correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*). If one reckons that correct wisdom and suchness exist, this immediately becomes a conceptualization of names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, it is said that the five dharmas (*pañca-dharma*) and the three self-natures (*tri-svabhāva*) are all empty; the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*) and the two kinds of selflessness (*dvi-nairātmya*) are both discarded.

When there is emptiness, there is nothing further to be emptied; when there is discarding, there is nothing further to be discarded. This is what is called "detachment" (*viveka*), and it is termed the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya-jñāna*). 2. [Second Section]
This reveals the benefit:

the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is well-versed in the selflessness of phenomena will, before long, attain the Bodhisattva’s first stage (*bhūmi*), the contemplation of non-existence, and the observation of the characteristics of the stages.
Through this, they shall awaken with joy. (The Tang translation states: "Having attained this wisdom, one knows there are no objective realms and realizes...")

Regarding the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*): one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), and with a heart born of joy, proceeds gradually through the sequence until transcending the characteristics of the [remaining] nine stages and attaining the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
(The Tang translation further states: "All that was to be accomplished has been fully completed.

Therein, one establishes a great jewel palace in the form of a magnificent king of great jewel lotuses, adorned with immeasurable jewels. (The Tang translation states: "Having dwelt in this stage...")

There was a great king of precious lotuses, adorned with various jewels. Upon that flower was a jeweled palace, shaped like a lotus, produced through the cultivation of the realm of the illusory nature;
there he sat (the Tang translation states: "The Bodhisattva sat upon it, having achieved it through his previous cultivation of the Dharma-gate of the illusory nature").
He was surrounded by a retinue of sons of the Conquerors (*jina-putra*) of identical appearance.
Surrounded [by them]. (The Tang translation says: "Buddha-sons traveling together, surrounding him from before and behind.

Having come from all Buddha-fields, they receive the consecration from the hands of the Buddhas, just as the crown prince of a *cakravartin* king receives his consecration. (The Tang translation says:
"All Tathāgatas from all Buddha-fields extend their hands and consecrate his head according to the rite for the consecration of a *cakravartin* prince. He transcends the Buddhas...
This is the stage of the Son (putrabhūmi). Upon reaching the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization (Tang:

"attaining the dharma of self-attestation"), one shall attain the sovereign Dharma-body of the Tathāgata by seeing the non-self of phenomena (dharmanairātmya). This is called the characteristic of the non-self of phenomena.
You, all you Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, should practice and study this.
The Commentary states: "One shall attain the First Ground" refers to the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) for a Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).
Yet it says, "one shall attain it before long," and further states, "gradually advancing, one transcends the nine grounds and so forth.

This indicates that the Distinct Teaching is used to clarify the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*), and is not the same as the provisional practices of the sequential distinct stages, which require a fixed number of kalpas. The "palace of the Great Jewel Lotus King" is described in detail as follows: [text continues].

What is elucidated in the *Avataṃsaka* is not merely the manifestation of inferior and superior responses associated with the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. Section Seven concludes the clarification of the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness.
Section Eight: Refuting the Two [Extremes of] Establishing and Denigrating. I. The Question. II. The Answer. △ Now, the first part.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain the characteristics of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*), so that I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may be free from the evil views of the two extremes of superimposition and denial, and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having awakened, we shall be free from the eternalism of superimposition and the nihilism of denial."

The view of slander. Not slandering the true Dharma (the Tang translation states: "Having attained Bodhi, one destroys the established [views] of eternalism and slanderous nihilism, so that one does not give rise to revilement toward the true Dharma").
II. The Response, which has two parts: first, a brief response in verse; second, an extensive response in prose. △ Now, the first:
At that time, having received the request of Mahāmati Bodhisattva, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: “Establishment and slander...”

That "mind-only" does not exist; it is the body, the objects of enjoyment, and their establishment that cannot be known by the mind. The ignorant lack wisdom and thus engage in both affirmation and denial.
(The Wei translation says: "Within the mind there is neither annihilation nor permanence; the body, the means of subsistence, and the dwelling place are all but the deluded mind lacking wisdom;
where no object exists, one perceives it as existing. The Tang translation says: "The body, the means of subsistence, and that which is dwelt in are all but images of the mind. Ordinary people...")
The foolish cannot comprehend this; they give rise to both establishment and denial. What arises is merely the mind (for apart from the mind, nothing can be found).
The Commentary says: This clarifies that because they do not realize "Mind-Only," they establish the view of eternalism and slanderously deny the view of annihilationism.
Yet, in the ultimate sense, permanence is fundamentally not permanent, and cessation is also not ceased. There is neither that permanence nor that cessation; it is merely one's own [mind].

This is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the mind. For those two views do nothing more than take as their basis the present root-body, the resources it employs, and the vessel-world where it dwells, and then falsely conceptualize them as being either eternal or annihilated;
they fail to realize that the body, its enjoyments, and their establishment are all solely the mind. This is due to their ignorance.
It is only through wisdom that one establishes [theories] or engages in denigration, as well as regarding the mind and words—here "words" (*akṣara*) should be understood as "mere words.

II. The detailed answer in prose has three parts: first, the presentation of the four kinds of establishment and the explanation of denigration; second, the reiterated explanation of the four kinds of establishment; third, the conclusion and exhortation to remain detached. △ Now, the first part: It is only through wisdom that one establishes [theories] or engages in denigration, as well as regarding the mind and words—here "words" (*akṣara*) should be understood as "mere words.

(1) The presentation of the four kinds of establishment and the explanation of denigration. (2) The reiterated explanation of the four kinds of establishment. (3) The conclusion and exhortation to remain detached. △ Now, the first part:
At that time, the World-Honored One further elucidated the meaning of these verses and addressed Mahāmati, saying: "There are four kinds of establishment of what does not exist.
What are the four? They are: the establishment of non-existent characteristics (the Wei translation says 'establishment of non-existent characteristics';
the Tang translation says 'establishment of the characteristic of non-existence'), the establishment of non-existent views (the Wei translation says 'establishment of non-..."

The characteristics of right view: (The Tang translation says: "There is no establishment of views"; [the Wei translation says: "Establishing the characteristic of non-existence"]. It is not the establishment of a cause that does not exist.
(The Wei translation says: "Establishing the characteristic of a non-existent cause"; the Tang translation says: "There is no establishment of a cause").

It is not the establishment of a nature that does not exist. (The Wei translation says: "Establishing the characteristic of a non-existent essence"; the Tang translation says: "There is no establishment of a nature"). These are called the four kinds of establishment.
Furthermore, regarding slander: it refers to the arising of slander by observing what has been established by others as being non-existent and beyond one's scope.
(The Wei translation asks: "What are the characteristics of slander? Mahāmati, it is when one observes the dharmas established by false views and fails to see their true nature.")

One then slanders all dharmas, saying that "everything is non-existent. [The Tang translation states: "Slandering" means that regarding the dharmas established by various evil views, one seeks them and finds them unobtainable;
failing to examine them skillfully, one consequently gives rise to slander. This is called the characteristic of establishing [a view] through slander.

The Commentary states: All phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind; outside the mind there are no marks, outside the mind there is no seeing, outside the mind there are no causes, and outside the mind there is no nature.
Yet, through deluded conceptualization, one imagines that there are marks, seeing, causes, and natures.

This is called "establishment," which falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, when one seeks that which has been established and finds it unobtainable, one then concludes that everything is utterly non-existent;
this is called "denial," which falls into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

One does not realize that what exists outside the mind is actually non-existent; rather, whether it be marks, appearances, causes, or natures, they are all merely manifestations of the mind alone. It is not... [the case].
It is the negation of non-existence. △ Second, the double explanation of the four kinds of establishment.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of establishing the characteristic of that which does not exist? It refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), wherein one gives rise to attachment to self-characteristics and common characteristics that do not exist, thinking, "It is thus," or "It is not otherwise. This is called the characteristic of establishing the characteristic of that which does not exist. This...
The construction of false imaginings regarding non-existent characteristics arises from attachment to various habitual tendencies of beginningless falsehood.

The Commentary states: "Deluded by what is manifested by one's own mind, one falsely perceives the existence of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. It is like flowers in the sky seen by those with cataracts;
how could there be any self-characteristics or common characteristics to be found? Yet one falsely calculates, 'This is a self-characteristic, such as...'"
It is so. This common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is not different [from them]; it is merely produced by beginningless false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Mahāmati, as for the characteristic established by the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi-pratiṣṭhita-lakṣaṇa*): if one establishes views regarding those aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)—such as the self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), sentient being (*sattva*), life-span (*jīva*), nourisher (*poṣa*), or spirit (*puruṣa*)—this is called the characteristic established by the view of non-existence.
The Commentary says: The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are a false conjunction;
they are provisionally named "self," "person," "sentient being," "life-span," and even "individual" (*puruṣa*). Yet, within these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, a self cannot be found;
nor can a self be found apart from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Nevertheless, based upon this, sixteen types of views have been falsely established.
How is this different from imagining a rope to be a snake or suspecting a tree stump to be a ghost?
Mahāmati, that which is established as having no cause refers to the initial consciousness arising without a cause, while subsequent [consciousnesses] are unreal, like a magical illusion.
Fundamentally unarisen. The eye, forms, light, and the element of attention—having previously arisen and already come into being, they subsequently perish.

This is called the characteristic of establishing what is non-existent as having a cause (*abhūta-hetu-prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*). (The Wei translation says: "It means that the initial consciousness does not arise from a cause; it is fundamentally unarisen.

It arises at a later time, like a phantom which is originally non-existent but exists due to objects. Because of the eye, forms, light, and attention, consciousness arises; having arisen, it again ceases. This is called...")

Establishing the characteristic of causes that do not exist. (The Tang translation states: This means that prior to the initial consciousness, there is no cause for its arising; that initial consciousness is fundamentally non-existent.
Subsequently, with the eye, visible objects, light, and attention acting as causes, it arises like a magical illusion. Once arisen, it exists, and having existed, it ceases.
This is called "establishing causes where no causes exist").
The Commentary states: The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is unchanging yet conforms to conditions.

Therefore, since beginningless time, sentient beings have by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) possessed the eight consciousnesses along with their mental factors (*caitta*), including both essence and appearance, as well as all seeds, which are capable of giving rise to active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
These active manifestations, by the very nature of things, in turn perfume the seeds; they mutually serve as cause and effect, revolving without interruption. Furthermore,
The eighth consciousness and its various seeds have co-arisen and co-perished since beginningless time, revolving perpetually like a flowing stream.

Because it is perpetual, it is not annihilated; because it revolves, it is not eternal. Moment by moment, in relation to what precedes, it is termed the "effect"; moment by moment, in relation to what follows, it is termed the "cause.
Thus, cause and effect are perfectly distinct, yet both are devoid of intrinsic nature. This is because they do not understand the nature of the mind.
Regarding the meaning of having no beginning or end: one falsely claims that the initial consciousness-mind exists inherently and would not arise at all if it lacked other causes;

yet, it must take the eye, visible forms, light, and attention as its causes for consciousness to arise. Although once arisen it exists as a reality, this existence is subject to cessation and destruction;
therefore, it is ultimately unreal, like a magical illusion. This is called "falsely establishing [a self] without other causes."
This refers to the causal characteristic (*nimitta*). That is to say, they reckon that consciousness arises with the eye, forms, light, and attention as its causes;
thus, they do not understand the principle that seeds give rise to manifest activity (*pravṛtti*). They reckon that what has arisen subsequently perishes and is therefore called "like an illusion";

thus, they do not understand the principle that manifest activity perfumes the seeds. Not knowing that both seeds and manifest activity are entirely mind-only (*cittamātra*), they further reckon in terms of extraneous causes.

Based on delusion, one claims that what existed previously was originally non-existent, and that it subsequently undergoes destruction; thus, the state of arising in the interim is termed "truly existent.
Yet one fails to realize that the nature of the mind has no beginning and no end, being a single continuum throughout the three periods of time.
All phenomena are, in their very essence, like illusions; they are not called "illusory" only after they have been destroyed.

Mahāmati, the characteristic of establishing the existence of that which does not exist refers to the conceptual attachment to the establishment of space, cessation, and parinirvāṇa as being non-produced and non-substantial.
(The Wei translation says: "It refers to the establishment and attachment to space, cessation, nirvāṇa, non-action, and non-thing.

The Tang translation says: "It refers to the attachment and establishment regarding space, nirvāṇa, analytical cessation, and the nature of non-action. This is the departure from [the notion of] intrinsic nature.

It is not a nature. (The Wei translation says: Because those three dharmas are free from existence and non-existence. All dharmas are like the horns of rabbits and horses, or like the appearance of floating hairs;

they are free from both existence and non-existence. (The Wei translation says: Because all dharmas are like the horns of rabbits, horses, donkeys, and camels, or like [the optical illusion of] a tuft of hair;
because they are free from the characteristics established as existence and non-existence. The Tang translation says: All dharmas are free from existence and non-existence.)

It is like the appearance of a net of hair or the horns of a rabbit, a horse, and so forth; this is called the characteristic of establishing that which lacks existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*).

The Commentary states: It is called unconditioned space (*ākāśāsaṃskṛta*) because it is free from all obstructions. It is called cessation (*nirodha*) because it is pure by nature without depending on the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), or because it is manifested through the absence of conditions;
