There is arising; therefore, I speak by means of the teaching of non-arising (the Tang translation states: "I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent, and thus they are called non-arising").

Mahāmati, as for the teaching on nature (*svabhāva*), it is for the sake of gathering in [beings from] birth and death, for the sake of destroying the view of non-existence and the view of nihilism, and for the sake of causing my disciples to gather various karmic actions and places of rebirth; it is taught by means of the nature of sound.

They undergo birth and death. (The Tang translation says: "Those who teach all dharmas do so to cause their disciples to know that birth and death are grasped through various karmas, in order to prevent them from falling into the view of annihilationism.
Mahāmati, I speak of the characteristic of the self-nature of illusion in order to bring about detachment from the characteristic of self-nature.
(The Tang translation says: "Speaking of the characteristics of all dharmas as being like an illusion is to cause [beings] to detach from the self-nature of all dharmas.")
Because of [clinging to] signs, they fall into the signs and aspirations of the evil views of foolish commoners (*bāla*).

Not knowing that all things are merely manifestations of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), they destroy the causal efficacy of what is produced and become attached to the self-nature and signs of conditions.
[The Buddha] teaches that the self-nature and signs of all phenomena are like illusions and dreams (the Tang translation says: "In order to cause them to distance themselves from...").
They cling to the characteristics of arising through causes and conditions, asserting that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams;

they do not allow foolish people with evil views to abandon their cravings, and by conceptualizing attachment to themselves and all other phenomena, they fail to see things as they truly are and compose incorrect treatises.
(The Tang translation says: "Those foolish people cling to evil views and deceive both themselves and others; they are unable to clearly see the true abiding place of all dharmas.
Mahāmati, seeing all dharmas as they truly are means transcending the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*).
(The Tang translation says: "To see all dharmas as they truly are means being able to thoroughly comprehend that they are merely manifestations of the mind. Thus it is said.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Non-arising is the absence of nature (*abhāva*);
[the verse says 'non-action,' which in the Tang translation means 'because there is no action, there is no arising']. Existence-nature (*bhāva*) encompasses birth and death.
By observing [all things] as being like illusions and the like, one does not engage in false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding their marks."

The Commentary states: This clarifies that what has been taught—the non-arising of phenomena and the fact that all dharmas are like illusions—is entirely for the purpose of counteracting the dispositions of sentient beings;
there is no contradiction between them. To refute the false causes and causelessness posited by non-Buddhists, one speaks of "non-arising.
To refute the nihilistic view and the view of non-existence, one speaks of all causal dharmas as being manifestations of mind alone. This is to refute false conceptualizations.
All phenomena possess the characteristic of intrinsic nature; therefore, they are said to be like illusions and like dreams.

If one can thoroughly comprehend that which is the manifestation of one's own mind, then one will know that arising is itself non-arising. Although karma and birth-and-death do not perish or disintegrate, they all lack intrinsic nature, being like illusions and dreams.
However, by reflecting according to the Tang translation, the meaning of the text becomes clear. This concludes the second section: the Explanation of Non-Arising.

[End. △ Third, an explanation that also clarifies the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*). Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall explain the characteristics of the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who skillfully observe the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes enter accordingly into the meanings, phrases, and phonemes. [The Tang translation says: "All bodhisattvas skillfully..."]
Contemplating these marks and thoroughly comprehending their meaning, one will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having awakened in this way, one awakens all sentient beings.
Mahāmati, as for "name-bodies" (*nāma-kāya*), it refers to establishing names based upon things (*vastu*). (The Tang translation says:)
That which is established as a name based on a referent (*vastu*), and wherein the name itself constitutes the body, is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*). Regarding the "phrase-body" (*padakāya*):

it refers to a phrase that possesses a body of meaning, wherein its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is determined and finalized (the Tang translation reads: "those capable of manifesting meaning that are determined and finalized"). This is called a "phrase-body. Regarding the "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*):
it refers to what manifests names and phrases (the Tang translation reads: "it is because by means of these, names and phrases are established"). This is called a "syllable-body."
[The phrase] "is called the body of form" (rūpakāya). The Commentary states:

"Ordinary, ignorant people do not realize that [all things] are the manifestation of their own mind; they falsely conceptualize that there are real entities outside the mind consisting of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.

Therefore, it exhorts the Bodhisattva to skillfully contemplate their characteristics. A name (nāman) expresses its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva); therefore, it is said to 'rely on the thing' (vastu)."
Regarding the establishment of names: just as the name "eye" is established based on the faculty that sees, and the name "form" (*rūpa*) is established based on the object seen;
the name "ear" is established based on the faculty that hears, and the name "sound" (*śabda*) is established based on the object heard, and so forth.
A phrase (*pada*) expresses specific distinctions; therefore, it is said that the determination of meaning is finalized through it. For example, as in the statement, "The eye is impermanent."
Up to "the mind is impermanent," "form is non-self," and so on, up to "consciousness is non-self. Form is itself the written character;
because it serves as the basis for names and phrases, it is said that "it reveals names and phrases."

Furthermore, the "body of form" (*rūpakāya*) refers to length, shortness, height, and depth. (The Tang version previously states: "The body of phrases" [*vākyakāya*] refers to the completion of a phrase-meaning;
"the body of names" [*nāmakāya*] refers to the individual distinctions among various characters and names, such as from the letter *a* up to the letter *a*, which then connects this phrase.
[The Wei commentary also contains three points]. Furthermore, the "body of phrases" refers to a track or footprint. (The Tang version states: "As if...")
"Footprints" refers to the tracks left by elephants, horses, humans, beasts, and so forth (the Tang translation says: like the tracks of people, livestock, and animals on roads and alleys).
One attains what is called the "body of phrases. Mahāmati, as for "name" and "form," this means that names are used to describe the four formless aggregates (*skandhas*).

Therefore, it is called "name" (*nāman*); because its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) appears, it is called "form" (*vyañjana*). (The Tang translation states: "Name" refers to the four non-material aggregates (*skandha*), as they are expressed by names;
"form" refers to the own-characteristic of the name, as it is manifested by form. These are termed the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).
One should study the definition and boundaries of these sets of names, phrases, and phonemes.
The Commentary states: "The completion of the matter of a phrase" means that a phrase is only established once it has definitively expressed a matter to its ultimate conclusion.
"The distinction of characters" refers to [syllables] such as *a*, *i*, and *ha*; these can only express distinct matters and are therefore termed "names" (*nāman*).
"Length, shortness, high, and low" refers to the provisional characteristics of opposition inherent within the substance of the characters themselves. Directly...
"Traces" refers to footprints left by humans or animals where there is a path; it is like how, when names exist, there are the phrases and meanings revealed by those names.

Regarding the four formless aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—they possess only names and have no further essential nature or characteristics that can be manifested.
That the specific characteristic of a name is revealed through its written expression is because...
It is through these characters—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—that the names of the four aggregates and so forth are manifested.

As before, there are three levels of explanation, all of which are manifestations of mind-only. They exist as distinctions based upon vocal sounds and are termed "non-associated formations" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
They are neither identical to nor separate from those vocal sounds, for they possess no distinct intrinsic nature.
(For now, taking sound as the substance of the teaching in this land, it is said to be neither identical with nor separate from sound.
If, in other lands, form, fragrance, and so forth serve as the substance of the teaching, these too are likewise neither identical with nor separate. Therefore it is said:
"One should practice and learn regarding the boundaries of those physical forms; one must not recklessly conceive that there are dharmas existing outside the mind."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The distinctions between the body of names, the body of phrases, and the body of syllables— Foolish ordinary beings cling to them, like an elephant sinking into deep mud."

The Commentary says: When noble wisdom thoroughly realizes that all is mind-only, even the objective realms of the six sense-objects, such as form and so forth, do not exist separately outside of the mind;
how much less could the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes—which are provisionally established based upon form and the rest—exist separately?
Ordinary, ignorant people cling to them and fail to realize that the nature of names, phrases, and phonemes is empty, like an elephant mired in deep mud; how could it ever emerge?
This is a profound warning; one must not be attached to it. This concludes the section clarifying the three types of bodies: name, phrase, and syllable.
△ Fourth, the section clarifying the four kinds of formal doctrines.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in future ages, those of wisdom—having abandoned the views of identity, difference, both, and neither—will [realize] my...
Regarding the general meaning: When asked by one who lacks wisdom, he immediately replies, "This is not a correct question" (the Wei translation states:
"In future ages, those without wisdom, possessing minds of false views, do not know the Dharma as it truly is; because of worldly discourse, they claim for themselves to be wise").
When one who possesses wisdom asks about the Dharma as it truly is—free from the characteristics of false views such as identity, difference, both, or neither—that fool...
People speak thus: "This question is not correct; it is not a question asked with right mindfulness. [The Tang translation says:

"In future ages, there will be those with false wisdom and evil thoughts who, having departed from the Dharma of reality, ask wise ones about the characteristics of identity, difference, both, or neither.
They will then answer: 'This is not a correct question.'"
The Commentary states: The meaning of this passage must be understood by synthesizing the three translations; only then will its significance become clear.
Generally speaking, if a person of wisdom encounters someone posing a false inquiry regarding the characteristics of identity, difference, both, or neither, they should respond as follows:
This is not a correct question. Yet those people of perverted wisdom and evil discernment, when they see a wise person asking about the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) as realized by the Buddha—
free from the characteristics of identity, difference, both, or neither— also falsely answer that it is not a correct question.
That is to say, whether form and so forth are identical to or different from permanence and impermanence;

likewise, whether nirvāṇa and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are identical to or different from one another; and whether the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*)—that is, within the characteristic, the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived—are identical to or different from one another;
and whether the quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*)—[as translated in the Tang version]...
The derived based upon the primary (the Wei version says: the agent and the acted-upon; are they one or different?);

the seer and the seen (the Wei version says: the seer and the visible; are they one or different?); the gross objects and their atoms (the Tang version says: the earth and its atoms; the Wei version says:
among the four great elements, are color, odor, taste, and touch one or different? Is a lump of clay and its atoms one or different?).
"Cultivation and the one who cultivates" (the Tang translation says: "wisdom and the one who possesses wisdom"; the Wei translation says: "the knower and the known"—are they one or different?).
Questions such as these involve successive characteristics; [the Tang translation says: "questions such as these inquire about the sequence of non-conceptualized phenomena"].
The Commentary states: This is a detailed account of the erroneous questions of those lacking wisdom.

It says that the Buddha’s teaching on the "unanswered" (*avyākṛta*) is intended to bring discussion to an end; it is not something that such deluded people can understand. (The Tang translation reads:

"The World-Honored One taught that these [questions] should be left unrecorded; they are beyond the capacity of ignorant fools to know. This is because they do not possess the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, in order to cause them to leave behind phrases that provoke fear, speaks of these as "unanswered" (avyākṛta), and does not provide a definitive explanation.
(In the Tang translation: "The Buddha, wishing to cause them to leave behind states of alarm and terror, does not provide a definitive explanation.

Furthermore, he does not speak of them in order to cease the speculative views and treatises of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika). (In the Tang translation: "As for not providing a definitive explanation, it is because he wishes to cause the non-Buddhists to forever attain liberation.")
Because they are free from the view of a creator, Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists (tīrthakaras) speak as follows: "The life-principle (*jīva*) is identical to the body.
Such discourses are called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). [The Tang translation states: "The various groups of non-Buddhists, calculating that there is a creator, speak thus:
'The life-principle is identical to the body,' or 'the life-principle is different from the body. Discourses such as these are called indeterminate. Mahāmati, those various non-Buddhists...

"Regarding causes, the foolish hold indeterminate views, which is not what I teach" (the Wei translation states: "Because non-Buddhists are deluded regarding the meaning of cause and effect, they are thus indeterminate;
it is not that within my Dharma there is such a thing as the 'indeterminate' [*avyākṛta*]). Mahāmati, that which I teach is as follows:
When one is free from the grasped and the grasper, false conceptualization does not arise. How, then, can it be ceased? (The Wei translation says:

"In my Buddha-dharma, one is free from the illusory marks of the seer and the seen; there is no mind of discrimination. Therefore, in my teaching, there is no such thing as a 'set-aside' answer [avyākṛta]. The Tang translation says:
'In my teaching, it is said that by being free from the grasping subject and the grasped object, discrimination does not arise. How could it be ceased? Mahāmati!

If one is attached to the grasped and the grasper, it is because they do not understand that these are merely manifestations of their own mind; for the sake of such persons, I speak of four kinds of questions: those to be set aside and those to be answered with silence.

This does not apply within my own Dharma. (The Wei translation says: "Various non-Buddhists and others cling to the graspable and the grasper, not knowing that these are merely phenomena seen by their own minds.
For their sake, I say there are four kinds of questioning methods: the unexplained and the answer by setting aside. The Tang translation says: "If there are those who cling...")
They are attached to the grasped and the grasper, failing to realize that these are merely manifestations of their own minds;
thus, they should be refuted. The Commentary states: This clarifies that the heterodox questions of the non-Buddhists lack any real meaning and constitute *avyākṛta* (unanswered) propositions;

they should be set aside without answer. Therefore, one must stop them by not answering. If, however, it were a correct question within the Buddha-dharma, it would be appropriate to answer it extensively. It is not [the case here].

One might falsely consider this a matter of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and cease [the inquiry]. However, the heterodox questions regarding the indeterminate or erroneous doctrines do not exceed four alternatives:

namely, identity, difference, both, and neither. Even if they were to possess the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), one may then explain for them at length that all four alternatives are non-existent, thereby revealing the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the first principle as it appears within the measure of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya*).
Because they lack the wisdom derived from hearing, if they hear the Dharma that transcends the four propositions, they will inevitably become terrified and lose their composure.

As in the *Mahābuddhatoṣaṇī-sūtra* (The Great Buddha-Topknot Sutra), regarding the two phrases "there is no one who sees" and "there is no one who does not see," the Buddha sealed them both with the seal of suchness (*tathatā*).
The great assembly was not composed of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), yet they were all utterly bewildered and could not understand the meaning to its conclusion.
At its inception, even those within our own tradition were struck with alarm and lost their composure; how much more so for the non-Buddhists?
Furthermore, the non-Buddhists falsely calculate that an agent is the cause and the action is the effect, failing to realize that both cause and effect are merely manifestations of the mind alone.

Consequently, they formulate various indeterminate doctrines—such as whether things are identical, different, both, or neither—which must be set aside and left unanswered. These are not the correct principles within the Buddha-dharma.

Question: One may indeed employ the "direct answer" (zhidá). Why then do ignorant and foolish people, seeing that within the Buddha-dharma the errors of non-Buddhists are condemned as improper questions, go on to condemn the wise for doing the same? Alas!
The masters of antiquity employed the staff and the shout; such were those wise ones. Now, the masters of the present day imitate and employ them as well.
They are like those who lack wisdom.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the four kinds of formal responses (*vyākaraṇa*).
Mahāmati, as for the "response by setting aside" (*sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa*), I preach it from time to time (the Wei translation says: "I preach such a Dharma because of waiting for the proper time").

The Tang translation says: "I spoke of it at another time because their faculties were not yet mature; it was not for those whose faculties were mature" (the Wei translation is the same. The Tang translation further explains:
"Because their faculties were not yet mature, I temporarily ceased speaking of it").

The Commentary says: Based on the preceding discussion regarding the cessation of conceptualization (*śamatha*), it is here clarified that the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma consists of four general types;
one must not cling to any single one. As for these four types, their characteristics will be presented in the subsequent verses themselves; for now, we shall merely record this summary.
However, it is but one among four [teachings], intended merely for those whose faculties are not yet mature.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are devoid of the causes and conditions of production; because there is no agent, all dharmas are unproduced.
(The Tang translation states: "For what reason are all dharmas unproduced? Because they are devoid of the producer and the produced, and there is no agent.")

Therefore, Mahāmati, for what reason are all natures devoid of self-nature? Because when one examines them through personal realization, neither their individual nor their common characteristics can be apprehended;
thus, it is said that all dharmas are unarisen. (The Tang translation states: "For what reason are all dharmas without self-nature?")

Because when observed with realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*), neither specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) nor general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) can be apprehended. For what reason are all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) neither brought forth nor taken away?

Because, by way of their specific and general characteristics, one wishes to bring them forth but there is nothing from which they come, and one wishes to take them away but there is nowhere to which they go.
Therefore, all phenomena are free from bringing and taking. (The Tang translation states: "For what reason are all phenomena without coming and going?")
Because they come from nowhere and go nowhere by virtue of their specific and general characteristics. Mahāmati, for what reason are all phenomena not extinguished?
It is because the characteristics of intrinsic nature are non-existent, and because all phenomena are unattainable;
thus, all phenomena are not extinguished. (The Tang translation states: "It is because all phenomena lack the characteristics of intrinsic nature and are unattainable. Mahāmati, for what reason...
"All dharmas are impermanent" means that their arising as characteristics is of the nature of impermanence; therefore it is said that all dharmas are impermanent. (The Tang translation says:
"Because the arising of all characteristics is of the nature of impermanence. Mahāmati, why are all dharmas permanent?

It is because the arising of characteristics is non-arising, and their nature is eternally constant; therefore it is said that all dharmas are permanent. (The Tang translation says: "Because the arising of all characteristics is...")
It does not arise, because it is non-existent. Its impermanent nature is eternal; therefore, I say that all dharmas are eternal). The commentary states:
This clarifies the analytical response given for those whose faculties are matured. The text is readily intelligible.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "There are four kinds of formal responses (*vyākaraṇa*):
the categorical (*ekāṃśa-vyākaraṇa*), the interrogative (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa*), the analytical (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*), and the response by setting aside (*sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa*).

These were established to subdue the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Regarding existence and non-existence, the teachers of Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika (in the Tang language: the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools)..."
The Vaiśeṣika school says that "existence" does not arise from birth; all such [theories] are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). He thus demonstrates this:
[The Chinese translation says, "All such various explanations are entirely indeterminate. That which is discerned by the Perfectly Awakened One has no obtainable intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
[The Chinese translation says, "When examined with wisdom, its essence cannot be found. Because it is free from verbal expression, it is said to be devoid of intrinsic nature.

Regarding the nature [of these four types of answers], the Commentary states: To answer directly according to the question is called a "categorical" (ekāṃśa) response. To respond by means of a counter-question in order to lead the interlocutor to self-realization is called a "dialectical" (vibhajya) response.
To provide a detailed explanation is called an "analytical" (vibhajya) response. To set the matter aside and not answer is called a "refraining from discussion" (sthāpanīya).
If it is for those whose faculties are matured, one employs the first three types [of answers]. If it is for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), one employs all four types;

this is because among non-Buddhists there are also those to whom one should give a direct answer, a counter-question, or an analytical answer. This refers to that which exists and that which does not exist arising.
These are the two theories of false causes and no cause. As for the Sāṃkhya, they are the teachers of the Sāṃkhya school who establish twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
They falsely claim that twenty-three of these principles are all produced from *pradhāna* (the primal principle) and are enjoyed by the *puruṣa* (the self).

Furthermore, they calculate that the producer and the produced are necessarily identical. As for the Vaiśeṣikas, they are the proponents of the *Vaiśeṣika* school who establish six categories (*padārtha*) and calculate that the possessor and the possessed are necessarily distinct.
However, all such doctrines are merely empty words and possess no real meaning; therefore, they are entirely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
As for the noble wisdom of self-awakening, it thoroughly realizes that [all things] are manifestations of one's own mind.

Regarding the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): not even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena can be apprehended. This is realized solely through meditative correspondence; it is beyond the reach of language.
Therefore, it is figuratively described as being "devoid of intrinsic nature. The thirteenth section, the Gate of the Constant Sound Being Like an Illusion, concludes.
The fourteenth section, the Gate of the Distinctive Characteristics of the Four Fruits, has three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the granting of the teaching.
III. The Correct Exposition. △ Now, first:
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the specific characteristics of the various types of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterers), as well as their common characteristics" (both translations state: "the characteristics of the differences in their practice"). If...

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully understands the specific characteristics and general marks of the various paths of the Srotāpanna, as well as the expedient marks of the Sakṛdāgāmin, the Anāgāmin, and the Arhat.

Having discerned and known them thus, he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings in such and such ways—namely, the two marks of selflessness and the purification of the two obstacles (the Chinese text says: "causing them to realize the dharmas of the two forms of selflessness").
Having purified the two obstructions and transcended the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*), one ultimately attains thorough penetration. (The Wei translation says:
"Successively advancing to grasp the superior characteristics of each stage. The Tang translation says: "Gradually and successively penetrating the characteristics of all stages.
One attains the inconceivable, ultimate realm of all Tathāgatas, which—like a mani jewel of manifold colors—is well able to benefit all sentient beings through all phenomena.
The spheres of activity consist of inexhaustible body and wealth, which sustain and nourish all beings.
The Commentary states: The distinct characteristics of the practices of the four fruits are all the Tathāgata’s sublime skillful means for transforming others;
they are able to lead sentient beings from the provisional into the ultimate. Therefore, a Bodhisattva must understand them well. △ Second, the Promise.
[The Buddha] proclaimed. The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well. I shall now speak for you. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! Indeed, we shall listen and receive [your teaching]."

III. The Correct Exposition has two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the characteristics of practice; second, the conclusion that these belong solely to the Mind. The first part has four sections:
first, the explanation of the *srotāpanna* (up to) fourth, the explanation of the *arhat*. Now, the first section.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three types of *srotāpanna* with distinctions in the fruit of *srotāpatti*.

What are the three? They are the inferior, the middling, and the superior. The inferior attains parinirvāṇa after at most seven more births (the Tang translation says: 'at most seven rebirths among the various states of existence').
The middling attains parinirvāṇa after three or five more births. The superior attains it in that very birth (the Tang translation says: 'in this life')."
Parinirvāṇa. These three types [of persons] possess three fetters (saṃyojana) of inferior, middling, and superior grades (*Táng* says: "These three types of persons sever three kinds of fetters").
What are the three fetters? They are the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Through the progressive advancement of these three fetters, one attains the state of an Arhat.
The Commentary says: After the Srotāpanna has severed the three fetters of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they no longer apply themselves with diligence;

consequently, the nine grades of the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) within the Desire Realm collectively provide the moisture for seven births. Specifically, each of the higher grades—namely the superior-superior, superior-middle, and superior-superior—consisting of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, can provide the moisture for two births.
Each of the middle grades—the middle-superior, middle-middle, and middle-inferior—provides the moisture for one birth. The middle-superior grade of delusion can provide the moisture for one [birth].
The middle-middle, middle-middle, and middle-low grades of afflictions together moisten one birth; the three lower grades of afflictions together moisten one birth.
Upon reaching the seventh birth, the moisture of the afflictions is exhausted and the seeds of past karma wither, such that one will never again take birth within the three realms of existence.
Once a middling *srotāpanna* has severed the three fetters, they no longer delight in taking birth and further apply themselves to spiritual practice. If...

If one abandons the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra) grade of afflictions, two births are eliminated; five births remain. If one abandons the high-of-middle (madhya-adhimātra) grade, one necessarily abandons the upper-of-middle (adhimātra-madhya);
thus four births are eliminated, and three births remain. If one further abandons the middle-of-high (madhya-adhimātra) grade of afflictions, two births remain;

this is called "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula). If one further abandons the middle-of-middle (madhya-madhya) and middle-of-low (madhya-mṛdu) grades of afflictions, one is then designated as a "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin).
The fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin. If one further abandons the three lower grades of afflictions, it is then renamed the fruit of Anāgāmin.
Having already abandoned the three fetters as a superior Srotāpanna, one develops a profound revulsion toward the triple world and exerts great application; thus, within this very life—
By exhausting the eighty-one grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) across the nine stages, one attains entry into *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the "three fetters" (*trisaṃyojana*), these refer to the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) abandoned by those in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). There are ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) in total: namely, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Precepts, views, and wrongness: here, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) subsumes the extreme views; the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) subsumes the clinging to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa);
and doubt (vicikitsā) subsumes wrong views (mithyādṛṣṭi). Furthermore, these three fetters collectively subsume greed, hatred, delusion, and pride among the afflictions of view;
this is because greed and the other afflictions within the category of views necessarily arise only through these three fetters.

Mahāmati, there are two kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-body): namely, that which is innate (*sahaja*) and that which is conceptualized (*parikalpita*). [The second version says "discriminated" (*vikalpita*).

It is like the conceptualization of dependent origination, or the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). [The Tang translation says: "Just as based on the dependent nature, there arises the attachment to various conceptualized natures.

For example, based upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), various attachments to conceptualized natures (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arise; because they are neither existent nor non-existent, they are not existent.

It does not exist, because it lacks the characteristics of real delusive conceptualization. Fools, however, through their delusions, cling to various characteristics of the self-nature of conceptualization.
(The Tang translation states: "Those dharmas are merely the characteristics of false discrimination; they are neither existent nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent.
Foolish ordinary people recklessly cling to them. It is like a mirage, where a thirsty deer perceives it as water. This is the delusion of the *srotāpanna*.

The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). By means of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), one grasps its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) and eliminates long-standing ignorance and attachment. (The Tang translation says:

"This conceptualized view of a self-body, because of a lack of wisdom, has been associated with its characteristics for a long time; upon seeing the selflessness of persons, it is immediately abandoned.

Mahāmati, as for the innate [view of a self-body], it is the view of a self-body of a *srotāpanna* regarding the four aggregates (*skandha*)—both one's own body and those of others—which are formless.

Because they are characterized by mutual marks; because matter arises as both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāya-rūpa*); because they function as reciprocal causes for one another; and because the primary elements and matter do not aggregate [independently].

For a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), when observing the categories of existence and non-existence, these do not appear, and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is thereby severed. (The Tang translation states:

"The innate view of a self-identity is severed by universally observing that in one's own and others' bodies, the four aggregates such as sensation (*vedanā*) lack the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), and that form [arises] from the primary elements.")

Because they arise [from causes], because these great elements (mahābhūta) are mutually causal, and because form does not accumulate—having contemplated in this way, one clearly perceives existence and non-existence, and immediately abandons them.
Thus, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is severed, and craving no longer arises; this is the characteristic of the clear vision of the view of a self.
The Commentary states: This clarifies that the two types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) are distinct, and the contemplations for severing them are likewise distinct.
The innate *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is identical to the afflictions of thought (*cintā-kleśa*); it pervades both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Because it is subtle, it is difficult to sever.

One must wait until after the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), when one repeatedly contemplates the Truth and cultivates the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*), before being able to sever it. As for the conceptualized [view of a self-identity]...

The view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) through conceptualization is a delusion of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). It is restricted to the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and, being coarse, is easily severed;
it is abandoned immediately upon first perceiving the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

As for the "conceptualized view of a self-body," it arises based on the five aggregates (*skandha*) of form and mind, involving false imputations regarding twenty propositions, such as identity with or distinct from, large or small, and so forth. Now, the manifest...
The five aggregates of form and mind are fundamentally phenomena born of causes and conditions; they are neither existent nor non-existent, nor are they both existent and non-existent.
They are the self-nature of dependent origination, devoid of "self" or "what belongs to a self," yet through deluded conceptualization and attachment, one claims them as "self" or "mine.
This is like a mirage that is not water, yet a thirsty deer perceives it as water. This occurs at the moment a Srotāpanna first realizes the non-existence of a personal self.
One is then able to sever it. As for the innate view of a self-body (*sahaja-satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it does not first arise through conceptual discrimination;
rather, it spontaneously clings to the provisional aggregation of form and mind as being "self. Therefore, [it is severed] after the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, one should universally observe that one's own body and those of others are nothing more than the composition of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Within these, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) possess no material form whatsoever;
they exist only as names. As for the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*), it is likewise nothing more than the composition of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*):
earth, water, fire, and wind. These four elements, moreover, arise through mutual dependence and lack any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, if one were to analyze these four...

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) might still seem possible to form from atoms (*paramāṇu*) such as visible form; however, atoms such as visible form can never be aggregated to constitute the four great elements.
After the *srotāpanna* has thus observed them universally, he knows that these five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are definitively not the self.
Consequently, the innate view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed, craving for the three realms does not arise, and he immediately becomes an *arhat*.
Furthermore,

Mahāmati, the characteristic of doubt is said to arise from having attained the characteristic of right vision regarding the Dharma (the Tang translation reads: "because of the characteristic of right vision regarding the Dharma realized"),
and because the previously existing two kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi (the view of a self-identity) have already been severed through false conceptualization and discrimination.

Doubt regarding phenomena does not arise (the Tang translation says: "Among all phenomena, doubt cannot arise"). One does not give rise to the view of a Great Teacher in other [objects] as being pure or impure.
This is called the characteristic of doubt abandoned by a Srotāpanna.
The Commentary says: To give rise to hesitation without understanding the principle of the truths is called doubt; this is exclusively discriminative and lacks any innate (sahaja) form.

For a Srotāpanna, because they have already clearly perceived the true nature within the dharmas of the four truths realized through their attainment, and because their discriminative view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has been permanently severed, [they are free from doubt regarding] the dharmas of cause and effect, both mundane and supramundane.
Within this, one will never give rise to doubt. One attains indestructible faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
therefore, one no longer regards external paths, Māras, and the like as true teachers, nor does one harbor doubts as to whether they are pure or impure.

Mahāmati, regarding the attachment to precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*): why does the *srotāpanna* not grasp at precepts? It is because he clearly perceives the painful nature of the places where one is reborn;

for this reason, he does not grasp at them. Mahāmati, "grasping" refers to the foolish who, out of a fixed determination, practice asceticism for the sake of the pleasures of material requisites and thus seek rebirth.
He [the *srotāpanna*] does not grasp at such things. (The Tang translation states: "Foolish ordinary beings, within the various realms of existence, are greedy...")
Attached to worldly pleasures, they practice austerities and observe the precepts, vowing to be reborn there. A *srotāpanna*, however, does not grasp at these signs;

setting aside the expedient means of practicing the characteristics of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharmas—which involve dedicating [merit] toward one’s own superior self-realization and freedom from conceptual construction—they uphold the branches of the precepts.
(The Tang translation states: "Seeking only the most supreme, outflow-free, non-conceptual dharma that is to be realized, they cultivate the categories of the precepts. This is called *srotāpanna*.
The *srotaāpanna* abandons the grasping for precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*).
The commentary states: To observe various precepts while being greedily attached to future existence is all termed "grasping for precepts.

For example, because Nanda was practicing the monastic discipline with such diligent application for the sake of rebirth in heaven, the Buddha commanded Ānanda not to speak with him or sit together with him. This is because...

This is because their aspirations and inclinations are deviant and perverse. How could it be that only the precepts of cattle, dogs, and the like are called "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*)?

The *srotāpanna* has severed the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*), and thus greed and delusion do not arise. (The Tang translation states: "Because he has abandoned the three fetters, he is free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
If a *srotāpanna* were to think, "I am not possessed of these fetters," there would be two faults, and he would fall [into error].
The view of a self-identity and the various fetters are not severed. (The Wei translation says: "If a srotāpanna gives rise to such a thought as, 'These are the three fetters;
I have abandoned these three fetters,' this is called seeing two dharmas. Following from the view of a self-identity, if he were thus, he would not be free from the three fetters.")

The Commentary states: Regarding "the severing of the three fetters so that greed, hatred, and delusion do not arise," once the sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) have been severed, the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*) arising from those sharp ones are also severed.
These three fetters are fundamentally false and illusory phenomena.
It is like a young child who, in a dark room, cries out in fear, claiming there is a ghost; yet the ghost does not exist. If one were to say, "These are the three fetters," I—

To be free from the three fetters yet to falsely conceive that there are fetters when there are none, and to falsely conceive a self when there is no self—this is like a small child who says, "This is a ghost in the dark room;
I am not afraid of ghosts. How could such a person truly be without fear?
Therefore, one falls into the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) and fails to sever the various fetters; these are the two faults.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken of many kinds of desire (*rāga*).
Among them, which kind of desire is to be abandoned? [The Chinese translation says: "Desire is of many kinds; which desire is to be relinquished?

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It is the attachment to and passionate clinging toward women, employing various means to commit evil deeds of body and speech, seeking pleasure in the present while planting the seeds of future suffering. That [kind of desire] is not [to be abandoned].”
It arises. (The Wei translation says: "To distance oneself from union with women, not for the sake of present pleasure, but because it plants the cause of future suffering.
The Tang translation says: 'Abandoning the entanglements of female beauty and greedy desire, one sees that this present pleasure gives rise to future suffering.

Why is this so? Because one attains the bliss of the correct reception (*samādhi-samāpatti*) of samādhi. Therefore, that [desire] is severed; it is not the severance of craving for the attainment of nirvāṇa.
(The Tang translation says: "Furthermore, because he has attained the sublime bliss of samādhi, he abandons that [bliss]; it is not a craving for nirvāṇa. ○ The Wei translation says:
'The srotāpanna is far removed from such cravings as these; it is not that he is detached from the craving for nirvāṇa')."

The Commentary states: One who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has not yet exhausted the afflictions of desire within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), but has already clearly understood the causal relationship between the mundane world and its effects, and has further attained the pure meditative absorption of *samādhi*.
Therefore, regarding the sensual desires for women, they are able to relinquish them and remain far removed from them.
Furthermore, the mind that seeks *nirvāṇa* is precisely not yet fit to be abandoned. The first section, clarifying the *srotāpanna*, is concluded.
II. Clarifying the *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Mahāmati, what are the characteristics of the *sakṛdāgāmin*? It refers to the sudden illumination of the characteristics of form (*rūpa*). (The Wei translation says: "It refers to seeing form once.")

When the signs appear before him, he gives rise to the mind [of realization]; the signs of deluded conceptualization and the signs of views do not arise. (The Wei translation says: "It is not through false discriminative conceptualization or views.
Because he clearly perceives the characteristics of the progression toward dhyāna. (The Wei translation says: "Because he skillfully perceives the characteristics of dhyāna practice.

He comes suddenly to this world. (The Wei translation says: "In one more coming and going in the world. He reaches the end of suffering and attains nirvāṇa. (The Wei translation says: "He then cuts off suffering.")

Exhausted, he enters into *nirvāṇa*. For this reason, he is called a *sakṛdāgāmin* (in the Tang language: one who, failing to fully comprehend the characteristics of form, gives rise to conceptualization of form;
having come and gone once more, he skillfully cultivates the practices of *dhyāna*, exhausts the limit of suffering, and attains *parinirvāṇa*.
This is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*).

The Commentary states: Because those in the second fruit still possess the three lower grades of afflictions of the desire realm, they may, for the time being, perceive the manifestation of forms and give rise to thoughts;
yet this is not a view-affliction produced by conceptual discrimination.

Furthermore, because they have skillfully cultivated the practices of dhyāna, they enter nirvana after returning to the world only once more to exhaust their remaining afflictions. This must be understood according to the Wei translation.
Explanation: This clarifies how [this teaching] does not contradict the formal doctrines. Third, the explanation of the Anāgāmin. Mahāmati, what is meant by "Anāgāmin"?

It refers to the non-arising of false conceptualizations—driven by the views of arising and the afflictions (*anuśaya*) regarding the nature and non-nature of the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) in the past, future, and present.
(The Tang translation states: "It means that regarding the characteristics of form in the past, future, and present, [one does not give rise to... )

Because the faults of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, as well as the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), do not arise, and because the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been severed—(the Tang translation says:
"having forever abandoned all fetters, one does not return again")—one is called an Anāgāmin.
The Commentary states: "Delusive thoughts do not arise" reiterates the previous severing of delusions of discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*).

"Severing the fetters" specifically clarifies the severing of the residual afflictions of desire (*kāmadhātu-kleśa*), thereby proceeding to sever the afflictions of the two higher realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*). △ Fourth, the explanation of the Arhat.
“Mahāmati, an Arhat is one who has fully accomplished the powers and clarities of the various dhyānas, samādhis, and liberations;

because afflictions, suffering, and false conceptualizations no longer exist [as per the Tang translation: ‘afflictions, sufferings, and discriminations are forever exhausted’], he is called an Arhat.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken of three kinds of Arhats. This refers to—”
"What kind of Arhat is it, World-Honored One? Is it one who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility (the Wei translation says 'definitive cessation';
the Tang translation says 'exclusively tending toward tranquility')? Or is it a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifesting as an Arhat through skillful means?

Or is it an emanation created by a Buddha? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is the Śrāvaka who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility, and not others. As for the others, they are those who practice..."

This is the conduct of a bodhisattva, as well as the transformation of a Buddha’s emanations; by means of skillful means and original vows, he manifests birth within the great assembly in order to adorn the Buddha’s retinue.
The Commentary states: "The accomplishment of the various dhyānas and so forth is the establishment of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and the completion of what was to be done.
The exhaustion of afflictions and suffering is the end of birth for oneself and the non-acceptance of further existence. This refers exclusively to those śrāvakas of fixed nature;
it does not refer to those manifested by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. This concludes the first section: the correct elucidation of the characteristics of practice. △ Second, the conclusion.
It belongs solely to the mind.
Mahāmati, within the realm of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), various teachings are expounded—namely, the attainment of fruits and the attainment of dhyāna.

This is because those who enter dhyāna are entirely free from [such conceptualizations]. (The Tang translation reads: "Within the realm of the false, various dharmas are taught; namely, the realization of fruition and dhyāna.")

...and dhyāna, all because their nature is detached [from grasping]. Manifesting the attainment of the fruit through the realization of what is manifested by one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*), it is called "attaining the fruit" (in the Tang translation:

because one attains the signs of the fruit as seen by one's own mind). Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who wish to transcend the realms of dhyāna, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless (*ārūpya*) should detach from the signs of what is manifested by one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*).
(In the Tang translation: they should detach from all that is seen by one's own mind.)
"Mahāmati, it is not the case that the attainment of cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*) transcends the manifestation of one's own mind.

Why is this? Because there is the measure of mind (*citta-mātra*). [The Tang translation states: 'It is not the case that the samādhi of the cessation of perception and sensation transcends the objects seen by one's own mind, for it does not depart from the mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The various dhyānas and the four immeasurables..."
In the samādhi of form, all sensation and perception cease; even that mental measure does not exist there (the Tang translation says: "only mind cannot be apprehended").
The fruit of srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, and the arhat—all these are delusions of the mind (the Tang translation says:
"all exist falsely based on the mind"). For the meditator, both meditation and its object (the Tang translation says: "its object") are to be severed and known.
To sever delusions and perceive the True Truth—this is merely the measure of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If one awakens to this, there is liberation (the Tang translation says:
"to fully know is itself liberation").
The Commentary states: The twelve gates of worldly dhyāna, the supramundane samādhi of cessation, and the four fruits of the śrāvaka path—all these are but mind alone;
there is no phenomenon apart from the mind. The Bodhisattva realizes this, and therefore is able to remain free from grasping and attachment.

In accordance with the various capacities of sentient beings, they attain mastery whether in bestowing [teachings] or setting them aside. This is the fourteenth section: The Distinctive Characteristics of the Four Fruits.
The section on the gates concludes. ○ Chapter Fifteen: The Section on the Two Kinds of Awakening (3). First, the correct discernment of the two kinds of awakening;

second, clarifying the four great elements through skillful awakening; third, clarifying the five aggregates through skillful awakening. Within the first [section], there are three parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation;
third, the conclusion on benefits. △ Now, the first.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening (both of which function as gnosis): namely, the awakening of analytical observation (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*) and the awakening that establishes through the grasping of and attachment to the marks of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-parigraha-abhiniveśa-vyavasthāpanajñāna*).
[The Wei translation says: "the wisdom that dwells upon the grasping of marks through false discrimination. The Tang translation says:]...
[This refers to] the wisdom that apprehends signs, discriminates, clings, and establishes [concepts].
Part Two: A detailed explanation of these two. First, the explanation of observation; second, the explanation of clinging and establishment. Now, the first [section].

Mahāmati, as for "insight through observation," it refers to the realization that the intrinsic nature and characteristics of phenomena cannot be apprehended when analyzed through the exclusion of the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*).
(The Wei translation says: "Observing the essence and characteristics of all dharmas, one finds them free from the four extremes; no dharma can be apprehended. The Tang translation says:
"It means observing that all dharmas are free [from extremes], such that they cannot be apprehended through the four extremes. This is called insight through observation. Mahāmati, regarding that...
The "four positions" (catuṣkoṭi) refer to being free from identity, difference, both, and neither; existence, non-existence, both, and neither;
permanence and impermanence. These are called the four positions. Mahāmati, that which is free from these four positions is called all dharmas.

Mahāmati, one should study and practice by examining all dharmas through these four positions. (The Tang translation states: "I [teach] that all dharmas are free from these four positions; therefore...")
It is said: "All phenomena are detached; you should observe phenomena in this way and practice accordingly. The Commentary states:
All phenomena are manifestations of mind alone and are fundamentally detached from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*).

To observe them in this manner is the true skillful means of the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation); therefore, one is exhorted to practice and study. All phenomena are detached from the four extremes.
The characteristics [of this] have already been explained in detail in the ninth section. △ Second, the explanation of the establishment based on conceptual attachment.

Mahāmati, what is the awakening that establishes through the grasping and conceptual attachment to the characteristics of false imagination? It refers to the grasping of the characteristics of false imagination.
The conceptual attachment to the unreal marks of the four great elements—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion (the Wei translation says:
"so-called attachment to solidity, heat, moisture, and motion, because of falsely discriminating the characteristics of the four great elements"; the Tang translation says:

"referring to the grasping at marks and attachment to the natures of the various great elements such as solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, which is false discrimination"). This refers to conceptual attachment to the thesis, reason, characteristic, and example. It is not...

It is established by means of what is actually established. (The Wei translation says: "Because one clings to the characteristics of the cause, the reason, and the example, one establishes unreal dharmas as real.
The Tang translation says: "One falsely establishes [them] by means of the thesis, the reason, and the example.
This is called the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false imagination.
The Commentary states: The subsequent text extensively explains how the four kinds of false conceptualization give rise to the four great elements of the internal and external.

Thus, outside of the mind, how could the four great elements ever truly exist? Yet, all ordinary and ignorant people falsely establish the four great elements as having a real intrinsic nature through the formulation of propositions, reasons, and examples, asserting that earth possesses a real nature of solidity, water possesses a real nature of moisture, and so forth. Is this not mere false conceptualization?
Is it established by clinging to unreal phenomena? This concludes the second part, the detailed explanation. △ Third, the conclusion on the benefits:

These are called the two aspects of awakening. If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes these two aspects of awakening, they will thoroughly understand the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
Through the skillful means of the awakening to non-existence, they observe the stages of practice and attain the first stage (*bhūmi*).
(The Tang translation says: "The Bodhisattva, knowing these marks of wisdom, is then able to penetrate the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
By means of signless wisdom, he skillfully observes on the stage of practice and understanding, and enters the first bhūmi. He enters one hundred samādhis and attains the samādhi of differentiation.)
(The Tang translation says: "By the power of the supreme samādhi") one sees a hundred Buddhas and a hundred Bodhisattvas;

one knows the events of a hundred kalpas in both the past and the future; light illumines a hundred lands; one knows the characteristics of the progressively higher stages (*bhūmi*); and one possesses great vows, extraordinary spiritual powers, and mastery.
Through the empowerment of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghābhiṣeka*), one shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.

Firmly binding the mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases, one brings sentient beings to maturity through various transformations and the adornment of light. One attains the holy bliss of self-awakening and enters into the correct reception of samādhi (in the Tang translation:
"the ten inexhaustible vows; accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings; manifesting in various ways without ceasing, while constantly abiding [in this state]").
"The Samādhi of the Noble Bliss of the Realm of Self-Awakening.

The Commentary states: "If one knows that conceptual attachment and establishment are erroneous, then one knows what is to be relinquished; if one knows that observation free from the four extremes is correct, then one knows what is to be cultivated.
Thus, one is able to proceed from the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) into the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and so forth until [enlightenment] is accomplished."
The Buddha, throughout the entirety of the future, matures sentient beings while constantly abiding in the bliss of self-realized noble wisdom (*svapratyātmāryajñāna*).
This concludes the first section, the correct exposition of the two types of awakening. II. Clarifying the Four Great Elements of Good Awakening.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa). [The Wei translation says:

"One should skillfully know the characteristics of the four great elements and the four objects. The Tang translation says: "One should skillfully and thoroughly understand the primary elements and the derived matter.
How does a bodhisattva become skilled in the primary elements and the derived matter? Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this realization: [The Tang translation says: "One should be like..."]

This contemplation of that ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is as follows: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are unarisen. (The Tang translation states: "Those various primary elements are truly unarisen.
Regarding the non-arising of those four great elements, one performs such an observation.

Having observed them, one realizes that the limits of names, marks, and false imaginings (*vikalpa*) are merely the manifestations of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya*), and that external natures lack inherent existence. This is called the limit of the false imaginings manifested by the mind; namely, the three [realms].
The Realm. (The Tang translation states: "Because all three realms are merely conceptual constructions, seen only by the mind, there are no external objects.
Contemplating the nature of the derived matter produced from the four great elements, one finds it free from the four extremes and universally pure; it is devoid of self and what belongs to self.

It abides as its own characteristic and its own specific characteristics according to reality, and its unarisen specific characteristics are established. (The Tang translation states: "When contemplating in this way, the primary elements and their derivatives are all... )
By nature it is detached, transcending the four propositions, devoid of self and what belongs to self, abiding in the state of suchness, and characterized by non-arising.

Mahāmati, how do those four great elements give rise to derived matter? It is said that the great element of moisture—which is false conceptualization (the Tang translation says "the great element of moisture of false discrimination")—gives rise to the internal and external water element.
[The Tang translation reads "accomplishes" for "gives rise to. Capable of false conceptualization...

That is, the conceptualization of all natures (*sarva-bhāva*) through their characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion; this is called the conceptualization of characteristics. Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of benefit (*upabhoga-vikalpa*)?

That is to say, delighting in various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels—this is called the delusive discrimination of "desire. Mahāmati, what is the delusive discrimination of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*)?
It refers to maintaining this intrinsic nature as being thus and not otherwise—a delusive discrimination based on evil views (the Tang translation says:

What is the delusion of cause (*hetu-vikalpa*)? It refers to the arising of the characteristic of a cause through the conceptualization of existence and non-existence regarding causes and conditions (as the Tang translation states:
"it refers to the conceptualization of existence and non-existence within causes and conditions; because it is able to produce [the effect] by means of this causal characteristic").

This is called the delusion of cause. Mahāmati, what is the delusion of view (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*)? It refers to the false views of existence, non-existence, identity, difference, both, or neither—the delusions of the non-Buddhists.

Attachment to false conceptualization—(the Tang translation states: this refers to various non-Buddhists who, due to evil views, cling to existence and non-existence, identity and difference, both and neither, and so forth)—is called the conceptualization of views (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*).
Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of establishment (*siddhi-vikalpa*)? It refers to the formation of a definitive doctrine based on the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self";

this is called the conceptualization of establishment. Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of origination (*utpāda-vikalpa*)? It refers to that which takes the nature of existence and non-existence as its object-condition.
To conceive of attachment to arising—(the Tang translation says: this refers to calculating that all phenomena exist or do not exist, arising from conditions)—is called the delusion of arising.
Mahāmati, what is the delusion of non-arising? It means that all natures are fundamentally unarisen;

they are bodies without causes, produced by conditions that lack seeds. (The Tang translation says: this means calculating that all phenomena are originally unarisen and that no conditions have yet existed.)
If it possesses an intrinsic nature beforehand and does not arise from causes, this is called the "delusion of non-arising. Mahāmati, what is the "delusion of continuity"?
It refers to their mutual continuity, like gold and its thread (the Tang translation says: "it means that this and that are mutually interconnected").
This is called the conceptualization of continuity (*saṃtati-vikalpa*). Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of bondage and non-bondage?
It refers to the attachment to the causes and conditions of bondage and non-bondage, such as a person’s skillful means in either binding or releasing—[the Tang translation says:

The Commentary states: This explains the distinct characteristics of the twelve types of conceptualization;

There is an intrinsic nature (*vastutva*). Second, the delusion regarding the object of expression (*vācyavikalpa*) consists of clinging to the expressed meaning as having an intrinsic nature.
Third, the delusion regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇavikalpa*) consists of clinging to the four great elements and so forth as having an intrinsic nature such as solidity and so on.

Sixth, the delusion of causal factors (*hetu-vikalpa*) consists of clinging to false causes and conditions, or to the absence of causes and conditions, as being able to give rise to all phenomena. Eighth, the delusion of accomplishment (*niṣpatti-vikalpa*) consists of clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," falsely establishing what is erroneous.

This refers to the principle of the truths (*satya*). Ninth, the delusion of arising (*utpāda-vikalpa*) consists of clinging to the notion that all phenomena arise from false causes and conditions or from no cause at all.

In this transformation, all dependent origination—whether matter or mind, the environment or its inhabitants—is devoid of intrinsic nature.

It is only through the deluded conceptualization of worldly people that these are termed the "conventional truth" (saṃvṛti-satya). When the wisdom of supramundane sages penetrates and realizes them, they are the "ultimate truth" (paramārtha-satya).

Because it is the truth, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Yet, this natureless essence of phenomena arising through conditions cannot be called merely the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), nor can it be called the ultimate truth.

It is, for example, like saying that the sun does not move in response to one who, while intoxicated, perceives the sun as spinning; yet the solar disc itself cannot be said to be either [moving or non-moving].

This is "transformation," yet it cannot be called "non-transformation. That which is not transformation, yet the intoxicated perceive as transformation, is termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

That which is not non-transformation, yet the sober perceive as non-transformation, is termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Although the intoxicated perceive transformation, [it is not so in reality].
In reality, it has never undergone transformation. Seeing that it does not transform upon awakening is not because it is fixedly non-transforming;
rather, because it is neither transforming nor non-transforming, it is called the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*). This is two expressed as three, yet the three are precisely the two.

Furthermore, because it does not change while following conditions, there is both transformation and non-transformation, all of which are termed the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Because it follows conditions without changing, transformation is itself non-transformation.
To turn is not to turn; that which is neither turning nor non-turning is what is called "the Real.

The Commentary states: This clarifies that if one knows that the objects of false conceptualization are themselves the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is like knowing that a snake is merely a rope, or that a ghost is merely a tree stump.

The Tang translation says: "One falsely conceives various marks, discriminating within dependent origination. If it were different from false imagination...
This relies upon the treatises of the non-Buddhists. (The Tang translation says: "If one discriminates otherwise than this, one falls into the discourse of the non-Buddhists.

One speaks of what is imagined through false conceptualization; it arises from the conjunction of views. (The Tang translation says: "Because of various false views, one falsely calculates upon what is already falsely calculated.

For one who is free from these two forms of false conceptualization, such a state is established as the perfected reality. (The Tang translation says: "One who is free from these two calculations is the true reality.")
[The text says: "Dharma").
The Commentary states: This concludes the clarification that the dependent origination of deluded thoughts is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and is not fixed as a single entity.
That is to say, the various marks falsely conceptualized by worldly people are merely like painted colors; their dependent origination is not real, yet therein [they]—

They give rise to false discrimination. If one were to claim that apart from false discrimination there exist various distinct characteristics that can be apprehended, this would be the calculation that objects exist outside the mind, falling into the views of externalist treatises. It is nothing more than this:

because of the conjunction of various false perceptions, one uses false conceptualization to describe back what has been falsely conceptualized. That which is capable of false conceptualization is merely the duality of self and dharmas.
The sixth consciousness, which is associated with grasping, produces what is called "delusive conceptualization. This is merely the various phenomena of dependent origination, such as form and mind.
If one is free from the dualistic reckoning of subject and object, then delusive conceptualization is empty and dependent origination is quiescent;

this is precisely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). It is like the disappearance of flowers when the cataract is cleared away; it is simply the clear and bright sky. [The sixteenth is] Nirvana.
The section on the gate of discursive conceptualization is concluded. ○ Seventeenth: The Gate of the Single Vehicle of Self-Awakened Noble Wisdom.
Part Three: First, the inquiry; second, the granting of the teaching; third, the formal exposition. △ Now, the first.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna)—[the Tang translation reads:

'the characteristics of the practice of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the characteristics of the practice of the Single Vehicle']—so that I and the other bodhisattvas may thoroughly realize the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle."
The vehicle. Not dependent on others. Penetrating the Buddha-dharma (the Tang translation says: "I and all bodhisattvas have attained this skillful means;
within the Buddha-dharma, we do not attain awakening through another").
△ Second, the granting of the teaching.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well. I shall speak for you. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, we shall receive your instruction."

III. The Correct Exposition has two parts: first, the exposition of the noble wisdom of self-realization; second, the exposition of the One Vehicle. △ Now, the first part. The Buddha addressed Mahāmati:
"That which was known by the previous sages and transmitted from one to another is, in its nature, free from false discrimination (according to the Tang translation:
'based on the teachings of the various sages, there is no conceptual differentiation'). A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in a solitary and quiet place, should personally realize and observe it. (Tang)
It is said: "Observing through self-awakening, not depending on another, free from the delusions of views, ascending higher and higher, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata;
this is called the characteristic of the noble wisdom of self-awakening."
The Commentary states: This is precisely the direct advancement of the mind-only, the wondrous cultivation of the Perfect and Sudden [teachings].

"Deluded thoughts" refers to the object of contemplation. "Lack of intrinsic nature" refers to the truth of that object. It lacks intrinsic nature because it is empty; it lacks intrinsic nature because it is provisional; it lacks intrinsic nature because it is the Middle Way.
These three are each identical to one another, and being inconceivable, they lack intrinsic nature. "Abiding alone in a quiet place" refers to—
In terms of phenomena, this is the *āraṇya* (hermitage); in terms of principle, it is the wondrous truth that transcends all dependencies.
"Observing through self-awakening" means taking self-awakening itself as the object of observation. "Not depending on another" means that there is nothing other than oneself.
"Free from the delusions of views" means that since there is no other, there is no self; and since there is neither self nor other, there is nothing [to grasp].
This is an analysis. This refers to the initial stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), where one first realizes the essence of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svapratyātmāryajñāna*).

From this point onward, one ascends progressively, transcending the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), until reaching the perfect clarity of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and entering the stage of the Tathāgata.
II. Explaining the One Vehicle (2): A. Direct Explanation; B. Resolving Doubts. △ Now, the first part.
Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the One Vehicle? It is the awakening to the path of the One Vehicle; this is what I call the One Vehicle.
What is the awakening to the path of the One Vehicle? It is the non-arising of false conceptualization regarding the state of reality as it truly is—the grasped and the grasper.

This is called the awakening to the One Vehicle. (In the Tang translation: "What is meant by knowing the path of the One Vehicle? It means being free from the discrimination of the grasper and the grasped.")
"Mahāmati, the realization of the One Vehicle is not something that can be attained by other outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even by Brahmā and the other celestial kings;
it is attainable only by the Tathāgata. For this reason, it is called the One Vehicle."
The Commentary states: The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is fundamentally equal.

Due to the presence of deluded conceptualization regarding the grasper and the grasped, there subsequently arise the differing gradations of the six realms of ordinary beings and the four classes of noble ones. Nevertheless, these ten realms are themselves none other than the true reality.
What is called "non-differentiation yet differentiation" is such that differentiation is itself non-differentiation. Only the Tathāgata can exhaustively fathom this;
even the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot know it, let alone the non-Buddhists or Brahmā. [Section Two: Resolving Doubts, Part Two.]
First, the question; second, the answer. △ Now, the first:
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak of the three vehicles and not the one vehicle?"

II. The Response, which has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying the concealment of the ultimate truth and the manifestation of provisional means;
second, clarifying the entry from the provisional into the ultimate. △ Now, the first section.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Because they do not possess the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa by themselves—(the Tang translation states:
because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack the dharma of self-attained parinirvāṇa)—I do not teach that all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas belong to the One Vehicle.

This is because all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attain liberation through the Tathāgata’s taming and the bestowal of skillful means for tranquility, rather than by their own power. For this reason..."
