I do not speak of a single vehicle (*ekayāna*). Furthermore, Mahāmati, because the karmic habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*)—and the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*, as stated in version two)—have not been severed, I do not speak of a single vehicle for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is because they have not realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and they have not transcended death by fragmentation (*bheda-maraṇa*).

[The Wei translation states: "They have not yet attained the inconceivable transformation-birth" (*acintya-nirmāṇa-upapatti*); the Tang translation states: "They are not yet called those of inconceivable transformation."]
Because [beings] are subject to death easily, the Three Vehicles are taught.
The Commentary states: Those of the Two Vehicles must rely on the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma to be subdued;

they cannot enter nirvāṇa through their own power. Furthermore, while their afflictions (kleśa) are severed, their cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) are not. Even if these were severed, their karmic habitual tendencies would still remain unsevered.
For this reason, the reality of the One Vehicle was concealed and not taught.

Since they do not realize that all phenomena are without self, if the Three Vehicles were not taught as a skillful means, by what means could they depart from birth-and-death with fixed limits and enter birth-and-death through transformation?
Therefore, the provisional power of bestowing kindness and providing guidance was employed to teach the Three Vehicles. Question: What does the Pratyekabuddha rely upon in relation to the Tathāgata?

Tiaoyu (調伏) replied: "If it were not for having resolved upon the mind of a pratyekabuddha and received the teachings on dependent origination from the Tathāgata prior to four *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and a hundred *kalpas*, by what means could the fruit ripen and fall from its stem?
How else could one awaken to non-arising (*anutpāda*) upon seeing a flower fly or a bracelet move?
[The interlocutor] asked: "The Tathāgata likewise served various Buddhas over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and a hundred *kalpas* before realizing Bodhi. How could this be [the case for others]?"
Dānzhìlì replied: "The awakened one of the One Vehicle is free from the deluded thoughts of subject and object.

Having realized that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in their threefold nature, they possess no self-other or pervasive conceptual discrimination—even regarding events spanning eons as numerous as atoms or Buddhas as numerous as atoms.
This is what is meant by 'this mind creates the Buddha' and 'this mind is the Buddha. How could this be the same as the [view of] the Two Vehicles?"

Is it that you have realized the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and yet falsely imagine that there is a Buddha external to the mind? △ Second, clarifying the entry from the provisional into the real:

"Mahāmati, those who have severed all afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies, and who have awakened to the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*)—they have severed all afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies.
They do not savor the nature of attachment to the bliss of samādhi, but awaken to the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*). (Tang)

It is said: "If they can eliminate all habitual tendencies toward faults and realize the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), at that time they will depart from the intoxication of samādhi and attain awakening within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
Having awakened, they further enter the supramundane, most excellent, untainted realm."

Fulfilling all requisites (the Tang translation says: cultivating all meritorious virtues so that they are universally fulfilled), one shall attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and sovereign Dharma-body.

The Commentary states: From the grasping at a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-grāha*), the grasping at a self in persons (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*) arises. It is like being deluded by a tree stump and subsequently perceiving it as a ghost;

therefore, the grasping at phenomena is considered the habitual tendency for all faults. By eliminating this grasping at phenomena and awakening to the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one no longer relishes the samādhi of partial truth.
It is like the wine having been digested; thus, from the outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of partial truth, one awakens once again.

Entering into the middle way within the supreme, unsurpassed realm of outflowlessness (*anāsrava-dhātu*), one practices in accordance with the nature of reality until it is universally fulfilled, thereby realizing the ultimate *dharmakāya*.

The "realm of outflowlessness" refers to the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāyika-śeṣa-bhūmi*); the "supreme, unsurpassed realm of outflowlessness" refers to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*sukhāvatī*).

This is the partial realization of the *nitya-śānti-prabhāsa-kṣetra* (the land of eternal quiescent light), also called the *tathatā-vipāka-alaṃkāra-kṣetra* (the land of true retribution adorned with merit).
It is the fulfillment of all requisites, namely the two kinds of adornment—merit and wisdom—possessed by the forty-two stages.
It is the sovereign *dharmakāya*, which refers to the fundamental Buddha-nature of equal *tathatā*. The long prose section concludes here. II. Verse Recitation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The vehicle of the devas and Brahmās, The vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, And the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas— I have taught all these vehicles. (In the Tang translation: "All these vehicles are what I have taught.")
The Commentary states: This verse establishes the provisional teachings that are actually bestowed. The "Celestial Vehicle" refers to the ten wholesome dharmas.
The "Brahma Vehicle" refers to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless absorptions. The "Śrāvaka Vehicle" refers to the dharma of the four truths of arising and ceasing.
The "Pratyekabuddha Vehicle" refers to the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, both in their modes of arising and non-arising. As for the Buddhas...
"Vehicles" refers to the practices of the six perfections, the principles of the six perfections, and even the various dharmas such as the three successive contemplations.
As long as there is the movement of the mind (the Tang version reads "arising"), these various vehicles are not ultimate. If that mind is extinguished, there is neither vehicle nor rider;
there is no establishment of a vehicle. (The Wei version says "distinctions. I call this the One Vehicle.
The Commentary states: This verse refutes the provisional to return to the real. When discrimination is forever exhausted, one knows that all dharmas are the self-nature of the mind;

thus, the principle of suchness does not exist outside of wisdom, and therefore there is no vehicle. Since the wisdom of suchness does not exist outside of the principle, there is likewise no "one who rides" the vehicle.
The ten realms, the hundred realms, and the thousand suchnesses are all the true mark (dharmatā); therefore, there is nothing [that exists apart from it].
This establishment of distinctions is, in fact, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) that is absolute and without external counterpart.

For the sake of guiding sentient beings, it is taught that there are various vehicles (as the Tang translation states: "In order to gather in the foolish, the distinctions of the various vehicles are taught").
There are three kinds of liberation, as well as the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), and the equality of afflictions and wisdom; thus, liberation is—

Detachment (the Chinese translation says: liberation is of three kinds, namely: detachment from all afflictions, [detachment] through the selflessness of phenomena, and liberation through the wisdom of equality).

The Commentary states: This verse explains the intent behind teaching the three [liberation doors] as a skillful means. If one were not to distinguish and teach them as three, how could the ignorant be gathered and guided?
Therefore, it first clarifies the three liberation doors of the provisional teachings to enable the abandonment of afflictions;
it further clarifies the liberation door of the equality of the non-self of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) and the inconceivable to purify the objects of knowledge.
Just as a piece of wood floating on the ocean is constantly tossed by the waves, so too are the ignorant śrāvakas driven by the winds of signs.
When their afflictions arise and then cease, they remain deluded by residual habitual tendencies. Becoming intoxicated by the flavor of the bliss of samādhi—(the Chinese says:

"intoxicated by the wine of samādhi")—they dwell within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), yet there is no ultimate destination for them. (The Chinese says: "That is not the ultimate destination. Nor...
Furthermore, they do not regress. They attain the bodies of various samādhis and remain unaware for as long as an eon.

It is like a person who is intoxicated; only after the alcohol has worn off does he awaken. The awakening to the Dharma is likewise so. They attain the supreme body of a Buddha (the Tang translation states:
"Śrāvakas are also like this; after awakening, they shall become Buddhas").
The Commentary states: This verse correctly praises the entry from the provisional into the ultimate. The seventeenth section, the Gate of the Single Vehicle of Self-Aware Holy Wisdom, is concluded.
*Lengqie abaduoluo bao jing* (Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra), Fascicle Two, Exegesis Part Two.
Commentary on the Third Fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-ratna-sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Upper Tianzhu Monastery;
the meaning expounded by the Chinese Śramaṇa O-yi, Shi Zhixu.
The Third Chapter on the Heart of All Buddha-Speech (In the Wei translation: Chapter Four on the Buddha-Mind; in the Tang translation:
Chapter Three on Impermanence). Section Eighteen:
The Gate of the Mind-Born Body. Part One: Granting Permission to Teach. Part Two: The Actual Exposition. △ Now, the first part.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"I shall now explain the characteristics of the distinctions of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! So be it."
He received the instruction. ○ Second, the actual exposition has three parts: first, listing the names; second, explaining their characteristics; third, concluding with verses.
△ Now, the first part. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). What are the three? They are: [the body born of] the bliss of samādhi..."
The mind-made body born of the experience [of meditative concentration] (the Wei translation says: "the mind-made body born of the attainment of the bliss of samādhi";
the Tang translation says: "the mind-formed body entering the bliss of samādhi"). The mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas (the Wei translation says:

"the mind-made body that realizes the characteristics of all dharmas as they truly are"). The mind-made body born of spontaneous manifestation according to its kind, which is without effortful activity (both translations agree).
Regarding "the practice of non-action": the practitioner thoroughly understands the characteristics of progressive advancement through the stages, beginning from the first bhūmi.

They attain the three bodies (the Wei translation states: "The bodhisattva, from the first bhūmi, practices according to reality and attains the characteristics of the realized wisdom of the progressively higher stages.
The Tang translation states: "All practitioners, having entered the first bhūmi, gradually realize and attain [these stages]").
The Commentary states: "The three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) are accomplished through the three similar contemplations (*samādhi*).

*Samādhi* is translated here as 'equipoise' (*samādhāna*) and also as 'right concentration. It takes the mental factor of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) among the five object-specific mental factors as its essence.
Its nature is to cause the mind to focus intently on the object of contemplation without distraction; its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom. Therefore, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*..."

It is said: All sentient beings are fully endowed with the three concentrations (*samādhi*). If one focuses single-mindedly on the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), it is called the superior concentration.
If one focuses single-mindedly on the four dhyānas, it is called the middling concentration. If one focuses single-mindedly on worldly affairs, it is called the inferior concentration.
"Bliss" (*sukha*) refers to the supramundane bliss of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). "Right reception" (*samyaksamāpatti*) means not receiving any worldly sensations; that is to say—
The Wei dynasty translation renders *samāpatti* as "attainment" (*dengzhi*). Question: *Samāpatti* is what the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* calls *samāpatti*;
since it takes the arising of illusions as its practice, it should properly belong to the contemplation of the provisional (*jia guan*).

Why, then, is it explained here by means of "right reception" (*zhengshou*)? Answer: Precisely because it does not receive any sensations, it is able to give rise to all manner of illusions, just like clarity.
A mirror does not "accept" various images; therefore, it is able to manifest them. An empty valley does not "accept" various echoes; therefore, it is able to respond to them.
"Non-acceptance" refers to the essential nature of these things, while "arising as an illusion" refers to their functional activity. This refers to the Body Born of the Will in the Bliss of Samādhi.

It subsumes the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], extends from the stage of insight (darśana-bhūmi) upward, specifically includes the ten abodes (bhūmis), and encompasses the first stage of faith (ādikṣānti) in the Perfect Teaching—all of which are capable of attaining this.

If this were according to the *Zang* (Tripitaka) or *Tong* (Shared) teachings, it would already mean that the contemplation of true emptiness has been perfected. However, since we are now speaking in terms of the Perfect Path (*yuan dao*), it is said to be accomplished through the contemplation of semblance emptiness.
As for "awakening to the nature of the self-nature of dharmas," this refers to knowing their various distinct natures and characteristics.

This is common to the provisional emergence (*chujia*), the distinct stage of the ten practices (*shixing*), and the perfect stage of the eight stages of faith (*baxin*), all of which are able to attain it. If, however, one considers the Shared and Distinct [teachings], [the attainment] differs accordingly.

This refers to the completion of the contemplation of provisional reality through illusion; however, as this is discussed here in terms of the Perfect Path (*yuan dao*), it is called the "simulative contemplation of provisional reality.
Regarding the phrase "of the same kind, co-arising, without active agency": all bodily forms manifest simultaneously and universally, yet there is no deliberate activity.

Both the separate ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) and the Perfect ten stages of Faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are capable of attaining this. Because the Dharma-body has not yet been realized, it is still termed "mind-born" (*manomaya*).

Therefore, it is merely called "similar Middle Way. From the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), one practices according to reality and progresses through successive stages until one is finally able to attain it—what is known as penetrating into the Perfect [Teaching]. △ Second, the explanation of its characteristics.
Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body born of the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi? It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages.

Because of the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi, one dwells in the tranquility of the various manifestations of one's own mind; the waves arising from the ocean of the mind—the marks of consciousness—no longer arise.

One realizes that the nature of the objects manifested by one's own mind is neither existent nor non-existent. (The Tang translation states: "It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages. Entering into...")

In samādhi, one is free from various mental states; it is tranquil and unmoving. The waves of evolving consciousness do not arise in the ocean of the mind. One realizes that objects are manifestations of the mind and that they are all non-existent.
This is called the "mind-made body born of the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi."

The Commentary states: The third is the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*), who enter the *ānantarya-samādhi*. The fourth is the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), where they realize supramundane wisdom.

The fifth is the stage of refinement (*tanu-bhūmi*), wherein they contemplate the Truth through repeated reflection to sever the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), causing them to gradually thin out;

in all these stages, they are able to realize that phenomena are themselves emptiness, and thus the waves of consciousness do not arise, as they dwell securely in the bliss of supramundane meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas? It refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), wherein one observes and realizes that all phenomena, such as illusions and the like, are entirely non-existent.

Thereupon, the body and mind undergo a transformation, and one attains the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) as well as other gateways of samādhi, along with immeasurable marks, powers, masteries, and clarities (the second version says "supernatural powers"). Like the adornment of exquisite flowers, it is swift.

As one wishes. Like a phantom, a dream, the moon in water, or a reflection in a mirror; it is neither the creator nor the created, yet it appears as if created and created from. (The Wei translation says:
"It is not produced by the four great elements, yet resembles the characteristics of the four great elements. All forms are fully endowed with various limbs and ornaments.
Entering into the great assemblies of all Buddha-fields because one has thoroughly penetrated the nature of phenomena (in the Tang translation:
"comprehending the nature of all dharmas"), this is called the mind-made body that awakens to the self-nature of phenomena.

The Commentary states: "In the eighth Pratyekabuddha stage, even if one has completely severed the afflictions and further severed the residual habits (*vāsanā*), one is thus able to enter from emptiness into the provisional (*saṃvṛti*) through various samādhi-gates such as 'like an illusion,' manifesting immeasurable transformations and universally entering Buddha-fields.

This is said in reference to those of dull faculties who are received [into the Bodhisattva path] at the eighth stage. As for those of sharp faculties, this should also apply to the fifth, sixth, or seventh stages.
It can be attained, Mahāmati.
What is the body born of mental construction (*manomaya-kāya*), which arises simultaneously with its class and is free from effort?

It refers to the realization of all Buddha-dharmas and the characteristic of the bliss of self-attained realization (the Tang translation says: "it means thoroughly comprehending the characteristics of the dharmas realized by the Buddhas themselves"). This is called the "class."
"Similar to the spontaneously born, effortless mental body.

The commentary states: "The reason for not specifying which stage [of the path] it belongs to is that it refers to those who, from the eighth stage onward, enter the distinct direction toward perfect faith and practice Madhyamaka.
Although they have not yet personally realized the noble wisdom of self-awareness (*pratyātmāryajñāna*), they are already able to awaken to all Buddha-dharmas."

This is because they take as their object the marks of bliss attained through self-realization. This concludes the second section, the explanation of the characteristics. △ Third, the concluding verse:
"Mahāmati, you should observe, realize, and train yourself in those three types of bodily characteristics. At that time, the World-Honored One—
Wishing to restate this meaning, he spoke these verses: "My vehicle is not the Great Vehicle" (The Wei translation says: "My vehicle is not the Great Vehicle";
the Tang translation says: "My Great Vehicle is not a vehicle"). It is neither speech nor letters; it is neither truth nor liberation;
it is not a non-existent realm (the Tang translation says: "nor is it a signless realm"). Yet, one rides upon the Mahāyāna. Three.
"Mañjuśrī is sovereign; the various bodies born of mind are adorned with the flowers of mastery.
The Commentary states: "The meaning of this verse is to reveal that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is fundamentally not the three kinds of bodies born of mind;

rather, these three kinds of bodies born of mind are all emanations flowing forth from the Dharma-body. The first phrase should follow the two translations [of the *Ratnagotravibhāga*], which are complete.
The Sūtra states: "My Mahāyāna is not Mahāyāna; it is neither spoken by sound, nor is it composed of letters.
It is not the Four Truths, the Three Truths, the Two Truths, or the One Truth. It is not liberation, nor is it the realm of signlessness or non-existence.
Therefore, it cannot be called the three kinds of mind-born bodies (*manomayakāya*). However, if a practitioner is able to mount [it]..."
Within the Mahāyāna, upon entering samādhi and attaining mastery, the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) are spontaneously and first accomplished;
thereafter, one realizes great bodhi. This is like a tree producing fruit, which is first adorned by flowers.
The eighteenth section on the Mind-made Bodies is concluded. The nineteenth section: The Five Acts of Immediate Retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*).
The section has three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the granting of permission to teach; third, the actual exposition. Now, the first part:
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, if a man or a woman commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, they do not enter the Avīci Hell. World-Honored One, how is it that a man..."

If a woman commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, she does not enter the Avīci Hell (the Wei translation says "enters the Uninterrupted," while the Tang translation says "falls into the Avīci Hell").

The Commentary states: When the five heinous offenses (*pañcānantarya*) are discussed in terms of worldly affairs, they are definitively followed by the *anantarya* (immediate) retribution; thus they are called the "five immediate karmas.
When the five heinous offenses are discussed in terms of contemplating the mind, they are definitively able to lead one to immediately realize and enter the Buddha-dharma;
thus they are also called the "five immediate karmas. In one case, one falls into hell; in the other, one does not fall into hell. Therefore, Mahāmati intends to ask about both simultaneously. △
Second, the granting of the teaching. The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well. I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction."
III. The Correct Exposition has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, a general indication of the five names;
second, an explanation based on the contemplation of the mind; third, an explanation based on worldly affairs. △ Now, the first section.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "What are the five deeds of immediate retribution? They are: killing one's father, killing one's mother, harming an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha (alternatively:
destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha), and with an evil mind drawing blood from the body of a Buddha."
△ Second, the explanation by way of contemplating the mind: "Mahāmati, what is the mother of sentient beings?
It is craving for further rebirth, accompanied by greed and delight; it is established as the condition, like a mother.

Ignorance is the father, which gives rise to the sense bases. (The Tang translation states: "It refers to the craving that draws forth the body, accompanied by greed and delight, like a mother’s nurturing. Ignorance is the father, which produces the sense bases.
The village (in the Tang translation it says: "What is the father? It is ignorance, because it causes one to be born within the village of the six sense bases").
To sever these two roots is called "killing one's father and mother."
The Commentary states: Among the twelve links of dependent origination, the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is associated with greed and delight; because it can moisten rebirth, it is called the "mother.

The link of ignorance (*avidyā*) is able to initiate karma; therefore, it is called the "father. To sever these two delusions—the one that initiates karma and the one that moistens rebirth—is termed "killing father and mother.
By doing so, one attains the state of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) and realizes the fruits of the Three Vehicles.

Those latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) do not manifest, just as the poison of a rat manifests [after a long time]. (The Wei translation says: "It means that the latent proclivities are like the manifestation of rat-poison.
The Tang translation says: "It means that the latent tendencies are the enemy, like the manifestation of rat-poison. Having completely severed them—(the Wei translation says:
"Uprooting the roots of the enemy-like proclivities so they do not arise again")—this is called "harming an Arhat."

The Commentary states: Since the subsequent text regards the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as the Buddha through the principle of truth (*satya*), it now directly uses the mental factor of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) as a metaphor for the Arhat.
That which is not manifest is precisely the latent tendency. Uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are neither called "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) nor "latent tendencies.
Seeds that are contaminated wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) or non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) are merely called "coarseness," but are not called "latent tendencies."
The seeds of the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*) are also termed "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) and "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*).

What is now referred to as the "various proclivities" (*paryavasthāna-anuśaya*) specifically indicates the seeds of the unwholesome and obscured mental factors (*caitasika*). Regarding the phrase "the poison of a rat erupts":
when a rat bites a person, although the wound has already healed, its poison will erupt upon encountering a thunderclap. [This applies to] the various [afflictions] of sentient beings...
The seed is likewise: when it has not yet encountered conditions, it cannot be perceived; once it encounters conditions, it immediately sprouts.
Therefore, when one cuts it off at that moment, it is called "observing the mind and slaying an arhat."

What is the schism of the Saṃgha? It refers to the various aggregates (*skandha*) characterized by distinct natures (the Wei translation says: "the five aggregates have distinct natures"; the Tang translation says: "the various *skandhas* have distinct natures").
To completely sever that which has been combined and accumulated is called the schism of the Saṃgha.
The Commentary states: "Saṃgha" is named the "harmonious assembly" because those of different surnames dwell together without discord or contention.

By contemplating how the five aggregates (skandhas) of the mind, despite their differing characteristics, harmoniously combine to form a conventional designation of "self," one destroys this attachment to a self;
therefore, it is called "destroying the harmonious Saṃgha."

Mahāmati, because they do not realize that the seven bodies of consciousness—which are the manifestations of their own minds as external self-characteristics and common characteristics—are merely the measure of what appears from one's own mind (the Wei translation says:
"that is to say, seeing external characteristics of one's own mind through self-characteristics and common characteristics; the eight bodies of consciousness"; the Tang translation says:

"that is to say, the eight bodies of consciousness falsely give rise to conceptualization, seeing external to one's own mind self-characteristics and common characteristics"), they harbor impure notions regarding the three gates of liberation and the outflow-free state. (The Tang translation says: "impure...")

To ultimately sever those seven types of consciousness (the Buddha [in the Wei translation says "eight types of consciousness," and in the Tang translation says "the Buddha of the eight-consciousness-body"]) with the mind is called shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind.

The Commentary states: "Buddha" means awakening (*buddha*). "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) means discerning and distinguishing. Since all eight consciousnesses take discerning and distinguishing as their functional characteristic (*ākāra*), they are called "Buddha.
The first seven [consciousnesses] act as the perfuming agents (*vāsaka*), while the eighth acts as the object of perfuming (*vāsya*).
The first seven are that which is supported, while the eighth is the supporter. The first seven are the dependent, while the eighth is the basis. The first seven...

Manifest activity is that which is produced. Among the eight [consciousnesses], the seeds are the producers. All phenomena, whether characterized by their own-nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) or common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), are fundamentally manifestations of mind alone;
there are no phenomena external to the mind. The first seven [consciousnesses] are non-awakened, falsely giving rise to the two attachments to self and phenomena.

The seeds perfumed by the two types of grasping are stored within the eighth consciousness; as they again give rise to the active manifestations of the two types of grasping, they defile and pollute it, and are therefore called "blood.
When the blood of the first seven [consciousnesses] flows out, the blood of the eighth is likewise released.
Regarding the three gates of liberation: first, all is empty; the ten realms are all empty. Second, all is signless;
the ten realms are all signless. Third, all is wishless; the ten realms are all wishless.
Because its nature transcends the two extremes, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Because there is nothing it does not destroy, it is called "evil thought. This is the sublime contemplation.

Investigating the mental complex associated with wisdom, it can cause the seventh and the first five consciousnesses to permanently sever their active manifestation (*samudācāra*), and it can cause the eighth consciousness to permanently sever its seeds (*bīja*).
Therefore, it is said that this Buddha-seed severs those seven kinds of consciousness.
If a man or a woman commits these acts of immediate retribution, they are called the five *ānantarya* offenses;

they are also called the "equalities of immediacy" (the Wei translation says: "These are called the five kinds of internal *ānantarya* offenses. If a good son or a good daughter commits these acts of immediacy...").
It is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) because it refers to the realization of the Dharma as it truly is. [The Tang translation states: "These are the five internal *ānantaryas*.
If there is one who acts [thus], they shall immediately realize and manifest the true Dharma."
The Commentary states: This is explained in terms of the contemplation of the mind; therefore, it is called "internal," not because it refers to being within the physical body.
Entering the *anantara-samādhi*, one realizes *tathatā* without emerging from contemplation; there is nothing whatsoever that can create an interval between them.

Because the subject that realizes and the object realized are both equally equal, it is also termed "the equality of the immediate" (*anantarya*). The second section, explaining in terms of the contemplation of the mind, is concluded.
△ Third, the explanation by way of worldly affairs.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are external *ānantarya* [sins of immediate retribution]; I shall now expound them.
Having heard this meaning, you and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will not fall into delusion in future ages. What are the five *ānantarya*? They are as previously stated...
It speaks of the "uninterrupted" (ānantarya). [The Wei translation says: "This refers to killing one's father, mother, or an Arhat; causing a schism in the Saṃgha;

shedding the blood of a Buddha. The Tang translation says: "This refers to the uninterrupted [sins] taught in other teachings. If one commits these acts, one will not attain the dharma of "uninterrupted realization" (ānantarya-abhisamaya) regarding each of the three liberations.
[The Tang translation says: "If one does so, one cannot realize them through direct manifestation within the three liberations."]
The Commentary states: It is explained in terms of worldly affairs, and is therefore called "external"; it does not mean that they exist outside of the mind.

Among all offenses, these five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) are the most grave; even if one performs repentance through the realization of non-arising by grasping at signs, one can only transform the heavy into the light.
However, in the present life, one is certainly unable to enter the *ānantarya-samādhi* and realize the three liberations (*vimokṣa*).

Apart from this, there are other manifestations of transformative power that appear as the *ānantarya* [samādhi]—namely, the transformative power of śrāvakas, the transformative power of bodhisattvas, and the transformative power of Tathāgatas.
These are employed to remove the doubts and remorse of others who have committed the *ānantarya* sins, and to provide exhortation.
Because of their resolve, they manifest through supernatural power and transformation as those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*). (The Tang translation states:

"Except for the Tathāgatas, the great Bodhisattvas, and the great Śrāvakas, when one sees someone committing an immediate transgression, in order to exhort them and cause them to reform, they employ the power of supernormal faculties to manifest as if they were doing the same.
That person then immediately repents and eliminates [the karma], realizing liberation. All of these are manifested transformations; they are not [actual acts]. )
[This refers to] "actually committing [the act].
The Commentary states: This explains away a doubt. It asks: For instance, when the Buddha was in the world, Mañjuśrī wielded a sword to harm him, and Aṅgulimāla made a flower crown from fingers;
were these not also grave offenses of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)? Why, then, did they manifestly realize liberation?
Therefore, the present commentary explains: this is intended to exhort those who have actually committed sins to eliminate their doubts and repent;
it is a manifested transformation for that purpose, and does not mean that one who has actually committed a heinous crime can attain liberation in the present body.
There is no one who, by performing acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), fails to attain immediate realization (*ānantarya-samāpatti*). [The Wei translation says:

"If one commits the five grave offenses of immediate retribution, one will ultimately be unable to realize entry into the factors of the Path. The Tang translation says: "If there are those who actually commit the deeds of immediate retribution, they shall never attain liberation in their present body.

This is except for those who awaken to the fact that all is the manifestation of their own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*) and thereby abandon the false imaginings regarding the body and material wealth.

They are free from the grasping of "self" and "what belongs to self. (The Tang translation states: "Except for that which is manifested by one's own mind—namely, the body, requisites, and dwelling place—they are free from the views of conceptual attachment to 'self' and 'what belongs to self.
Or, at times, they encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and are liberated from the deluded thoughts that cause the continuity of other realms of existence.
(The Wei translation states: "Throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, having encountered a spiritual friend, they leave behind [the cycle] within the bodies of other paths.")

The fault of seeing one’s own mind as false and illusory. ○ The Tang translation says: "Or, in a future life or another place, one may encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and, free from the faults of conceptual discrimination, finally realize liberation."

The Commentary states: This clarifies that while ordinary, ignorant people truly commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) of the mundane world and will inevitably fall into the Avīci Hell, they will never, in their present bodies, realize the *ānantarya-samādhi*.

Alternatively, if such a person has planted the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna in past lives, although they are currently deluded and commit the five heinous crimes, they immediately awaken to the realization that both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*) are manifestations of mind alone, and are thus free from the notion of self.

Regarding the view of grasping at a self: furthermore, by encountering a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), just as King Ajātaśatru saw the Buddha, repented, and attained rootless faith (amūlakā śraddhā), he was then able to transform his body and immediately realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). This concludes the initial long passage.
△ Second, the verses in praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Craving is called the mother; ignorance is the father.
The consciousness that perceives objects is the Buddha; the various latent tendencies are the Arhats. The accumulation of the aggregates is called the Sangha; the uninterrupted..."
They are severed in succession; that is to say, these five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) do not lead to entry into the Avīci Hell.
The Commentary states: This is merely a reiterative verse (*geya*) explaining the contemplation of the mind. The nineteenth section, the Gate of the Five Immediate Transgressions, is concluded.
○ Section Twenty: The Gate of the Buddha’s Knowledge and Awakening. Part Two. First, the explicit elucidation of the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening;
second, the incidental explanation of the intentional terminology (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*). Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the question; second, the answer. △ Now, the first.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the enlightened awareness of the Buddhas” (the Wei translation says:
“the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s enlightened awareness”; the Tang translation says: “the essence-nature of all Buddhas”). World-Honored One, what is this enlightened awareness of the Buddhas?
△ Second, the answer.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "To realize the selflessness of persons and phenomena, to fully understand the two obstacles, to be free from the two kinds of death, and to sever the two afflictions—this is called the awakening of a Buddha.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who attain this Dharma are also called Buddhas."
For these reasons, I teach the One Vehicle. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, Severing the two obstacles and the afflictions, Forever departing from the two kinds of death— This is called the awakening of a Buddha."
The Commentary states: The grasping at a self of persons (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*) obstructs Great Nirvāṇa; the grasping at a self of phenomena (*dharma-ātma-grāha*) obstructs Great Bodhi.

Therefore, by awakening to the two kinds of selflessness, one thoroughly understands the two obstructions. The afflictions of the four abodes (*catur-vihāra-kleśa*) induce birth-and-death with distinct segments (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*);

the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*) induces birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-saṃsāra*). Thus, one departs from the two types of death by severing these two afflictions. [This applies to those of] dull faculties.

Such a person first contemplates the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), realizes the obstacles to *nirvāṇa*, severs the afflictions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsana-kleśa*), and becomes free from birth-and-death in segmented portions (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*);

therefore, they are called Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. When the wine of samādhi has been digested, they enter again into the supramundane, unsurpassed realm of outflow (*anāsrava-dhātu*), fulfill all requisites, and are likewise named Buddhas. The verse that follows may be understood accordingly.

The first section, which correctly clarifies the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening, is concluded. The second section, which additionally explains the intentional terminology, has two parts: first, the explanation of the meaning of "one Buddha";

second, the explanation of the meaning of "not speaking. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, the posing of the question; second, the answer and explanation. Now, the first [part]: the posing of the question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason did the World-Honored One proclaim these words in the midst of the great assembly:
'I am all the Buddhas of the past,' and [described] various births, such as:
'At that time I was the Cakravartin King Mandhātṛ' (both versions say King Mūrdhaja), the six-tusked great elephant, and the parrot Śuka?"
Śakra Devānām Indra (translated in Tang as Diśì). The *Sūtra on the Hundred Thousand Births* speaks of such figures as the Rishi Sunetra and others.
The Commentary states: Since these are past Buddhas, they should not undergo further various births.
Yet, since the *Jātaka-sūtras* describe hundreds of thousands of distinct births, they cannot be identical to those past Buddhas.
Therefore, he asks about it. Part Two: The Response and Explanation, in three sections. First, the presentation of the fourfold equality; second, the explanation of the fourfold equality;
third, the concluding verse. Now, the first section.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Because of four kinds of equality (the Wei translation says: 'relying on four kinds of equality'; the Tang translation says:
'relying on the secret intention of the four equalities'), the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words in the midst of the great assembly:
'At that time, I was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Buddha. What are the four equalities?"

That is to say: equality of letters, equality of speech, equality of dharmas, and equality of bodies (based on the two translations and the subsequent commentary, these should all precede the dharmas).
These are called the four equalities. Because of these four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words amidst the great assembly:
The Commentary states: This merely explains that "I" refers to the Buddhas of the past; it is a statement of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*).
Thus, one should know that the hundreds of thousands of *jātaka* tales are all manifestations produced through the power of vows, and are not themselves statements of intentional meaning.
K Krakucchanda is translated as "that which should be severed," and is also translated as "activity"; he is the first Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. Kanakamuni is translated as... [text continues]
Kanakamuni (Jinji) is also translated as "Golden Immortal" (Jinxian); he is the second Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. Kāśyapa is translated as "Drinking Light" (Yinguang);
he is the third Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. △ Second, the explanation of the four kinds of equality.
What is the equality of syllables? If the syllable that designates me as a Buddha also designates all Buddhas, then the intrinsic nature of those syllables is without distinction.
(The Tang translation says: "That is to say, my name is Buddha, and all Tathāgatas are also named Buddha.")

The names of the Buddhas are without distinction; thus their names are equal. What is meant by equality of speech? It refers to the manifestation of sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice sounds in my own speech.
Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise manifest these sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice sounds;
they neither increase nor decrease, and there is no difference between them, such as the *kalaviṅka* Brahma-voice.
The nature of sound (śabda-svabhāva). [The Tang translation says: "I produce sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds; all Tathāgatas also produce these sounds.
The nature of the Brahma-sound of the kalaviṅka bird neither increases nor decreases, and there is no distinction between them.
This is called equality of speech. What is equality of body? It means that my Dharma-body and form-body, including their marks and signs, are no different from those of all Buddhas.

They are distinct. Excluding those instances where various distinct physical bodies are manifested in order to discipline sentient beings across their various different realms of existence—these are called the distinctions of body and so forth.
What are the distinctions of dharma? This refers to myself and those Buddhas attaining the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
briefly stated, these are the unobstructed wisdoms of the Buddha-dharmas.
The Commentary states: Regarding the sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds, there are eight grammatical transformations (*vibhakti*) in the sounds of the Western Regions:

first, the substance (*svabhāva*); second, the action (*karman*); third, the agent (*kartṛ*); fourth, the purpose (*sampradāna*); fifth, the source (*apādāna*); sixth, the possession (*sambandha*); seventh, the location (*adhikaraṇa*); and eighth, the vocative (*āmantraṇa*). The Buddha, regarding these eight types of transformed sounds—
Each possesses eight qualities: first, harmony; second, softness; third, clarity; fourth, ease of understanding;
fifth, absence of error; sixth, absence of feebleness; seventh, vastness; and eighth, profundity. Thus, there are sixty-four characteristics, eight for each.
*Kalaviṅka* is translated here as "the bird of wondrous voice. Among humans, devas, and others, no voice can equal its. Therefore...
This is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s voice; the rest may be understood accordingly. △ Third, the concluding verse:
These are called the four immeasurables. Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words amidst the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni...
"The Anāgāmin is I. By means of these four kinds [of statements], I have taught for the sake of my disciples, the sons of the Buddha.

This concludes the first explanation of the meaning of "one Buddha. Second, the explanation of the meaning of "not speaking" has two parts: first, the posing of the question; second, the answer and explanation.
△ First: Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has said:

'From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, in the interval between them, I have not uttered even a single syllable, nor have I [taught anything] in the past.'"
"What should be said has been said; what is not said is not the word of the Buddha. "World-Honored One, for what reason does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha say:
'What is not said is not the word of the Buddha'? (The Wei translation says: "Based on what meaning is such a statement made—that the Buddha's words are not words"?
The Tang translation says: "Based on what underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) is such a statement made?")
II. The Response and Explanation, in three parts: first, the presentation of the two dharmas; second, the explanation of the two dharmas; third, the concluding verse. △ Now, the first:
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "It is because of two dharmas (the Tang translation says: 'by relying on two secret dharmas') that I speak in this manner."
What are the two dharmas? They are the dharma of self-attainment (in the Tang translation: the dharma of self-realization) and the primordially abiding dharma.
These are called the two dharmas. It is because of these two dharmas that I speak in this way.
△ Second, the explanation of the two dharmas.
What is the dharma of self-attainment through conditions? It is that whatever has been attained by those Tathāgatas, I too have attained; it is without increase and without decrease.
Based on the ultimate realm of the Dharma realized by oneself, one is free from the conceptualization of verbal expression and free from the two paths of letters (the Chinese translation states:

"That which all Buddhas have realized, I too have realized equally—neither increasing nor decreasing; it is the domain of realized wisdom, free from the marks of verbal expression, free from the marks of discrimination, and free from the marks of names").
The Commentary states: This clarifies that the wisdom which realizes cannot be expressed in words. Regarding the two aspects of "letters" (*akṣara*), these are the signifier and the signified;
as previously explained, both speech and that which is spoken are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
What is the primordially abiding dharma (*pūrvasthita-dharma*)? It refers to the ancient path of the sages, such as the nature of gold and silver. The *dharmadhātu* is eternally abiding;

whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the *dharmadhātu* remains eternally abiding. (The Tang translation states: "It refers to the original nature of dharmas, like gold remaining within its ore.
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the abiding of dharmas, their station, the *dharmadhātu*, and the *dharmatā* are all entirely [present].")
It is eternally abiding, like the path leading to that city. For example, it is as if a man traveling through a vast wilderness sees a level, direct road leading toward an ancient city;
he then follows it into the city and experiences bliss according to his wishes. (The Tang translation says: "For example, it is as if there were a person traveling through a vast wilderness...")
Seeing an old, level path leading toward an ancient city, they immediately followed it in and stayed there to enjoy themselves.
"Mahāmati, what do you think? Did they create that road and the various pleasures within the city? He replied, "No.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "I and all the Buddhas of the past abide eternally in the *dharmadhātu*. (The Tang translation says: "The *tathatā* realized is eternal.")
The abiding in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is likewise so. Therefore it is said:
"From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I entered parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken therein; nor has anything been spoken, nor will anything be spoken."

The Commentary states: This clarifies that the principle realized cannot be expressed in words. Nevertheless, because of the four *siddhāntas*, both the means of realization and the object realized can also be explained;
yet such explanation is itself non-explanation. It is not that silence and the binding of the tongue constitute non-explanation.
Those who are hindered by words and stuck on phrases—how could they not reflect deeply upon this? The two explanations of the two dharmas are concluded.
△ Third, the summary verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"From the night I attained enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa, during the interval between these two, I have said nothing at all. Because the Dharma realized by myself abides, I..."
He spoke thus: (The Tang translation says: "Because one personally realizes the primordially abiding Dharma, he thus utters this esoteric word.
That Buddha and I are entirely without distinction.
The twentieth section, "The Buddha’s Door of Knowledge and Awakening," is concluded. ○ The twenty-first section, "The Door of Transcending Existence and Non-existence," has three parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the granting of the teaching; third, the formal exposition. △ Now, the first part.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the World-Honored One: "I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena,
so that I and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may be free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
△ Second, the promise to teach.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it. I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
III. The Correct Exposition has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the explicit clarification of the two views;
second, a further refutation of the view of non-existence. △ Now, the first section.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "This world has two kinds of dependence, namely dependence on existence and dependence on non-existence.

(The Tang translation states: 'Sentient beings in the world mostly fall into two views, namely the view of existence and the view of non-existence. They fall into the views of intrinsic nature and the absence of intrinsic nature, and thus do not depart from the appearance of departure.

(The Wei translation states: 'Because they see the existence of all dharmas and the non-existence of all dharmas, these are not ultimate dharmas, yet they give rise to the notion that they are ultimate. "
Mahāmati, what is meant by the world depending on existence? It means that the world arises from causes and conditions;

it is not non-existent. It arises from existence, not from non-existence. (The Tang translation says: "It means that all phenomena arise from truly existent causes and conditions; they are not non-truly existent.")
"Mahāmati, truly existent dharmas arise from causes and conditions; it is not that non-existent things arise.
Those who speak in such a manner are asserting that the world is without cause."
The Commentary states: All dharmas are manifested solely by the mind; therefore, they are neither existent nor non-existent, and are free from false views.
Sentient beings in the world do not realize that all is but mind, and thus they sometimes fall into the view of existence, reckoning that all dharmas possess an intrinsic nature.

Alternatively, one may fall into the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*), whereby one calculates that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). First, to explain those who fall into the view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*):

they maintain that there exist real causes for the production of all phenomena, such as a supreme principle (*pradhāna*), a sovereign lord (*īśvara*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), time (*kāla*), space (*dik*), or a self (*ātman*).
It is not that causes do not exist; truly, all phenomena arise from those causes. It is not that phenomena do not exist.
Now, the *puruṣa* (primordial spirit) and so forth are fundamentally not the causes of phenomena, yet they are falsely conceived as such; thus, one is ignorant of the true cause, which is "mind-only.
Furthermore, worldly phenomena are fundamentally not effects produced by the *puruṣa* and so forth, yet they are falsely conceived as arising from those causes.
Thus, they are ignorant of the illusory fruits that arise solely from the mind. Therefore, they categorically declare: "This explains that the world is without cause.
How could they know that all phenomena of worldly suffering and pleasure have as their cause the good and evil within one's own mind?

Mahāmati, what is meant by the worldly reliance on non-existence? It refers to having first experienced the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, and subsequently engaging in conceptual construction and attachment regarding whether that nature of greed, hatred, and delusion exists or does not exist.
(The Tang translation states: "What is the view of non-existence? It means knowing that one has already experienced greed, anger, and delusion...")

Yet they falsely calculate that [things] do not exist. Mahāmati, if one does not grasp at the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is because the characteristics of intrinsic nature are quiescent.
(The Wei translation says: "If there are people who speak thus: 'All dharmas do not exist, because the characteristics of all things are not perceived. The Tang translation says:
"And as for their conceptualization of the characteristic of existence, they do not accept the existence of dharmas. This refers to the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
Awakening does not grasp at the nature of greed, anger, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent. (The Wei translation says:
"If there is another person who says that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have no greed, no anger, and no delusion, yet further says they previously existed. The Tang translation says:
"Furthermore, there are those who know that all Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas possess the nature of no greed, anger, and delusion, yet reckon it to be non-existent.")
The Commentary states: Those who fall into the view of non-existence are unable to permanently sever the roots of all afflictions and karmic actions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
They merely maintain that when the active manifestations of greed and so forth cease without interval, their nature is itself non-existent.

Furthermore, although they falsely conceptualize the practice of greed and so forth, if they do not grasp at the existence of a nature, then the characteristics of that nature will naturally become quiescent. Moreover, they falsely claim:
The Buddhas and those of the Two Vehicles likewise do not grasp the nature of greed, anger, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent;

what greed, anger, and delusion is there, then, that could be severed? This is precisely the false meditation of the degenerate age, which erroneously interprets the principle that "the sought-after offense is ultimately unobtainable.
Consequently, they fall into the view of nihilistic emptiness (*mithyā-śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), falsely claiming to sit and sever both extremes of existence and non-existence. Not so.
Knowing that he speaks emptiness with his mouth while practicing existence in his conduct, he will surely fall together with Shanxing.
This concludes the initial clarification of the two views. △ Second, further refuting the view of non-existence.

“Mahāmati, what herein is meant by ‘one who destroys’? Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, if one grasps at the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, and subsequently no longer grasps at them” (the Tang translation says:

“if there is the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, and later one grasps at their non-existence, this is called a destroyer”), the Buddha told Mahāmati, “Excellent, excellent! You understand it thus. Mahāmati, it is not only greed...”
One who destroys the nature or non-nature of hatred and delusion is also a destroyer of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas (the Tang translation reads:
"is also a destroyer of the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas"). Why is this? It is because neither the internal nor the external can be apprehended.
Because the nature of the afflictions is neither different nor non-different. (The Tang translation says: "For what reason? Because the afflictions cannot be apprehended internally or externally;
their essential nature is neither different nor non-different. Mahāmati, greed, anger, and delusion cannot be apprehended whether internally or externally.
Because the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is without body and without grasping (the Tang translation says:

because they lack intrinsic nature and are not graspable), the Buddha, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are not destroyers [of these states]. This is because the Buddha, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are by their very nature liberated;
for both bondage and the cause of bondage are without intrinsic nature (the Tang translation says: śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas are liberated by their original nature).
Because there is neither that which binds nor the cause of binding. Mahāmati, if there were one who is bound, there would necessarily be binding;
for that is the cause of binding. (The Tang translation states: "If there were that which binds and the cause of binding, then there would be that which is bound.
Mahāmati, to speak in this manner of destruction is called the characteristic of non-existence. (The Tang translation states: "To speak thus is called a destroyer; this is non-existence.")

"Mahāmati, for this reason I say: it would be better to hold a view of a person (pudgala-dṛṣṭi) as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness (śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi) based on the overweening pride (adhimāna) of non-existence.
Mahāmati, [this refers to] the overweening pride of non-existence."

Pride is called "destruction. It consists of falling into the hope of views regarding self and common characteristics (the Tang translation says: "falling into the midst of attachment to views of self and commonality").
It is the failure to know that all things are merely manifestations of one's own mind (the Tang translation says: "not realizing that all phenomena are only what is manifested by the mind").

Because of this lack of realization, one perceives external natures as impermanent, undergoing moment-to-moment disintegration (the Tang translation says: "because of not understanding, one sees the existence of external dharmas...").

That impermanence, through its successive differentiations, is the continuous flow and transformation-cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—[the Tang translation says:

"The characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and bases; their continuous circulation, arising and then ceasing"]—which is free from the characteristics of words and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

This is called "that which undergoes destruction" [the Tang translation says: "False discrimination, being free from the characteristics of words, is likewise that which undergoes formation and destruction"].
The Commentary states: Since the two views—existence and non-existence—have already been fully set forth above, he asks which of these two views is capable of destroying all roots of goodness.
Mahāmati, having a profound understanding of the faults of the view of non-existence, answers with certainty; the Buddha likewise confirms this with his seal of approval.
This means that while those [who hold the view of existence] currently manifest the faults of greed, anger, and delusion, they falsely claim that their nature is itself non-existent.
In its essential nature, it is not only a denial that greed, anger, and delusion have any functional activity;
it is also a denial that the Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas attain liberation through their own Dharma. Why is this? Because the nature of the afflictions fundamentally does not exist within.
Nor does it exist externally, for upon investigation, its origin cannot be found. Furthermore, its essential nature is like an illusion, being neither different nor non-different [from that nature].
If one thoroughly realizes that both internally and externally it is unattainable, lacking any essential nature and nothing to be grasped, then one realizes the liberation of self-nature;
there is no binder, nor is there a cause for binding. This is what is called...

Because the Buddha, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas [have transcended these], they are not those who destroy [the bonds]. If those [ordinary beings] manifest the arising of greed, anger, and delusion, then there are clearly those who are bound.
If there are persons who are bound, then there must be that which binds, as well as the causes of bondage.
Furthermore, to falsely claim that [the self] does not exist is like covering one's ears while stealing a bell, or like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail;
is this not a form of destruction? This is called the mark of non-existence into which worldly people fall;

it is even worse than the arising of the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), for the latter has not yet reached the point of repudiating cause and effect or severing the roots of goodness. This is the first instance of the evil grasping of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by those of overweening pride (*abhimāna*).
They nevertheless fall into the hope of perceiving self-characteristics and common characteristics. How could they understand that all phenomena are merely manifestations of mind?

Because they do not understand this, they falsely perceive external natures as momentarily impermanent; they reckon them to be emptiness and reckon them to be free from the marks of words and letters, yet they do not know that what is called "emptiness" and what is called "being free from the marks of words and letters" are both mere false imaginings.
It is merely a conceptual construction. Therefore, although both the views of existence and non-existence are erroneous, the view of emptiness as "nothingness" is particularly toxic;
this is what is called "destruction. The preceding long prose section concludes. II. Verse Summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Existence and non-existence are two extremes;
even the realm of the mind (the 'sphere of activity' according to the Tang translation) is likewise so. By purifying that realm, the mind becomes equal and quiescent.

When the nature of the objective realm is not grasped, it is neither extinguished nor is it non-existent (according to the Tang translation: 'not grasping the realm, neither extinguished nor existent'). Existence..."

All phenomena are entirely suchness (tathatā), like the sphere of experience of the noble ones (*ārya*). [The Chinese translation states: "There is the wondrous substance of true suchness, as practiced by the various sages.
Without seeds yet there is arising; having arisen, they again cease. Conditioned by causes and conditions, they exist and do not exist; they do not abide within my teaching.
They are neither non-Buddhists nor Buddhas; they are neither I nor others. They arise through the gathering of causes and conditions. [The Chinese translation states: "They are able to..."]

If existence is established through conditions, how can it be non-existent? Who assembles the causes and conditions for existence (the Tang translation asks: "Who establishes existence by means of conditions") and yet further declares it to be non-existent?
Such views arise from false doctrines; they are mere deluded imaginings of existence and non-existence. If one knows that nothing is produced, [one transcends these extremes].
Nor is there anything to be extinguished. Contemplating this [the world], one sees it is entirely empty and quiescent; one is free from both existence and non-existence. The Commentary states:
The first two lines clarify that the two extremes of existence and non-existence are both objects traversed by the mind; there is no object external to the mind.
The next two lines clarify that by not grasping at objects, one is inherently and originally quiescent. The following four lines...
If one clearly does not grasp [at things], then they are neither subject to extinction nor are they anything at all.
All phenomena are, in their very essence, *tathatā* (suchness), just as it is realized by the noble ones (*ārya*).

The next four lines mean that if one falsely calculates that things arise from non-existence or perish after having existed, or calculates existence and non-existence, none of these are the Buddha-dharma. The next six lines...
The principle of dependent origination is clearly understood as being entirely the manifestation of one's own mind. The Dharma-realm is eternally abiding;
since it cannot be created by Buddhas, non-Buddhists, or any other group, how could one falsely deny it as non-existent?

Moreover, when one observes with discernment that dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature, who is there to accumulate [the causes]? Since there is no accumulator, why further claim it to be non-existent? Next...
The first two lines generally clarify that if one speaks of arising, it is a false view; if one calculates existence or non-existence, it is a deluded thought.

The subsequent four lines conclude by clarifying that since one knows there is no arising, there is likewise no ceasing. Being without arising and without ceasing, its very substance is empty and quiescent.
Because there is no arising, it is free from existence; because there is no ceasing, it is free from non-existence. (20)

The first section, the Gate of Departing from Existence and Non-existence, is concluded. ○ The twenty-second section, the Gate of the Universal Penetration of the School, has three parts: first, the inquiry;
second, the granting of the teaching; third, the formal exposition. △ Now, the first part.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle (zongtongxiang).

If the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle are skillfully distinguished, I and all the bodhisattvas will thoroughly understand these characteristics; having understood them, [we shall attain liberation].”
Having realized these marks, one swiftly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. One does not follow discursive thoughts or the various māras and non-Buddhists (the Wei translation says:
"because one does not fall into any false conceptualizations, observations, or demonic matters"; the Tang translation says:
"one does not fall into any of the various heterodox delusions").
The Commentary states: "The 'Principle' (zong) is the essential framework for spiritual practice. The 'Penetration' (tong) is the correct path from cause to fruition.
Since the Principle Penetration pertains to one's own cultivation and the Teaching Penetration pertains to transforming others, the following text provides answers to both.
△ Second, the granting of permission to proclaim."
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"Yes, I shall receive your instruction."
III. The Correct Exposition has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary.

△ Now, the first part. The Buddha told Mahāmati: “All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two kinds of general characteristics: namely, the penetration of the ultimate principle (zongtong) and the penetration of the teaching (shetong).
(The Wei translation says: “First, the characteristic of establishing the true dharma; second, the characteristic of explaining the establishment of the true dharma.”)
In the Tang language: *Zongqu Faxiang* (The Essential Goal of the Dharma Characteristics). [Regarding] the "Dharma Characteristics of Verbal Expression":

Mahāmati, as for the "penetration of the essential goal" (*zongtong*), it refers to the characteristics of supreme advancement attained through personal realization (*zide shujing zhi xiang*). It is far removed from the delusions of verbal expression and written words.
They proceed toward the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and the stage of self-awakening (*svayambhū-bhūmi*), characterized by their own specific marks (*svalakṣaṇa*).

They remain far removed from all false conceptualizations and perceptions, subduing all external paths and demonic hosts. Taking the path of self-awakening as their object, they radiate brilliant light. (The Tang translation states:

"Free from the discrimination of words, letters, and language, they enter the untainted realm, accomplish the practices of their own stage, transcend all improper thoughts and perceptions, and subdue the demons.")

"O outsider, the arising of the light of wisdom" refers to the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle (*zongtong*). What are the characteristics of the penetration of verbal teaching (*shetong*)?

They refer to the preaching of the various teachings of the ninefold canon, which, through skillful means, accord with sentient beings while remaining free from such dualistic characteristics as difference and non-difference, or existence and non-existence.

One should preach the Dharma as appropriate, so that beings may attain liberation; this is called the characteristic of the penetration of teaching (*deśanā-pratisaṃvid*). Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this.

The Commentary states: Taking one’s own practice as the primary principle, it transcends verbal expression, written characters, and deluded cognition, subdues Māras and externalists, and brings forth the light of self-awakening.
Taking the transformation of others through teaching as its function, there exist the ninefold teachings of the Great and Small Vehicles;

these transcend the four logical extremes, employing skillful means according to individual capacities, administering medicine in accordance with the illness, so that beings may attain liberation. Second, the deficiency...
The first is untenable; therefore, it is cautioned that one ought to practice and study [this]. II. Verse Summary.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The characteristics of the fundamental doctrine and the teaching of the vehicle, The objects of perception, the self-nature, and the teachings— One who clearly perceives and skillfully discriminates these, Does not follow various conceptualizations.
There is no such thing as a truly existent nature, Just as with the delusions of a fool."
Now, as for deluded thought—(the Tang translation says: "as that which is discriminated by the foolish is not the true characteristic")—how does one give rise to deluded thought?
Liberation is the absence of intrinsic nature. (The Tang translation says: "How could they not seek to attain the Dharma of non-existence?
One observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as a continuous succession of arising and ceasing; this increases the two views, leading to inverted ignorance. This is the first [point].
The Truth: Nirvāṇa is the state of being without fault. (In the Tang translation: "Nirvāṇa is free from mind and intellect; this alone is the one true Dharma.
One observes that worldly delusions are like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees. Although there is no greed, anger, or ignorance, in reality there is no person.
From craving arise the aggregates (*skandhas*); all that exists is like an illusion or a dream.

The Commentary states: "The first verse correctly eulogizes both the penetration of the principle (*zongtong*) and the penetration of the teaching (*shuotong*). The subsequent four verses all clarify the intent of these two penetrations.
As for the 'penetration of the principle,' it is simply the thorough realization of the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-pratyakṣa*).

As for the 'penetration of the teaching,' it is simply the instruction and revelation intended to lead others to realize the manifestation of their own minds. As for the deluded commoners who, through false conceptualization, discriminate between existence and non-existence..."
Distinctions such as "different," "simultaneous," or "not simultaneous" have no ultimate reality. Even if one seeks liberation through them, they will ultimately not be the dharma of liberation.

If one fails to realize that all is mind-only and merely observes the continuous succession of the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena, then upon seeing the place of arising, one needlessly increases the view of existence;
and upon seeing the place of cessation, one needlessly increases the view of non-existence. Thus, being inverted, one ultimately possesses no true knowledge.
Yet they do not know that this oneness is the true reality (*tattva*), and that the absence of transgression is itself *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, all worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) belong entirely to delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Greed, anger, and ignorance, as well as the person, appear to exist, but in truth there is no greed, anger, ignorance, or person.

Although it is said that the aggregates (*skandha*) arise from craving, they are merely like illusions and dreams. To awaken to this is what is called the penetration of the fundamental principle (*zong-tong*).
To demonstrate this is what is called the "Expedient Teaching" (deśanā-pratisaṃvid). The twenty-second section, the Gate of the Penetration of the Fundamental Tenets, is concluded.

The twenty-third section, the Gate of the Characteristics of Unreal False Imagination, has three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the granting of the teaching; third, the formal exposition. Now, the first part.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of unreal conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
How does unreal conceptualization arise? What kind of phenomena are called unreal conceptualization?
Within what kind of phenomena does unreal conceptualization occur? (The Tang translation says: "I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of false discrimination. This false...")
Discrimination: how does it arise? From what does it arise? By what cause does it arise? By whom is it produced?
For what reason is it called "false discrimination"?
The Commentary states: "The characteristic of unreal imagination" refers to the characteristic of false discrimination; this is the general question. First, it asks how [this] arises;
second, it asks what kind of dharma is taught as its essence—this corresponds to the phrase "from what does it arise" in the Tang translation;
third, it asks within what dharma it arises—this corresponds to the phrase "by whom and from what" in the Tang translation.
