The Tang translation says: "That which is established by the non-Buddhists. They all lack liberation because of their foolish delusions.

All these foolish non-Buddhists falsely perceive the agent and the acted-upon, and they debate the categories of existence and non-existence. (The Tang translation says: "They all cling to the doctrines of existence and non-existence.")
They possess no liberation at all; the foolish and ignorant delight in false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and do not hear of true wisdom.

Words are the root of the three kinds of suffering (both [versions] state they are the root of the three realms). True reality is the cause for extinguishing suffering. It is like an image in a mirror: although it appears, it does not exist.
Within the mirror of the deluded mind, the ignorant perceive duality. (The Tang translation reads: "Within the mirror of the mind of habitual tendencies, the foolish and ignorant...")
Seeing duality—failing to recognize the mind and its objects—one gives rise to two kinds of false conceptualization. (The Tang translation says:

"Because one does not understand that these are manifestations of Mind-only, one gives rise to dualistic discrimination. When the mind and its objective realms are understood, false conceptualization does not arise. (The Tang translation says: "If one knows that these are merely the mind, discrimination will not arise.
The mind is itself manifold; it is far removed from the characteristics of the signifier and the signified, yet phenomena appear.
There is no manifestation; it is like the false conceptualization of the ignorant (the Tang translation says: "as that which is discriminated by the ignorant, though seen, there is no seeing").

The three realms of existence are merely conceptual construction; external objects do not exist at all. Conceptual construction manifests in various ways, yet the foolish and ignorant cannot comprehend this.
Sūtra after sūtra speaks of conceptual construction, for it never transcends names (the Wei translation says: "various different names"; the Tang translation says: "merely...").
"These are different names; if one is apart from verbal expression, there is also nothing that can be expressed" (the Tang translation says: "their meaning cannot be apprehended").
The commentary states: The final verse clarifies that deluded conceptualization and discrimination possess only names, but have no substantial reality from the beginning.
The remainder may be understood accordingly. This concludes the twenty-eighth section, the Gate of Further Discernment on Nirvāṇa.

Are they different or not different? This is because the Tathāgata intends to manifest the Dharmakāya as being beyond the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).

[Section 4: The Response, in two parts. First, the long prose section; second, the verse summary. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, a general negation of all propositions; second, a specific analysis of their meaning;
third, a concluding response to the question. △ Now, the first.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding such phrases as these, is neither an entity nor a cause.
Why is this? Because both [positions] entail faults. (The Wei translation states:

"The marks of the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—such phrases as these—are neither created phenomena nor uncreated phenomena; they are neither cause nor effect. Why is this? Because...")
Because both extremes involve faults. (The Tang translation states: "The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is not an agent, nor is he a non-agent; he is not an effect, nor is he a cause;

he is not a characteristic, nor is he that which is characterized; he is not speech, nor is he that which is spoken; he is not awakening, nor is he that which is awakened. Why? Because both [extremes] involve faults.)"
II. A detailed analysis of its meaning has five parts: first, an analysis based on causal phenomena; second, an analysis based on the meaning of non-self (*anātman*) and so forth;

third, an analysis based on the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*); fourth, an analysis based on liberation (*vimukti*); and fifth, an analysis based on gnosis (*jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*). △ Now, the first [part].
"Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were a conditioned thing, he would be either created or impermanent. Because he would be impermanent, all conditioned things would be the Tathāgata.
This is something neither I nor the Buddhas would accept. (The Tang translation states: "If the Tathāgata were a product of creation, he would be impermanent;
if he were impermanent, then all created phenomena would be the Tathāgata. (The Wei translation states: "We do not sanction this teaching.")
The Tang translation says: "All are unable to endure or affirm it. If it is not that which is produced, there is nothing to be attained; thus, skillful means are empty, identical to a rabbit's horn.
The son of Pāṇḍu [is so called] because he possesses nothing; (the Tang translation says: "If it is not a created dharma, then it has no essential nature.
The skillful means practiced are entirely empty and useless, identical to a rabbit's horn or a stone woman. It is not a cause of creation.")
Therefore, Mahāmati, if there were no entity and no cause (the Chinese translation says: "if it were neither cause nor effect"), then it would be neither existent nor non-existent.
If it were neither existent nor non-existent, it would transcend the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). These four propositions are merely worldly discourse.
If one transcends the four propositions, one does not fall into the four propositions. Because one does not fall into the four propositions, it is that which is taken up by the wise.
The meaning of the phrases of all Tathāgatas is likewise so; the wise should know this.
The Commentary states: First, it clarifies the faults of being "produced" (*kṛta*) or "unproduced" (*akṛta*); subsequently, it clarifies the principle of being neither cause nor effect.

That which is capable of producing is the cause; that which is produced is the effect. The essence of the effect is termed "phenomenon" (*vastu*); a phenomenon is termed "existence. What exists is impermanent. That which is unproduced is termed "non-existence.
Non-existence is identical to a rabbit's horn or the son of a barren woman. How could the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body be like these?
It is so! Since cultivation arises from the fullness of nature, it is not non-action; since cultivation is fully present within nature, it is not something created.
The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; therefore, the cause is itself no-cause. The fruit of the Mahāyāna is the true reality of all phenomena;
therefore, the fruit is itself no-fruit. Because it is neither cause nor fruit, it is not existent; yet because it is both cause and fruit, it is not... [non-existent].

It is not non-existent, for it does not contradict [existence]. Therefore, it is neither existent nor non-existent. It is not neither-existent-nor-non-existent, for it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
To transcend the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) is called "emergence. To speak by means of the four propositions without falling into error is called "non-falling.
This is the meaning of the phrase regarding the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which those possessed of wisdom should understand. △
Second, it is distinguished according to the meaning of "selflessness" (*anātman*) and so forth.
As I have taught: "All phenomena are selfless. One should know that this meaning is that the very nature of being selfless (*anātmatā*) is selflessness (the Tang translation says:
because there is no nature of self within all phenomena, they are said to be selfless). All phenomena possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). (The Tang translation says...)
It is said: "It is not that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*), like [the case of] oxen and horses.

(The Wei translation says: "All dharmas exist as their own bodies and do not exist as other bodies, just like oxen and horses. Mahāmati, it is, for example, like how what is not an ox does not have the nature of a horse, and what is not a horse does not have the nature of an ox.
(The Tang translation says: "For example, an ox lacks the nature of a horse, and a horse lacks the nature of an ox. In reality, they are neither.

"It is not non-existent. That [nature] is not a non-existent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, Mahāmati, all dharmas do not lack their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); they possess their own characteristics.

However, it is not that this is something which can be known by the deluded worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*). (The Tang translation says: 'There is no self-characteristic, yet it is not non-existent; it exists.
It is not something that can be known by the various foolish worldlings. The Wei translation says: 'Foolish worldlings do not know it. "
All phenomena lack a self-nature and characteristics because they arise from false conceptualization. (The Tang translation asks: "Why is this not known? Because of discrimination.
Thus, all phenomena are empty; all phenomena are unarisen; all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. (The Wei translation says: "They lack substance and characteristics.
One should understand it in this way.

The Commentary states: When the Tathāgata constantly says that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*), it is precisely because the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha remains immutable while conforming to conditions, such that its entire substance manifests as all phenomena.
Therefore, all phenomena, while conforming to conditions, remain immutable; their very essence is the Tathāgatagarbha.
One must not call this a "real self" or "real phenomena," and thus it is said to be without self. This does not mean that [the Tathāgatagarbha] itself is non-existent.
There is the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* which serves as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena. There is only this nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, and no other nature.
It is, for example, like a cow having only the nature of a cow and no nature of a horse, or a horse having only the nature of a horse and no nature of a cow.
From the perspective of the cow, the nature of a horse does not exist, yet the nature of a cow is not non-existent. From the perspective of...
In that case, while the nature of the ox is not present and the nature of the horse is not absent, it is not that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

One should know that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise: they do not lack the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *tathāgatagarbha*, nor do they possess the self-characteristic of a personal self (*ātman*).
It is only because of the false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of all deluded beings that they fail to know the *tathāgata* as being without self (*anātman*).
It is like covering one's ears. Thus, while it is constantly said that "all dharmas are empty," one should know that the Tathāgatagarbha is not empty.
While it is constantly said that "all dharmas are unarisen," one should know that there is nothing within the Tathāgatagarbha that is not arisen.
While it is constantly said that "all dharmas lack self-nature," one should know that the Tathāgatagarbha is not devoid of self-nature. △ Third, [the section] concerning the aggregates and elements.
[The Buddha] entered into analysis:
"In this way, the Tathāgata and the aggregates (skandhas) are neither different nor not different. [The Wei translation says: "The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is also like this;
within the five aggregates, it is neither one nor different. If he were not different from the aggregates, he would have to be impermanent. [The Wei translation further...]

It is said: Because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). [The Tang translation further states: "Because the various phenomena of the five aggregates are conditioned.
If they were different, then skillful means would be empty. [This sentence is absent in both translations. If they were two distinct things, there should be a difference, like the horns of an ox.
[The Tang translation states: "If they were different, it would be like the two horns of an ox; there is both difference and non-difference. Because they are similar, they are not different.
There is difference due to the distinction between long and short; all dharmas are likewise.

Mahāmati, it is like the right horn of an ox being different from the left horn, and the left horn being different from the right horn; in this way, length, shortness, and various colors are each distinct. (The Tang translation says: "Length and shortness are not the same;
their color-forms are each separate. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, in relation to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, is neither different nor not different.

The Commentary states: This is a comparative analysis by way of person and dharma, clarifying that they are neither different nor not different, thereby transcending the four propositions and not falling into the four propositions.
"Tathāgata" is a provisional name for a person; the "five aggregates" are dharmas of form and mind.

If one were to claim that the Tathāgata is definitively identical with the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), then because the five aggregates are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and subject to arising and ceasing, the Tathāgata would likewise be conditioned and subject to arising and ceasing;

this is certainly untenable. If one were to claim that the Tathāgata is definitively distinct from the five aggregates, then the Tathāgata would necessarily lack the five aggregates—both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)—and his physical marks, wisdom, and so forth would all be unattainable. [As stated in] the *Saṃghīti-sūtra*...
"Would that not then be in vain? That too is impossible. Furthermore, if the Tathāgata’s five aggregates were dual, they would be like the two horns of an ox.
Yet even the two horns of an ox possess both difference and non-difference; one cannot say they are definitively different.
How much less so for the Tathāgata and the five aggregates? This is intended to show that the five aggregates, when examined in relation to one another, are already [empty] of self-nature."

There is both difference and non-difference. How much more so regarding the Tathāgata and the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Could they be said to be exclusively different or exclusively non-different?
As for the statement that "all dharmas are also like this," it is as with the five aggregates: because they share the common name "aggregates," they are not different.
Form is not sensation and so forth; sensation is not perception and so forth; therefore, they are different. As for the eighteen *dhātus*, they are all equally termed "elements" (*dhātu*);

therefore, they are not different. The faculties are not the objects and so forth; the objects are not consciousness and so forth; therefore, they are different. As for the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), they are all equally termed "bases" (*āyatana*); therefore, they are not different. The eye is not the ear and so forth;
visible form is not sound and so forth; therefore, they are different. △ Fourth, [the classification] according to liberation.
[Śāriputra] said:
"In this way, the liberation of the Tathāgata is neither different nor not different. Thus, the Tathāgata is designated by the name 'liberation' (the Wei translation says:
'Thus, because he relies upon liberation, he is called by the name of the marks of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body'). If the Tathāgata were different [from liberation]..."
Liberation should be constituted by the characteristics of form; because it is constituted by the characteristics of form, it should be impermanent. (The Wei translation says:

"Then it would be identical to the characteristics of form, and thus it would be impermanent. The Tang translation says: "If it corresponds with the characteristics of form, it is precisely impermanent.

If it were not different [from the characteristics of form], then practitioners would attain a state of non-differentiation through correspondence, yet practitioners perceive differentiation. (The Wei translation says: "Then there would be no capacity...")
There is a distinction between the realization and that which is realized; yet the practitioner perceives both the realizer and the realized. (The Tang translation says:
"The practitioner should see them as without distinction, yet there is a distinction. Therefore, they are neither different nor not different.
The Commentary states: The Tathāgata is that which realizes, and liberation is that which is realized. Since neither the subject nor the object possesses intrinsic nature, they are not different;
yet since the subject and object appear distinctly, they are not non-different. To speak of "cultivation" and "seeing" as having distinctions involves two meanings.

First, there is the sense that the subject which realizes and the object realized are non-dual yet dual. Second, within the object realized itself, there are distinctions of partiality versus completeness and deficiency versus fulfillment;
this is as in the realization of the ten suchnesses across the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and as stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*:
"All worthies and sages have their differences based on the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). △ Fifth, [the classification] by means of wisdom.
And that which is the object of cognition (*jñeya*)—thus, wisdom (*jñāna*) and its object are neither different nor not different.
Mahāmati, as for why wisdom and its object are neither different nor not different: it is because they are not permanent.
It is not impermanent; it is neither created nor a creation; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither awakening nor that which is awakened to;

it is neither characteristic nor that which is characterized; it is neither the aggregates nor distinct from the aggregates; it is neither speech nor that which is spoken; it is neither one nor different, neither both nor neither.
The Commentary states: Whether ordinary or noble, the objective poles (*viṣayabhāga*) of all minds and mental factors are termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Whether ordinary or noble, the objective poles of all minds and mental factors are termed "suchness-flame" (*tathatā-jvālā*). In this way, all phenomena are subsumed without exception.

Since they both take self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) as their essence, they are not different. However, because the distinction between these two poles is provisionally established, they are not identical.

They are not different. Since they are fundamentally neither different nor non-different, they are also fundamentally neither permanent nor impermanent, neither agent nor action, and even fundamentally neither both nor neither. All these phenomena are fundamentally free from the four extremes.
Because it is neither one, nor different, nor both, nor neither, it is entirely free from all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

(The Tang translation says: "For this reason, it transcends all means of valid cognition. Being free from all means of valid cognition, it is beyond verbal expression. (The Wei translation says: "It possesses only its name.
The Tang translation says: "There is only verbal expression. Being beyond verbal expression, it is without arising. (The Wei translation says: "If there is only a name, that dharma...")
Non-arising. (The Tang translation says: "Because there is only verbal expression, there is no arising. Where there is no arising, there is no cessation.
Where there is no cessation, there is quiescent extinction. (The Wei translation says: "Because it does not cease, that dharma is equal to space.
The Tang translation says: "Because there is no cessation, it is like space. Quiescent extinction is the self-nature nirvāṇa. Self-nature nirvāṇa...
Then there is no activity and no cause. When there is no activity and no cause, there is no objective support (*ālambana*).
When there is no objective support, one transcends all falsehood. To transcend all falsehood is to be the Tathāgata.
(The Wei translation states: "Space is neither cause nor fruit. If a dharma is neither cause nor fruit, that dharma is unobservable. That which is unobservable... )
That Dharma transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). That which transcends all conceptual proliferation is called the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya.
The Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha (in the language of Tang, "the Tathāgata is the essence of Perfect Enlightenment").
The Commentary states: Since all phenomena (*dharmas*) are already free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), they transcend all measures (*pramāṇa*).
That which possesses names and words is, in itself, not names and words. They are without arising and without ceasing, just like empty space. They are neither effect nor cause;
the sphere of mental activity is extinguished, and the path of language is cut off. Therefore it is said: "All phenomena are none other than the Buddha-dharma. Even walls, tiles, and...
The pebbles are all the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body. How could they be distinguished by such phrases as "created" or "uncreated"?
This concludes the second section, the detailed analysis of their meaning. △ Third, the conclusion answering the question.
Mahāmati, this is called the Buddha of Samyaksaṃbuddha. Mahāmati, as for the Buddha of Samyaksaṃbuddha, he is free from all faculties and measures (the Wei translation says:
"because he has transcended the spheres of all the sense-faculties"; the Tang translation says: "Because he has transcended the spheres of all the sense-faculties").
"Permanently detached from all realms of the sense faculties.

The Commentary states: "The term 'Buddha' is repeated here to clarify the essence of awakening—the awakening of Right Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). Sentient beings are deluded regarding this essence of awakening;
its entire substance manifests illusorily as the realms of the sense faculties. This is what is meant by 'the unchanging conforming to defilement.'"
It is due to conditions (*pratyaya*). The Tathāgata has awakened to these realms of the sense faculties (*indriya-viṣaya*):
they do not change according to conditions, and their very substance is the essence of awakening (*bodhi-tattva*). They cannot be restricted to being merely the realms of the sense faculties.

Therefore, within this, the one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes the one. The faculty is both the illuminator and the illuminated; the object is both the illuminated and the illuminator. Thus...
This means that the unchanging follows along with pure conditions. The initial long prose section concludes. II. Verse Summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Completely detached from the measures of the sense faculties, There is no object and no cause.
(The Wei translation says: Detached from all dharmas and faculties, neither effect nor cause. Already detached from the perceiver and the perceived,"

It is also free from the characterized and the characteristics; it is the perfect awakening regarding the aggregates and conditions. Neither identity nor difference can be perceived, nor is there any perceiver.
How then could one make distinctions? It is neither created nor uncreated; it is neither an effect nor a cause; it is neither the aggregates nor residing within the aggregates.
Nor does it exist as something else distinct; (as the Wei translation says: "It is neither the aggregates nor separate from the aggregates, nor does it abide elsewhere. The Tang translation says:
"It is neither the *skandhas* nor not the *skandhas*, nor is it separate from other things. Nor does it possess any inherent nature as it is perceived through false imagination.
(As the Tang translation says: "There is not a single dharma-essence as seen through such conceptual construction") one should know that it is also not non-existent.
This dharma and its nature are likewise so. (As the Tang translation says: "Nor is it again non-existent; the nature of all dharmas is thus. Because of existence there is non-existence;

because of non-existence there is existence. (As the Tang translation says: "In dependence on existence, non-existence is established; in dependence on non-existence, existence is established. If it were non-existent, it should not [be so].
Regarding sensation: if there is that which should not be conceptualized—(the Wei translation says: "Therefore it is not said to be non-existent, nor can it be said to be existent";

the Tang translation says: "Since non-existence cannot be grasped, existence likewise should not be spoken of")—or if one lingers in the conventional expressions of self and non-self (the Tang translation says:
"Not understanding self and non-self, one merely clings to words"), one becomes immersed in the two extremes and ruins oneself.
Destroying the world and liberating one from all faults, correctly observing the penetration of the self—(the Tang translation says:
"If one can see this Dharma, then one will be free from all faults")—this is called correct observation; it does not disparage the Great Teacher.

The Commentary states: The first verse praises the preceding general negation of all [categories]. The next two verses skip ahead to praise the analysis based on the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
The following two verses retrospectively praise the analysis based on non-self (*anātman*). The next verse rebukes the errors of those who are deluded.
The final verse extols the realization of those who have awakened. "Not the aggregates" means it is not identical with the aggregates; it does not exist within the aggregates.
This is not different from the aggregates (*skandhas*), nor is there anything else remaining or mixed within it. It should be understood as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in its own essence.

Since the Dharma-realm has nothing external to it, there is nothing remaining; since the Dharma-realm has no remainder, there is no mixture. The other two translations may be understood by comparison.
The twenty-ninth section, "The Gate of the Tathāgata’s Self-Nature," concludes. Thirty: Non-Arising and Non-Cessation.
Section Two. First, the explicit elucidation of the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing. Second, the differentiation [of this teaching] in contrast with the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Within the first section, there are three parts: first, a brief answer in response to a question; second, a request for further instruction following a repeated inquiry; third, the full and detailed exposition. △ Now, the first part.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, the sūtras uphold the teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has stated that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is another name for the Tathāgata.

World-Honored One, is it because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) that you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, or is it indeed another name for the Tathāgata? (The Tang translation says: "Not...")
"Arising is non-extinction; this is the absence of dharmas. Why, then, is this said to be another name for the Tathāgata? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I teach that all dharmas are neither arising nor extinguishing, for the categories of existence and non-existence do not manifest. [The Wei translation asks:

"Yet the Buddha-Tathāgata constantly says that all dharmas are neither arising nor extinguishing, because he is free from the establishment of the categories of existent and non-existent dharmas. The Tang translation asks: "As..."]
The World-Honored One says: "All dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished; one should know that this [view] falls into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
The Commentary states: In the ordinary sūtras, it is frequently said that all dharmas are like illusions and dreams, fundamentally without production or extinction;
thus, "neither produced nor extinguished" is precisely the meaning of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of all dharmas. Furthermore, it is said that this is the Tathāgata...
Because these are different names, one asks out of doubt. My brief answer now is based on the two translations, which are indeed interrogative in nature, yet their underlying meanings differ.

The Wei translation holds that since the Tathāgata constantly teaches non-arising and non-ceasing, being fundamentally free from the establishment of existence and non-existence, it should not be pointed out as a different name for the Tathāgata.
The Tang translation holds that if one speaks of non-arising and...

To say that cessation is the absence of intrinsic nature still falls into the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*). To say that non-arising and non-cessation are alternative names for the Tathāgata still falls into the view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*).
Songze answered that non-arising and non-cessation fundamentally transcend both existence and non-existence;

therefore, although they manifest the absence of intrinsic nature, they are not non-existent, and although they are alternative names for the Tathāgata, they are not non-existent. II. Repeated Questioning.
Xu Xuan.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-arising, then the apprehension of dharmas cannot be obtained (the Wei translation says:
'this cannot be called all dharmas'), because all dharmas are non-arising" (the Tang translation says: "If dharmas...").
That which is unarisen cannot be grasped; there is not even the slightest dharma. Who, then, is the Tathāgata?

If there were any dharma within these names, I pray that you would explain it for me. (The Wei translation says: "If this name exists based on other dharmas, World-Honored One, you should explain them to me.")
The Commentary says: Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are fundamentally unarisen, how could there be any phenomenon that can be grasped?

Since there is no phenomenon that can be grasped, how can this be an alternative name for the Tathāgata? If it were an alternative name for the Tathāgata, there must necessarily be a referent for the name;
ultimately, what phenomenon or meaning does one point to when calling it "unborn and undying"?
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it.
I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "So be it; we receive your instruction."
The permission granted for the double questioning is concluded. III. The actual extensive response has three parts: first, directly clarifying the faults avoided in what is taught;
second, extensively revealing the various names of the Tathāgata; third, meticulously distinguishing the differences in the meanings of the words. △ Now, the first part.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I say that the Tathāgata is not non-existent; nor is he the unarisen and undestroyed [nature] that encompasses all dharmas;
nor is he unarisen and undestroyed because of depending on conditions; nor is he without meaning. (The Wei translation says: "The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.")
It is not that there is no thing; nor is it that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing. Nor can it be said that they exist by depending on causes and conditions.
Nor is it a false statement to say they are neither arising nor ceasing. [In the Tang translation it says:

"I say that the Tathāgata is not a non-existent thing, nor is he one who grasps at neither-arising-nor-ceasing, nor does he depend on conditions, nor is he without meaning. Mahāmati, this is what I mean by "mind."
The name of the Tathāgata of the Dharmakāya is "Unborn. That which is unborn is not within the realm of any non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas abiding in the seventh stage.
(The Wei translation states: "I have always said that what is neither born nor extinguished is called the Mānasikāya, the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata;
it is not the realm of any non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas who abide in the seventh stage.")
It is also not the domain of Bodhisattvas. ○ [The Tang translation says: "I say that 'non-arising' is a distinct name for the mind-made Dharma-body (*manomaya-dharmakāya*).
All non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas up to the seventh stage do not understand its meaning. — Mahāmati.
"That non-arising is another name for the Tathāgata.
The Commentary states: "The Tathāgata is not without nature (niḥsvabhāva). This refutes the view that taking the absence of nature to be non-arising and non-ceasing.
"Nor does non-arising and non-ceasing encompass all phenomena. This refutes the grasping at the apprehension of phenomena as being subsumed [under those categories]. Furthermore...
"It does not depend on conditions" refutes the notion that there is a distinct dharma existing within names.

"Nor is it without meaning" refutes the further calculation that names exist while meanings do not. Among these, the phrase "neither arising nor ceasing encompasses all dharmas" is somewhat difficult to understand;
I shall now explain it. For all dharmas, arising is fundamentally non-arising, and ceasing is fundamentally non-ceasing.

That which is called the true, eternal nature—within which one seeks, in vain, for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death—is precisely the original Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous True Suchness-nature.
This wondrous True Suchness-nature is a synonym for the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata;
it does not mean that all phenomena exist within the fruit, and that [the fruit] is further grasped by means of non-arising and non-ceasing.
This is so. Now, as for the statement that there is no intrinsic nature and thus neither arising nor ceasing, this refers to the meaning of emptiness regarding causes and conditions.

That the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) is called neither-arising-nor-ceasing refers to the meaning of the provisional (*prajñapti*). That the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is called neither-arising-nor-ceasing refers to the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyama*).
Although the mind-made body possesses three characteristics, it is nonetheless accomplished through the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) in their semblance.
Because they have not yet realized the Middle, these are subsumed as the "Provisional. Although the Dharma-body possesses the three virtues, it is the body of partial realization and perfect fusion;
because its essence is non-dual, it is subsumed as the "Middle. All externalists do not yet know that things are empty;
how then could they know the Provisional and the Middle? Although Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage of the Shared Teaching know emptiness, they have not yet...
Because it is not seen as non-empty, it is likewise not within its domain. Regarding the statement "the seventh stage," this refers to those of the most dull faculties;
they must reach the eighth stage before they can receive the empowerment. II. Extensively Revealing the Various Names of the Tathāgata (in three parts):
First, citing an analogy; second, indicating the Dharma; third, applying the correspondence. △ Now, the first [citing an analogy]:
Mahāmati, it is like Indra, Śakra, Purandara, and so forth—such things each have many names.
(The Wei translation says: "For example, Śakradevendra, Śakra, Rāja, Purandara, and Hasta.")
"Grasping," "body," "earth," "pṛthivī," "space," "unobstructed"—such various names as these differ in name but are one in meaning.
(The Tang translation states: "For example, Śakra, earth, space, and even hands and feet—each individual thing has many names.
Nor does having many names imply having many natures; (both function as the substance. Nor is it that they lack intrinsic nature. (Tang)
[The text] says: "Nor is it without substance.
The Commentary states: For example, Śakra, Lord of Devas, has a thousand names;

likewise, the hand is also called a "claw," the body is also called "substance" (*tǐ*), the earth is also called "Pṛthivī," and empty space is also called "unobstructed. A single thing in the world has many [names].
As for names, they are beyond counting. Although their names are many, their substance is not many, nor is it without substance.
One should know that the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is also like this. △ Second, the demonstration of the Dharma.
"In this way, Mahāmati, I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names in this Sahā world.
The commentary states: "Sahā is also called Soka and also called Saha; this is translated as 'Enduring' (*kṣānti*).
It is the general name for the trichiliocosm presided over by Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Within the world-systems..."

It consists of layers as numerous as the atoms in thirteen buddha-fields, surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in thirteen buddha-fields, just as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The sentient beings therein endure all afflictions.
One is called "Kṣānti" (Endurance) because one performs various deeds and endures manifold sufferings;
furthermore, it is called Kṣānti because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas liberate sentient beings through the power of great endurance. *Asaṃkhyeya* is translated here as "innumerable."
Fools hear all these names and each speaks of them as my name, yet they do not understand that these are alternative names for me, the Tathāgata. (In the Tang translation:
"Though all foolish commoners hear and speak of them, they do not know they are alternative names for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, there may be some sentient beings...
Those who know me as the Tathāgata, those who know me as the Omniscient One, those who know me as the Buddha,
those who know me as the Savior of the World, those who know me as the Self-Awakened One, those who know me as the Guide, those who know me as the Broad Guide,
those who know me as the Guide of All, those who know me as the Rishi, those who know me as Brahmā, and those who know me as Viṣṇu (here translated as "Great Power"). There are...

Some know him as the Sovereign of Knowledge; some know him as the Victorious One of Knowledge; some know him as Kapila (the name of the city where the Buddha was born, thus named after the sage Kapila);
some know him as the Limit of Reality; some know him as the Moon; and some know him as the Sun.
There are those who know the Lord; those who know non-arising; those who know non-ceasing; those who know emptiness; those who know suchness;
those who know the truths; those who know the limit of reality; those who know the nature of phenomena;
those who know nirvana; those who know permanence; those who know equality; those who know non-duality; and those who know signlessness.
There are those who know liberation; there are those who know the Way; there are those who know the mind-born. The Commentary says:
These are briefly cited as thirty-three names to serve as examples for the rest.
The Wei edition has forty-six names, and the Tang edition has fifty; these may likewise be inferred, so there is no need for an exhaustive explanation.
Mahāmati, such as these are the three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names, neither increasing nor decreasing.
In this world and in other worlds, all know me to be like the moon in water—neither emerging nor entering. (The Tang translation reads:
"In this and other worlds, there are those who can know me to be like the moon in water, neither entering nor emerging. As for those foolish commoners...

They cannot know me, because they fall into the two extremes (the Chinese translation says: "Only the various ordinary fools have their minds submerged in the two extremes and thus cannot understand").
The Commentary states: "Neither increasing nor decreasing" means that the nature of all names is identical to the nature of a single name;

therefore, there is no increase. The nature of a single name is identical to the nature of all names; therefore, there is no decrease. The Dharma-body abides in ultimate emptiness, like the full moon.
According to the purity of the water of the minds of sentient beings, its reflection appears. This...
The reflected image that appears does not depart from the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, and thus it does not emerge;
nor does it depart from the water of the sentient beings’ minds, and thus it does not enter. Being neither emerging nor entering, it is neither existent nor non-existent.

Those foolish people, some of whom reckon that the Buddha exists outside the mind, and others who reckon that the Buddha has no essence or characteristics, are therefore unable to know that the Dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished.
This is the meaning.
Yet, although they all respectfully honor and make offerings to me, they do not skillfully understand the meaning and intent of words and phrases;

they do not discern names, nor do they understand self-realization. They cling to various verbal expressions and textual passages, and regarding that which is neither born nor extinguished, they conceive of it as non-existent.
[The Wei translation says: "Because they do not skillfully understand the meanings of names and phrases, they grasp at differentiated characteristics and cannot know themselves.
Because they are attached to names, their false discrimination [concerning] non-arising and non-ceasing is called 'non-existence. [The Tang translation says:

"Because they do not skillfully understand the meanings of names and phrases, they are attached to verbal teachings and are obscured regarding reality. They falsely claim that non-arising and non-ceasing is 'non-existence.'"
[The essence of the nature].

The Commentary states: "Those who all reverently make offerings to me" explains that although [the Dharma] has been heard and preached, those who do not understand it well—this and so forth—explain that they do not know this is an alternative name for the Tathāgata; they do not distinguish the names.

This refers to being unable to discern the meaning expressed by names. "Not understanding one's own penetration" means not knowing that the Dharma-body is inherently possessed by every person, and that there is no difference among the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings. This concludes the second section, "Showing the Dharma.
△ Third, the "Application."

They do not know the distinctions among the names and titles of the Tathāgata—such as Indra, Śakra, or Brahmā—and fail to understand that these are self-referential designations ultimately converging upon the same absolute reality.
Regarding all dharmas, they become attached to whatever is spoken [of them]. (The Wei translation states:
"Because they cannot determine the true nature of names and titles, taking up dharmas according to the sounds of words is likewise so. The Tang translation states: "Because..."
They believe the verbal teachings but are obscure regarding ultimate reality; they grasp the meaning of all phenomena according to the words alone.
The Commentary states: If one knows that the primordially existing Dharmakāya is equal to that of the Buddhas, then every word reveals the Truth and every character returns to the Source.
This constitutes the final convergence, which is what is meant by the definitive, true meaning of the Name.

Because they do not understand that all names and titles ultimately refer to the *dharmakāya* as the supreme refuge, upon hearing [the term] "neither arising nor ceasing," they immediately form a conceptual attachment to it as being "without nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*).
This is like hearing the name "Purandara" and immediately assuming he is not Śakra.
Part Two concludes the extensive explanation of the Tathāgata’s various names. Part Three: A detailed analysis of the distinctions between words and their meanings.

There are five further sections. First, the refutation of deluded views; second, the revelation of the well-spoken; third, the exhortation to rely on the meaning; fourth, the admonition against clinging to literal expressions;
fifth, the exhortation to draw near to those of great learning. △ Now, the first section.
"Mahāmati, those deluded people speak thus: 'The meaning is identical to the verbal expression; the meaning and the expression are not different. Why is this?
Because they claim that meaning has no body [the Wei version says: because meaning has no essential nature or characteristic].

Apart from verbal expression, there is no further meaning; it is merely verbal expression. [The Tang version says: These people do not understand the intrinsic nature of sounds and words, and thus claim that the word is itself...]"
[Meaning: there is no separate essence of meaning. Mahāmati, those who are burned by evil views—[the Wei version says: "those foolish people"; the Tang version says:
"that person is foolish"]—do not know the self-nature of verbal expression, nor do they know the arising and ceasing of verbal expression; yet meaning neither arises nor ceases.
Mahāmati, all verbal expressions fall within the realm of letters, but the meaning does not so fall, because it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Thus, there is no taking of birth, nor is there a body (both [versions] say: because it is free from existence and free from non-existence, because it is without birth and without essence).
The Commentary states: "Verbal expressions and sounds arise and perish momentarily; they can be heard by the ear-consciousness and apprehended as objects by the mental consciousness.

Therefore, deluded people reckon them to be existent. The true meaning of the Dharmakāya is neither existent nor non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, and does not fall within the sphere of discriminative, deluded consciousness.
Therefore, deluded people reckon it to be non-existent. It is not so.
To know non-arising is to have nothing that does not arise; to have no substance is to have nothing that is not its substance.

○ Second, revealing the excellence of the teaching, which has two parts: first, clarifying that speaking is itself non-speaking; second, clarifying that there is speaking without speaking. △ Now, the first part.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not teach a dharma that falls into words, because the existence or non-existence of words cannot be apprehended.

This is with the exception of that which does not fall into words. (The Tang translation says: "Except for that which does not fall into words. The Wei translation says: "The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma.")
This is spoken according to the word "self," because one does not perceive that various syllables are either existent or non-existent, and thus does not cling to names and words.
Mahāmati, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata teaches a dharma that falls into [the trap of] words and letters, this would be a false statement. (The Wei translation says:

"If a person clings to names and words when speaking, that person is not called one who speaks the Dharma well. The Tang translation says: "If a person, when preaching the Dharma, falls into words...")
"Regarding 'syllables' (akṣara): this is a deceptive teaching, for dharmas are free from syllables. (The Tang translation states: 'Because the self-nature of all dharmas is free from syllables.
Therefore, Mahāmati, we Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas do not speak a single syllable, nor do we answer with a single syllable.
Why is this? Because dharmas are free from syllables."
The Commentary states: To realize and accord with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the path of language is severed and the sphere of mental activity ceases.

[The] Place. (The Tang translation says: "Then one attains a supreme and wondrous place. When one perceives that the nature of things does not give rise to conceptual discrimination within its own essence, all worldly activities are forever stilled.

Foolish ordinary people engage in the affairs of deluded imagination; this is not the case for the noble sages. (The Tang translation states: "Conceptual discrimination is the business of the foolish and ignorant;
it is not that of the wise and holy. Unreal imagination is like a city of Gandharvas or a conjured person. (The Tang translation states: "The deluded mind divides...")
It is distinct from unreal objects, such as a city of the *gandharvas* or a person created by illusion.
Mahāmati, it is like a city of the *gandharvas* or a magically conjured person where various beings, merchants, and others appear to enter and exit;

yet, due to the deluded imaginings of fools, they think there is real entering and exiting, whereas in reality there is no one who enters or exits—it is merely their own deluded imagination. (The Tang translation says: "For example, it is like small children...")
One sees a city of Gandharvas and illusory people engaged in commerce coming and going; with a deluded mind, one discriminates and says these are real things.
In this same way, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings give rise to the delusion of arising and ceasing. Yet for them, there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned.
Just as an illusory person is born, in reality there is neither birth nor cessation; their nature and non-nature are both non-existent.
Therefore, all dharmas are likewise free from arising and ceasing. (The Tang translation states: "What is seen by the ignorant—arising and non-arising, conditioned and unconditioned—is all likewise.
Like the birth of an illusory person, like the death of an illusory person; yet the illusory person in reality neither arises nor ceases.
All dharmas are also thus, being free from arising and ceasing. Foolish ordinary beings fall into what is not as it truly is.
The arising of delusive thoughts of birth and cessation does not belong to the noble sages (the Chinese text says: ordinary people falsely give rise to views of birth and cessation;

this is not the case for the noble ones). Those who do not accord with reality do not perceive things as they truly are in their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*); nor is delusive thought different from that [nature]. If it were different, [it would not be delusion].
(As translated by Tang: To speak of "falsehood" means it does not accord with the *dharmatā*, giving rise to perverted views.

"Fanciful conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) refers to clinging to all phenomena as having intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), failing to perceive tranquility. (As translated by Tang: "Perverted views" refers to grasping at the existence of a nature in phenomena, failing to perceive cessation.
"Failing to perceive tranquility" means that one will ultimately never be free from fanciful conceptualization. (As translated by Tang: One cannot distance oneself from falsehood.)

Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of signlessness (*animitta*) is superior, not the vision of signs (*nimitta*). Mahāmati, because the vision of signs is the cause for receiving birth, it is not superior.
Mahāmati, as for signlessness: when false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise, there is neither arising nor ceasing;
this I call *nirvāṇa*. (The Tang translation says: "If there are no signs, then there is no discrimination; non-arising and non-ceasing is *nirvāṇa*"). Mahāmati, *nirvāṇa*...

"Parinirvāṇa" means seeing according to the true meaning (the Chinese translation says: "seeing the place as it truly is"). It is the departure from the prior deluded thoughts and mental factors (the Chinese translation says:
"abandoning the discriminating mind and mental concomitants"), and the attainment of the Tathāgata’s self-realized noble wisdom.
This, I say, is Nirvana.
The Commentary states: Regarding the "unborn and undying" taught by the non-Buddhists, they falsely conceptualize that phenomena exist outside the mind;

therefore, when grasped, they seem to exist, yet when scrutinized, they are non-existent. As for the "unborn and undying" taught by the World-Honored One, one realizes that all is manifested by the mind alone:
arising is itself non-arising, and thus it is not existent; ceasing is itself non-ceasing, and thus it is not non-existent. It is, for example, like an illusion or a dream.

Because various manifestations appear, it is not non-existent; because there is no real external form, it is not existent. Furthermore, that which appears is not non-existent, and that which does not appear is not existent.
That which is subsumed is not non-existent, and that which is not subsumed is not existent. For example, like a city of the gandharvas or a conjured person:
their arising is not a real arising, and their ceasing is not a real ceasing. Since both arising and ceasing—being conditioned phenomena—are entirely unreal, they are neither arising nor...
Cessation is termed "non-existence. Furthermore, how could there be any separate reality?

To say that deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is not different [from its object] means that if it were different, one would fail to realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and give rise to inverted conceptualization. Conceptualization has no intrinsic nature;

it is like waves arising upon water, and is therefore not different. While the nature of water is motionless, conceptualization is the movement of the waves; thus, if they were different, it would be merely this delusion.
This is the perversion of perception. Because one clings to the existence of an intrinsic nature within the essence that is by nature empty and quiescent, one ultimately fails to see that quiescence.
Regarding the statement that "seeing the supreme is signless": it is seeing without the signs of arising and ceasing; seeing without the signs of non-arising and non-ceasing;
seeing without the signs of the two extremes; and seeing without the signs of the middle way. Thus, all conceptual discrimination [is transcended].
When false conceptualization does not arise, and when false conceptualization does not arise, then all dharmas are from the beginning neither born nor extinguished;
this is called nirvāṇa. To thoroughly understand this mark of original, eternal quiescence is called the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
How could this be the same as the non-arising and non-extinction of the nine substances imagined by the non-Buddhists? [The second part consists of two verses in praise. First, the direct verse:]
The first meaning. Second, a restatement of the question and answer. △ Now, the first [part].
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "To eliminate that doctrine of arising, He establishes the principle of non-arising.
[The Wei translation says: "In order to negate the arising of all dharmas, he establishes the dharma of non-arising. The Tang translation says: "To remove..."]

There is the grasping at birth; [yet] I teach such a Dharma to establish the meaning of non-arising. The foolish cannot understand that all dharmas are unarisen, without intrinsic nature, and non-existent.
(The Wei translation says: "Nor can one say they are non-existent. The Tang translation says: "Nor are they non-dharmas.
Like a *gandharva-city*, a phantom, or a dream, those who hold to an intrinsic nature have no cause. (The Wei translation says: "All dharmas exist without a cause.")
[Tang]: Although they exist, because there is no cause, they do not arise; they lack intrinsic nature. For what reason is emptiness?

Please explain this. [Wei]: All dharmas are empty and signless; for what purpose do you speak of them to me? [Tang]: Emptiness is non-arising and lacks intrinsic nature; for what purpose do you speak of it to me?
Because one is detached from conjunction, the nature of cognition does not manifest. [Second version]: Detached from all conditions of conjunction, wisdom...

Because wisdom cannot perceive it, emptiness is non-arising; therefore, I say it has no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). (The Wei translation says: "Because emptiness is fundamentally non-arising, I therefore speak of its lack of substance.

This means that when things are combined one by one, their nature appears yet does not exist. (The Wei translation says: "One sees that things are unobtainable. The Tang translation says: "Though they appear, they do not exist.
When analyzed, there is no combination; this is not like the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
[The World] Is Seen. (The Wei translation says: "It is not what is seen by non-Buddhists; a composite cannot be apprehended.

Like dreams, illusions, falling hairs, mirages, and *gandharva*-cities—these various phenomena of the world appear without cause. (The Tang translation says: "They falsely appear without cause; all worldly affairs are thus.
Having refuted those who argue for the existence of causes, he expounds the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). To expound non-arising means:
The flow of the Dharma shall never be interrupted. (In the Tang translation: "If the meaning of non-arising exists, the eye of the Dharma will forever not perish.

Blazing forth, I refute the doctrine of no-cause, striking terror into all the non-Buddhists. (In the Tang translation: "I proclaim the doctrine of no-cause; the non-Buddhists are all filled with alarm.")
The Commentary states: The Buddha taught non-arising (*anutpāda*) merely to refute the attachment to arising; it was not to establish a doctrine of non-arising.
Yet, ignorant people do not understand this and falsely interpret non-arising as meaning the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

How could they know that what is called the "non-arising of all phenomena" does not merely mean the absence of intrinsic nature? Even the absence of intrinsic nature is itself non-existent; one must not hold to it exclusively.
To say that these exist is like a city of the gandharvas, an illusion, or a dream; though they appear as if they were real, in truth there is no other cause for them.
Next, he further inquires: "For what reason do I say that all phenomena are unarisen, empty, and without intrinsic nature?
It is because when causes and conditions combine, there is a false arising. If one is separated from all combined conditions, then through the observation of wisdom, [it is determined that]...
It cannot be seen; thus, emptiness is fundamentally unarisen, and it is for this reason that it is said to be without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

One must understand that at the very moment of correct conjunction and manifestation, the essence itself is non-existent. This is not like the heterodox schools (*tīrthika*), which claim things are unobtainable only after analyzing them through disjunction.

Observe, for instance, how dreams, illusions, and floating hairs manifest falsely without cause; thus, all [phenomena]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the philosophical context of Yogācāra thought regarding the non-substantiality of phenomena and the distinction from non-Buddhist analytical methods.*

All matters in the world are without exception like this. For this reason, he subdues the heterodox arguments on causal conditions of the non-Buddhists and proclaims the meaning of the True Dharma—that arising is itself non-arising.
This meaning of non-arising is the flow of the True Dharma; it is the Eye of the True Dharma.
Therefore, when the non-Buddhists hear it, they are inevitably struck with terror, just as the brains of the hundred beasts burst upon hearing the roar of a lion. ○
II. A Reiteration of the Questions and Answers (in four parts): First, the question; second, the answer; third, the further question; fourth, the further answer. △ Now, the first part.
At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse: "What is it? What is its cause? By what reason does it arise?
In what place do they combine to form the doctrine of causelessness?"
The Commentary says: This follows from the preceding passage concerning dreams, illusions, and floating hairs appearing as causeless phenomena, and thus raises a question.
Therefore it asks: "What is this matter? By what cause do such things as dreams and illusions exist?
Furthermore, for what reason are dreams and illusions seen to arise? Each of these combinations—where, ultimately, do they combine? And...
"Does the Buddha, then, propound a theory of causelessness? △ Second, the answer.
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered in verse: "Observing conditioned phenomena, they are neither causeless nor possess a [fixed] cause;
thus is extinguished the view held by those who debate arising and ceasing."
The Commentary states: This clarifies that the Buddha refuted the heterodox teachings on false causes by propounding the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).

This is because he observed that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) within the three realms are manifestations of one's own mind; therefore, they are not without cause. Since there are no phenomena outside the mind, they are not caused by something external.
When the mind arises, phenomena arise in that very place; their arising has no point of origin. When the mind ceases, [phenomena] likewise...
The phenomena of the bases cease; in their cessation, there is no place to which they go.
Thus, the perceived characteristics of conjunction held by those proponents of arising and ceasing are forever extinguished from this point on. △ Third, the repeated questioning.

At that time, Mahāmati spoke in verse, asking: "What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it because of the absence of intrinsic nature? (The Tang translation says: 'Is it because they do not exist that they do not arise?
Or is it because one observes various conditions that a phenomenon is called 'non-arising'? (The Tang translation says: 'Is it because it depends upon various conditions?

Should a name not correspond to its meaning? (The Tang translation says: 'Is it that there is a name but no meaning? It is merely for the sake of analytical explanation. (The Tang translation says...)
[The interlocutor] says: "I pray that you will explain this for me. The Commentary states:
This raises three points of difficulty regarding the name "non-arising" (*anutpāda*). First, does it mean that things do not arise because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?

If so, then they would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; therefore, this is untenable. Second, [does it mean that things do not arise] because they depend upon various conditions (*pratyaya*)? And so forth...
If it were produced, it would be like a scorched sprout or a rotten seed; this too is unacceptable.
Third, if that which is called "non-arising" (ajāta) were in fact devoid of meaning, it would become a hollow, deceptive fabrication; this is even more unacceptable.
Only when these three difficulties are resolved can the Tathāgata’s sublime purport of non-arising be fully expounded. △ Fourth, the second response.
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered in verse: "It is not that there is no nature and thus no arising (the Tang translation says:

'It is not that non-existent dharmas do not arise'); nor is it that [things] depend upon conditions. It is not that there is a nature and thus a name (the Tang translation says: 'Nor is it that one waits for conditions; nor is it that there is a substance and thus a name').
Furthermore, the name is not without meaning."
The Commentary states: This first passage generally brushes away the errors of the questions posed.
"All externalists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—these are not the domain of the seventh stage; this is called the mark of non-arising."
The Commentary states: This reveals that the Dharma-body of the Middle Way is termed "non-arising.
Therefore, it is not the domain of the non-Buddhists who cling to existence, nor of the followers of the Three Vehicles who realize emptiness.
Far removed from all causes and conditions, and likewise detached from all phenomena (the Tang translation says:
"there is no agent"), there is only the subtle mind abiding (the Wei translation says: "it is taught that it is established as mind-only"; the Tang translation says: "established by mind-only").

Both the perceiver and the perceived are abandoned (the Tang translation says: "the distinction between subject and object is abandoned"), and its body undergoes transformation (the Wei translation says: "transforming the body and its environment").
Characteristics. [The Tang translation says: "Thus transforming the basis. I declare this to be non-arising. There is no external nature, nor is there a lack of nature.
[The Wei translation says: "Externals are neither real nor unreal. The Tang translation says: "External objects both exist and do not exist.
Nor is there mental appropriation. [The Tang translation says: "That mind has nothing to grasp. Severing all views, I declare this to be non-arising. Thus, there is no self-nature...
The nature [of phenomena], emptiness, and so forth should be analyzed. (The Tang translation states: "Sentences such as 'emptiness' and 'the absence of intrinsic nature' all have this same meaning.
It is not because they are empty that they are called empty; it is because they are unarisen that they are called empty.

The Commentary states: This precisely clarifies "Mind-Only," which is the true meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Since it is called "Mind-Only," it is far removed from external causes and conditions;
it is also free from the activity of a creator; there is no duality of subject and object; and one is able to realize the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Furthermore, it does not grasp at views concerning the existence or non-existence of things external to the mind. Therefore, it is named "Non-" (i.e., Non-arising).

Arising is also called "absence of nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) and is also called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). Because there is no arising, there is emptiness; this emptiness is not a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
True emptiness is precisely the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Because there is no arising, there is no nature; this absence of nature is not a nihilistic non-existence.
This absence of nature is the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). Thus, it clarifies that it is neither a mere absence of nature nor a mere absence of arising.
This is the essential meaning [of the teaching].

When the various conditions and factors harmoniously combine, there is arising and ceasing. (The Tang translation says: "When causes and conditions assemble together, there is therefore arising and ceasing.
Apart from these various conditions and factors, there is no separate arising or ceasing. (The Tang translation says: "When separated from causes and conditions...")

When extinguished, there is nothing; one abandons the enumeration of causes and conditions. There is no other distinct nature. To speak of identity or difference is the false conceptualization of externalists.
(The Wei translation says: Apart from causes and conditions there is no dharma; apart from combination there is no attainment. Externalists falsely discriminate and perceive identity and difference.
The nature of existence and non-existence does not arise; it is neither existent nor non-existent. This excludes the shifting of numerical categories.
These transformations are entirely unattainable. (The Tang translation says: "Neither existence nor non-existence gives rise to dharmas; the same applies to that which is neither.
Only when various conditions assemble can one perceive arising and ceasing within them. There are merely conventional designations that link together like a chain.

Apart from that causal chain, the meaning of "arising" cannot be found. (The Tang translation says: "Following worldly convention, they are provisionally expressed; causes and conditions link together in succession.")

If one is separated from the chain of causes and conditions, the meaning of "arising" cannot be established. Since arising lacks intrinsic nature, it does not occur; thus, one is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists. I speak only of the hook and the chain: because arising has no [intrinsic] existence, there is no arising.

This is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists, yet it is not understood by the foolish and ignorant. (The Tang translation states: "I say that there is only the hook and the chain. Because arising does not exist, there is no arising.
It is free from the errors of all non-Buddhists, and is not something understood by the foolish and ignorant.")

The Commentary states: This clarifies that when one is deluded regarding the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way, the entire substance [of reality] falsely manifests as the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
If one knows that the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination is itself non-arising, then one perceives the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way.
Because these twelve links of dependent origination are a false conjunction based solely on the mind, one perceives arising and ceasing within that which is devoid of arising and ceasing.
If one knows that the nature of causes and conditions is empty and does not falsely assemble them, then arising and ceasing are quiescent in their very substance.

It is like when the cataracts of the eyes have vanished, the flowers in the sky naturally disappear. Therefore, apart from these causes and conditions of the "mind-only," no other distinct nature can be found.
If one falsely calculates the existence of a single nature or a distinct nature, all such views belong to the outsiders.

This is merely a mistaken conceptualization of the Path. Therefore, it is not that all phenomena arise from an existent nature, nor do they arise from a non-existent nature, nor do they arise from a nature that is neither existent nor non-existent.

Rather, it is simply the transformation of the twelve links of dependent origination within the mind-only that appears as arising and ceasing. Apart from this numerical transformation, there is no arising or ceasing.
All of these are ultimately unattainable. Nevertheless, the transformations of these twelve factors are merely conventional designations following worldly usage.

Because it is solely the mind that gives rise to delusion, solely the mind that creates karma, and solely the mind that experiences suffering, yet one fails to realize that suffering is itself nothing but the mind, further delusions arise.
Therefore, it is said that they function like a chain of interlocking links; once one is separated from those delusions of the "solely mind" (cittamātra), [the cycle ceases].

Within the fetters of the suffering of karma, how could there be any possibility for the meaning of "arising"? Since this is the hook and fetter of mind-only, and there are no phenomena external to the mind, arising is itself devoid of intrinsic nature.
Thus, dependent origination is non-arising, free from the errors of the non-Buddhists regarding annihilation, permanence, existence, and non-existence.
Yet ordinary beings of the three realms and those of the two vehicles who are deluded are all unable to comprehend this.
If there were a nature of birth existing apart from the hook-and-chain of conditions, that would be a doctrine of causelessness, which destroys the meaning of the hook-and-chain.
The Commentary states: This refutes the false causes imagined by non-Buddhists, which are in fact causeless.

If one departs from the chain of dependent origination of "mind-only" and separately imagines that atoms, a self-existent lord (*īśvara*), or other such entities constitute the nature of arising, then distinct causes would produce distinct effects.
Consequently, all phenomena would not arise from correct causes and conditions, but instead become causeless.
This argument destroys the meaning of the "hook-and-chain" (saṃdhāna) metaphor.
Just as a lamp reveals various forms, if the hook-and-chain were manifested in such a manner, then there would be various natures existing separately, apart from the hook-and-chain itself.
The Commentary states: This refutes the externalist’s counter-argument.

The externalists argue that although all phenomena each possess their own nature, they nevertheless depend upon a "hook and chain" (causal conditions) to be manifested. It is like objects in a dark room, which require a lamp to be seen;

thus, they maintain that the principle of the hook and chain remains intact. The Buddha therefore restates their position and says: "This, then, is divorced from the hook and chain of causes and conditions."
There are no other dharmas apart from their nature, just as there is no object existing separately outside of a lamp.
Below, this is refuted: "Without nature, there is no arising; its self-nature is like empty space. If one were to depart from the hook and chain, wisdom would have nothing to differentiate.

(The Wei translation says: "Arising dharmas originally have no substance; their self-nature is like empty space. If one seeks dharmas apart from the hook and chain, the foolish have nothing [to grasp].")

[He] knew. ○ The Tang [dynasty] translation says: "Where there is no arising, there is no nature; its essence is like empty space. To seek the Dharma apart from hooks and locks is the discrimination of the foolish."
The Commentary says: This precisely reveals that apart from the causal chain of dependent origination, there is no separate dharma;
this is to refute false conceptualizations. We observe in the world that all phenomena cannot arise without depending on causes and conditions.
Since they are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature and lack arising, their self-nature is like empty space. How could it be said that various [phenomena] existed beforehand?
Is it the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? Therefore, those who seek the Dharma apart from the causal chain of dependent origination are ignorant and deluded, engaging in false discrimination;
this is not the discrimination of the wise.
All of the above clarifies the principle that [the Dharma] neither attends to various conditions nor possesses an inherent nature, yet is so designated.

Furthermore, there is another non-arising, the dharma attained by the noble ones (*ārya*). That which is the arising of that non-arising is precisely the patience toward non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
If one were to observe the hooks and chains of all the worlds, one would find that all are free from hooks and chains;

from this, one attains samādhi. (In the Tang translation: "All the worlds are nothing other than hooks and chains; if one can understand them in this way, the mind of this person attains [liberation])."
[Concentration].
The Commentary states: From here below, the intent is to clarify that even names are not devoid of meaning. The twelvefold dependent origination is fundamentally non-arising;
this principle of non-arising is the Dharmakāya of inherent virtue. To observe it as a linked chain—
Knowing that birth is itself non-birth, one dwells securely in patient acceptance and enters samādhi; this is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This is the manifestation of the nature through cultivation. Only when one realizes the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and the partial and complete Dharmakāya does one truly grasp the actual meaning of this term.

Ignorance (*moha*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and the various karmas (*karman*) and so forth constitute the internal chain. The fire-drill, the lump of clay, the potter’s wheel, the seed, and so forth are termed external. The Commentary states:

"Ignorance" refers to the ignorance that initiates karma (*karma-samutthāna-avidyā*), which is the projecting member (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*). "Craving" refers to the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*janma-snigdha-avidyā*), which is the productive member (*abhinirvartaka-aṅga*).

"Various karmas" refers to the members of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*). "And so forth" includes the members of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The five members induced by the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*), together with the two members produced by birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), are called "internal" because they are appropriated;
they are real dharmas within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Just as fire arises from the causes and conditions of a fire-drill, yet that fire has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
or as a vessel arises from the causes and conditions of a lump of clay, a wheel, and so forth, yet that vessel has no [intrinsic nature].
Nature [is such that] sprouts arise from conditions such as seeds, earth, and water. The sprout has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for it is not grasped;

thus it is called "external. This is a conventional designation within the relative truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The environments and inhabitants of the three realms arise solely from these internal and external, provisional and real causes and conditions.
That which arises is non-arising, because when analyzed through the four types of intrinsic nature, it cannot be found.
Observing in this manner, one realizes that the nature of things is free from mutual dependence like a chain and its links;

thus, one can realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If there were a "self-nature" (*parabhāva*) that arose from causes and conditions, it would not accord with the meaning of the chain and its links.

This, then, would not be established. (The Tang translation states: "If one says there is another dharma that arises from causes and conditions, being divorced from the principle of the chain and its links, this is not the teaching.")
[The Principle].
The Commentary says: If the drawn-out and the produced effects possessed their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why would they depend on that which draws them forth and that which produces them?

If vessels, sprouts, and so forth, as effects, possessed their own intrinsic nature, why would they depend on lumps of clay or seeds? Furthermore, even if there were a Supreme Nature (*pradhāna*) or Īśvara...
[They] are able to produce all internal and external phenomena; furthermore, what reliance could they have on internal and external causes and conditions?
Therefore, apart from the principle of the "hook-and-chain" (gōu-suǒ), the teachings and principles cannot be established.
If arising has no intrinsic nature, what could serve as its hook and lock? (The Tang translation says: "If the dharma of arising were non-existent, what would be its causes and conditions?
Because they arise through mutual succession, one should understand the meaning of causes and conditions.

The Commentary states: Non-Buddhists do not reckon that things truly exist, and thus they reckon them to be non-existent through annihilation. Previously, their reckoning of "other-nature" (parabhāva) was refuted;
now, their reckoning of "non-self-nature" (niḥsvabhāva) is further refuted. Delusion, karma, and suffering arise from one another in a continuous cycle;
therefore, they are called the twelve links of dependent origination, like a chain of hooks and locks. How could it be that there is no self-nature consisting solely of mind?
