That which can cause harm and disadvantage for this life and future lives is called an unwholesome dharma (*akuśala-dharma*); it is exclusively contaminated.

That which cannot be definitively characterized as either wholesome or unwholesome is called an indeterminate dharma (*avyākṛta-dharma*). This is further divided into two types: if it is defiled and obscure, [it is categorized as such].

That which can obstruct the Noble Path is called obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). If it is pure and stainless, and does not obstruct the Noble Path, it is called unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Both of these are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*). Material and mental phenomena that possess the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Space, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and so forth, lack arising.

Those phenomena in which the four characteristics—arising, abiding, change, and cessation—are not perceived are called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The causes and effects of the three realms are called worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*).

The four noble dharma-realms, whether as cause or as fruit, are called supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*). Those that inflict harm upon oneself or others are called blameworthy phenomena (*sāvadya-dharma*).

Those that do not inflict harm upon oneself or others are called blameless phenomena (*anavadya-dharma*). Those that induce the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are called contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Those that do not induce...

Birth and death are called untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). That which possesses the capacity [to act] and that which is the object [of action] is called phenomena with appropriation (*sopādāna-dharma*).

To penetrate the absence of capacity and object is called phenomena without appropriation (*anupādāna-dharma*). Among these, conditioned, tainted, and appropriated phenomena possess moments (*kṣaṇika*).
If they are unconditioned and untainted, or conditioned and untainted, and do not undergo any appropriations, this is called right reception (*samyag-upādāna*); thus, they are not momentary.
That is its nature. △ Second, specifically showing what is destroyed and what is not.

Mahāmati, to speak briefly, the mind (citta), the intellect (manas), the consciousness (vijñāna), and their habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are the causes of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha). These are nourished by the habitual tendencies of the mind, intellect, and consciousness;
they are the false imaginings (parikalpa) of the ignorant regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome. (The Tang translation says: "To state the essentials, the five aggregates of clinging...")

The dharmas of the aggregates increase by taking the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of mind, intellect, and consciousness as their cause. In this regard, the ignorant give rise to conceptual discrimination, claiming them to be "wholesome" or "unwholesome.
Mahāmati, [there is] the cultivation of the bliss of samādhi, the meditative absorption of samādhi, and dwelling in the happiness of the present life.
It is called the "Noble, Wholesome, and Untainted" (in the Tang translation: "The Noble Ones' dwelling in the bliss of samādhi through direct realization;
this is what is called the wholesome, untainted dharma").
The Commentary states: The five aggregates (pañca-skandha), both material and mental, all arise from the perfuming and growth of the eight consciousnesses;
as such, they are conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) and thus possess distinctions such as wholesome and unwholesome, all of which belong to the out-flowing (sāsrava).
However, the supramundane samādhi realized by the sages is wholesome and without out-flows (anāsrava); it is not momentary (akṣaṇika).
“Mahāmati, as for the wholesome and the unwholesome, they refer to the eight consciousnesses. What are these eight?

They are the Tathāgatagarbha—which is called the *vijñānagarbha*—the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñānakāya*). These are not as described by the non-Buddhists.

Mahāmati, the five groups of sensory consciousnesses, together with the mind, intellect, and mental consciousness, possess both wholesome and unwholesome characteristics; they undergo successive transformation and disintegration, flowing on in a continuous stream. (The Tang translation reads: “Wholesome and unwholesome...”)

Good sir, through successive distinctions and an uninterrupted continuity, an indestructible body arises; it both arises and ceases. (The Tang translation says: "It arises without a distinct substance, and having arisen, it immediately ceases.
Failing to realize that what appears is one's own mind, the [preceding] consciousnesses cease in succession as other consciousnesses arise.
(The Tang translation says: "Not understanding that objects are manifestations of one's own mind, when they cease in succession, distinct consciousnesses arise. This is the characteristic of form.

They are separately grasped. The mental consciousness arises in conjunction with the five [sensory] consciousnesses; it does not abide for even a moment, and is thus called "momentary" (in the Tang language:
"The mental consciousness, together with those five consciousnesses, apprehends various distinct forms and characteristics;
because it does not abide for a moment, I call these 'momentary phenomena'").

The Commentary states: Although the eighth consciousness is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), it is capable of receiving the pervasive perfuming of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and furthermore serves as the fundamental support for wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
Although the seventh consciousness is obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), it serves as the defiled support for wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
The sixth consciousness pertains to all three natures and serves as the support for the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The basis for the differentiation of phenomena consists of the eighth and seventh consciousnesses; there is never a time when they do not arise.

If the first five consciousnesses arise, they necessarily arise simultaneously with the sixth, assisting in the formation of the sixth’s wholesome or unwholesome karma. Therefore, it is said that "wholesome and unwholesome" refers to the eight consciousnesses.
At times the five consciousnesses perform wholesome acts, and at times they perform unwholesome acts; from the beginning, there is no fixed certainty, and thus [the distinction exists].
They undergo successive transformation and disintegration; from birth to birth, and from eon to eon, they never cease for even a moment.

Therefore, it is said that they flow in a continuous stream without interruption. These aforementioned five consciousnesses, if explained according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) in terms of their non-disintegrating characteristics, are as follows:
Each [aspect of consciousness] possesses an internal twofold essence that transforms into an external twofold function; from the beginning, there is no difference between them.
This essence and function of consciousness are like the flow of water or the flicker of a lamp’s flame; they do not abide for even a moment, and thus it is said that they "arise and cease.

Failing to realize that the five sense-objects, such as form and so forth, are merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested by the essence of consciousness, one instead grasps at them through the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect).

Therefore, although they perish immediately upon arising, once extinguished, they arise again—such as when visual consciousness has just perished and auditory consciousness arises in its wake, or when a preceding moment of visual consciousness has just perished and a succeeding moment of visual consciousness arises in its wake.
These are all instances of what is called "the sequential extinction of one consciousness followed by the arising of another.
The simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must necessarily coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses before it can [engage its objects].
The five sense objects arise as false discriminations of distinct forms and characteristics, which are then grasped;

yet both the perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga) that is able to grasp them and the perceived aspect (nimitta-bhāga) that is grasped are nothing other than states that do not abide for even a single moment. For this reason, they are called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
"Mahāmati, 'moment' (kṣaṇa) refers to the ālayavijñāna. It is the momentary nature of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the Tathāgatagarbha and the co-emergent manas-consciousness.
(The Chinese version says: 'The Tathāgatagarbha is called the store-consciousness; it is together with the various habitual tendencies of the manas and so forth, and these are momentary phenomena.

The untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) are not momentary; they are not perceived by ordinary, ignorant people because of their attachment to the doctrine of momentariness. (The Chinese version says: 'This is not...')"
Ordinary fools who hold the doctrine of momentariness do not realize that all phenomena are both momentary and non-momentary (the Tang translation states:

"They cannot know that among all phenomena, some are momentary and some are non-momentary"). Because they hold the view of annihilationism, they destroy the unconditioned dharmas (the Tang translation states:
"They reckon the unconditioned to be the same as other phenomena and thus destroy it, falling into the view of annihilationism").
The Commentary states: "The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* is eternally abiding; why then is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) termed 'momentary' (*kṣaṇika*)?
It is because it receives the permeation of tainted habitual tendencies (*sāsrava-vāsanā*), whereby its entire substance becomes subject to arising and ceasing.

If, however, it is permeated by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), causing it to form supramundane untainted habitual tendencies and to realize the unconditioned Dharma-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as manifested through the two kinds of emptiness, then..."
Its very essence is neither arising nor ceasing; how could it be something that ordinary, ignorant people can perceive?
Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate (the Tang translation states: "The five bodies of consciousness do not transmigrate");

they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure, is accompanied by their causes, and undergoes both birth and cessation. (Tang)
It is said: "They are intoxicated by the four stages of abiding (catur-vāsabhūmi) and the stage of ignorance (avidyā-vāsabhūmi)—[the Tang translation says:

'deluded and obscured by the four kinds of habitual tendencies']—and ordinary fools do not perceive this. Their minds are perfumed by the conceptualization of momentary views (kṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi-vikalpa)—[the Tang translation says:
'while ordinary fools have their minds perfumed by discrimination, they cannot understand it, and thus give rise to the view of moments']."
The Commentary states: This is a further explanation of the reason why that which is called "momentary" (kṣaṇika) is named the "storehouse consciousness" (ālayavijñāna).

Now, the storehouse consciousness is permanent, whereas the preceding seven [consciousnesses] are subject to arising and ceasing; thus, one might expect the seven to be called momentary and the storehouse consciousness to be called non-momentary.
Why, then, is that which is momentary named the storehouse consciousness? It is because the active manifestations (pravṛtti) of the seven arise from seeds, and having arisen...
They cease immediately and do not abide for even a moment; there is no possibility for them to move from this place to another location, and thus they do not circulate.
Since they do not circulate, suffering and pleasure likewise perish moment by moment, and therefore cannot give rise to sensation.
Since one does not experience worldly suffering or pleasure, these are not the causes for supramundane nirvāṇa. This demonstrates that the preceding seven [elements] lack intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is just as waves take water as their substance, for no separate self-substance can be found.

The Tathāgatagarbha takes its entire substance as the sovereign of the collective retribution; thus, although it is associated only with neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is precisely because of it that one experiences pleasure and pain.
Furthermore, because it is capable of receiving perfuming and maintaining seeds so they are not lost, it coexists with the causes.

Furthermore, because the seeds of all dharmas sustained by the ālayavijñāna perpetually flow like a torrential stream, they are subject to arising and ceasing, yet are neither annihilated nor eternal.
Ordinary worldlings are intoxicated by the four abodes of attachment and ignorance; foolish-dharma śrāvakas are intoxicated by the ground of ignorance.
Thus, they are unable to realize that arising and ceasing lack intrinsic nature; therefore, [the cycle of existence] persists.

The moments of分段生死 (paricchinna-utpāda-maraṇa, fragmented birth-and-death) and the moments of 變易生死 (pariṇāma-utpāda-maraṇa, transformative birth-and-death) are in reality all merely false conceptualizations.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, just as gold, the diamond, and the Buddha’s *śarīra* attain extraordinary qualities and are ultimately never destroyed, Mahāmati, if there were such a thing as a moment (*kṣaṇa*) in the attainment of the Uninterrupted [Path] (the Chinese text says:
"if one attains the realization of the Dharma"), then the Sage would not be a Sage. And yet...

The Noble is never anything other than noble. Just as gold or a diamond, though passing through the course of eons, does not diminish when weighed, why do the foolish and ignorant—being unskilled in my hidden teachings (the Chinese translation says:
"not understanding my secret teachings")—conceive the notion of momentariness regarding all internal and external phenomena?
The Commentary states: This borrows from phenomena currently perceived in the world that are non-perishing to illustrate that the essence of supramundane, untainted dharmas is not momentary.

Regarding "attaining the uninterrupted": by means of the *anantarya-samādhi*, one severs delusions and directly realizes *tathatā* (suchness), wherein there are no dual characteristics of a subject that realizes and an object that is realized.
The first section, defining the meaning of the momentary, is concluded. II. [The second section follows].
Distinguishing the Characteristics of the Six Perfections (2). Part One: The Question. Part Two: The Answer. △ Now, the first [section].
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, there is the fulfillment of the six pāramitās."
One attains perfect enlightenment. What are the six? (The Tang translation says: "What are the six? How are they fulfilled?"). The Commentary states:
Having attained perfect enlightenment, one realizes that [the Buddha-nature] is like a vajra and is not of a momentary nature;

yet this must necessarily depend upon the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). These six perfections are simply the two types of adornment—merit and wisdom—and this is stated in reference to the cultivation of virtuous qualities.
This refers to conditioned, untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena. Are they momentary (*kṣaṇika*), or are they non-momentary?
If they are momentary, how can one attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) by means of them?

If they are non-momentary, how can there be six [categories], and how can there be the distinction between fulfillment and non-fulfillment? The intent of the question lies herein; it must not be overlooked.
II. The second part consists of two sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation. △ Now, the first:
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of distinctions regarding the pāramitās, namely: worldly, world-transcending, and world-transcending supreme."

The Commentary states: The six perfections of the mundane world are conditioned and with outflows; they are momentary phenomena. The six perfections of the supramundane world are conditioned but without outflows;

in relation to the mundane, they are not momentary, yet in relation to what is superior to them, they are momentary, because they only transcend the suffering of birth and death (分段) and do not transcend the suffering of transformation (變易). Furthermore, these supreme supramundane six perfections may also be termed "conditioned."
It is untainted (*anāsrava*). It may also be called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted. When the entirety of the nature gives rise to cultivation, it may be termed conditioned;
when the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature, it may be termed unconditioned. This reality is not a momentary phenomenon. △ Second, the explanation.
Mahāmati, as for the worldly pāramitās: they are characterized by grasping and attachment to "self" and "mine," and by adhering to the two extremes.
For the sake of various places of rebirth, and because of delighting in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, one fulfills the dāna-pāramitā;

the same applies to śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, and prajñā. These include the supernatural powers of ordinary people, as well as birth in the Brahma heavens (the Tang translation says: "that is to say...").
All foolish commoners, attached to "self" and "what belongs to self," grasping at the two extremes, seeking various bodies of existence, and craving objects such as forms,
practice the perfection of generosity, as well as ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, thereby accomplishing supernormal powers and being born in the Brahma world.
The Commentary says: *Pāramitā* is translated here as "crossing over to the infinite" (*du wuji*) and also as "reaching the other shore.

Ordinary fools falsely reckon such things as the Brahma-world and other future, superior retributions to be the "other shore"; therefore, they practice the six dharmas, such as giving, as the means by which one can cross over and reach [that shore].

Mahāmati, as for the supramundane pāramitās: because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the grasping of nirvāṇa, they practice the six pāramitās while delighting in their own personal nirvāṇic bliss (the Tang translation says: "clinging to nirvāṇa and longing for self-bliss").
"Thus one cultivates the various pāramitās. The Commentary states:
"The followers of the Two Vehicles falsely reckon the partial truth as the 'other shore,' and therefore they cultivate the six perfections as the means to reach it."

The supramundane, supreme *pāramitā* consists in the non-arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) because one realizes that the objects of grasping are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind and that these two [subject and object] are of one's own mind.
Thus, one does not grasp at the various realms of existence as being real, nor does one cling to the forms and characteristics of one’s own mind.

(The Tang translation states: "That is to say, the Bodhisattva understands that the two dharmas within his own mind are manifested solely through discrimination; he does not give rise to [false conceptualization]...")

Without giving rise to deluded thoughts, without producing attachment, and without grasping at the marks of form, one gives rise to the *dānapāramitā* for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
(The Tang translation states: "Desiring to benefit and bring joy to all sentient beings, one constantly practices the *dānapāramitā*").
Thus, when deluded thoughts do not arise regarding those very conditions, this is the *śīlapāramitā*.
(The Tang translation states: "Not giving rise to discrimination regarding any objects is the practice of the *śīla-pāramitā*.
This means that when those false imaginings do not arise, one patiently knows the grasped and the grasper; this is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*. The Tang translation states:
"At the very moment when discrimination does not arise, one patiently knows the intrinsic nature of the subject-grasper and the object-grasped; this is called the *kṣānti-pāramitā*.)

To apply diligent effort during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, and to practice in accordance with skillful means so that false conceptualizations do not arise—[the Chinese translation says:
"to accord with true understanding and not give rise to discrimination"]—this is the *vīryapāramitā*.

When all false conceptualizations are completely extinguished, one does not fall into the grasping for the *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvakas*—[the Chinese translation says: "not giving rise to discrimination, nor conceiving the *nirvāṇa* of the non-Buddhists"].
This is the dhyāna-pāramitā. Through the wisdom of observation, one realizes that the false imaginings of one's own mind lack inherent nature; thus, one does not fall into the two extremes.

One’s prior body becomes increasingly superior and indestructible, attaining the noble path of self-realization. (The Tang translation states: "By observing with wisdom, the mind is free from discrimination and does not fall into the two extremes.
The basis of support is transformed into purity without being destroyed, thereby attaining the internal realization of noble wisdom.")
[The sphere of] objective conditions is the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Commentary states: Not giving rise to deluded thoughts, not giving rise to attachment, and not grasping at the marks of form—this transcends the views of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings—this transcends the views of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). One gives rise to the most supreme skillful means (*upāya*).
Within a single gateway of giving, the six perfections are instantaneously perfected. One should know that this is likewise true for morality, patience, and the others.
One perfection is all perfections; all perfections are one perfection. Practice arises in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*);
practice is entirely within that nature. This transcends the views of the provisional Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is called "fulfillment" and is not merely momentary (*kṣaṇika*). All phenomena...
The first long prose section within the "Momentary Gate" is concluded. II. Verse Summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Empty, impermanent, and momentary—these are constructed by the deluded thoughts of fools.
(In the Tang translation: "Fools discriminate conditioned things as empty, impermanent, and momentary. They are like a river, a lamp, or a seed.
One should form the conception of the *kṣaṇa* (the Chinese translation says: "discerning the meaning of the *kṣaṇa*, like a river, a lamp, or a seed"). In the *kṣaṇa*, agitation and confusion cease;
it is quiescent and free from activity. All phenomena (*dharma*) do not arise; this, I say, is the meaning of the *kṣaṇa*.

(The Chinese translation says: "All phenomena do not arise; they are quiescent and without activity. The nature of all things is entirely detached—this is my meaning of the *kṣaṇa*"). The arising of things...
Then there is cessation. (The Tang translation says: "Immediately upon arising, it ceases. This is not taught for the sake of the ignorant.
The nature of uninterrupted continuity is permeated by false conceptualization. (The Tang translation says: "It arises from the discrimination of the various realms of existence.

Ignorance is its cause; the mind arises from that. Until form has yet arisen, what division exists in the interim? (The Tang translation says: "Before one can discern the coming of form, in the middle...")
In the interval between what ceases and what arises, where does it abide? The preceding moment ceases in continuous succession, and another mind arises following it.
(The Tang translation says: "It ceases in uninterrupted succession, yet a distinct mind arises. When it does not abide in form, by what object of perception (*ālambana*) is it produced?
Since it arises from that [preceding mind], it does not arise from a true cause. (The Tang translation says: "If that mind arises by taking that as its object, then its cause is false. How so?
There is nothing established, yet one perceives momentary disintegration. (The Tang translation says: "Because the essence of delusion is not established, how can there be momentary extinction?
The Commentary states: This verse addresses the delusion regarding the *tathāgatagarbha* that results in [the perception of] moments. Moments are fundamentally without intrinsic nature.

It means that because foolish people use deluded conceptualization to differentiate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), their essence is fundamentally empty and inherently impermanent from the beginning.
Therefore, it is called a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*). Like the flow of a river, like the flame of a lamp, or like the growth of a sprout from a seed, there is transformation from moment to moment;
thus, one forms the notion of a "moment" therein. If one knows that the moment is quiescent and unarisen, [one realizes the ultimate].
Thus, all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature. This is why I speak of the "momentary":
it precisely reveals the meaning that arising is itself non-arising. Indeed, all things perish at the very moment of their birth and do not abide for even an instant;
yet the deluded do not know this, falsely perceiving them as an uninterrupted succession. This is permeated by the conceptualizations of the various realms of existence, and all possess ignorance.
Ignorance acts as the cause; there is no other cause. Ignorance grasps at the objects of form, and it is conventionally said that the mind arises [therefrom].
Before form exists, what could the mind possibly possess? When form and mind perish moment by moment, they continue to arise in each successive moment.
If one does not abide in form, from what object of perception (*ālambana*) could it arise?
If the mind arises by taking that form as its object, then its cause is false and unreal, and its substance is not established. Since it has no establishment, how can there be destruction?
Thus, one knows that moments have no intrinsic nature; they are merely the deluded conceptualizations of the ignorant.

The practitioner’s meditative absorption, the diamond-like relics of the Buddha, the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and the indestructible phenomena of the world—all these are attained by abiding in the True Dharma.
Possessing the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the bhikṣu attains equanimity. How does one perceive the momentary? (In the Tang translation:
"The perfect wisdom of the Tathāgata and what the bhikṣu realizes: the nature of all dharmas is eternally abiding; how does one perceive the momentary?")
The Commentary states:

This verse indicates that untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) are not momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Because the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven are not reached by the calamity of fire, they are said to be "indestructible.
However, both the calamities of water and wind can destroy them. Here, worldly affairs are specifically cited as an analogy.
This is merely a partial analogy. It is the same with the vajra. That which is realized by the Tathāgata refers to the true suchness (tathatā) of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā);
that which is attained by the bhikṣu refers to the true suchness of the emptiness of self (ātma-śūnyatā). How can suchness be seen as momentary?
Gandharvas, illusions, and the like—forms have no momentariness. (In the Tang translation: "Why are forms such as those of a *gandharva-city* or an illusion not momentary?

Regarding unreal forms and the like, one views them as if they were real. (In the Wei translation: "If there are no four great elements (*mahābhūta*) yet form is seen, what function do the four great elements serve?
In the Tang translation: "The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) lack a real nature; how can it be said that they are the creators [of derived matter]? )
The Commentary states: This passage generally reveals that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; that which is momentary is, in itself, non-momentary.

This means that just as the illusory forms of a city of Gandharvas, having already arisen and ceased, are neither arising nor ceasing, so too all derivative matter composed of the four great elements arises and ceases and is, in itself, neither arising nor ceasing.
Why, then, do you regard them alone as being real? (30)
The seventh section, "The Gate of the Momentary Nature of All Dharmas," is concluded. **Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Gate of Resolving Doubts.** (In the Wei translation, this is titled "Chapter Fifteen:
Transformation"; in the Tang translation, it is "Chapter Seven: Manifestation. This text is divided into three parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the granting of permission to teach; third, the formal exposition. △ Now, the first part: the inquiry.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has prophesied that Arhats shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, being no different from all Bodhisattvas. (In the Tang translation:
'For what reason does the Tathāgata bestow upon Arhats the prophecy of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? All sentient beings..."
"Beings subject to birth do not enter parinirvāṇa; who, then, attains the Buddha-way? (The Tang translation asks:

"For what reason is it further said that there are sentient beings without the nature for parinirvāṇa who attain the Buddha-way? "From the initial attainment of Buddhahood until parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken therein, nor was anything answered.
(The Tang translation asks: "And for what reason is it said that from the initial attainment of Buddhahood until parinirvāṇa...")
Within this interval, not a single word is spoken, for the Tathāgata is eternally in samādhi; thus there is neither vitarka nor vicāra (the Chinese translation states:

"Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata is always in samādhi, without applied thought or sustained thought"). The emanation-Buddha performs the Buddha-work through emanation (the Chinese translation states:

"Furthermore, it is said that all Buddha-works are merely emanations"). For what reason, then, is it said that consciousness has the characteristic of momentary, successive destruction? (The Chinese translation...)
It says: "Furthermore, it states that the various consciousnesses undergo momentary transformation and decay, yet the Vajrapāṇi spirits constantly follow and guard them" (the Tang translation says:
"Furthermore, it states that the Vajra-spirits constantly follow and attend to them"). Why is the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) not established? (The Tang translation says:

"Furthermore, it states that the prior limit is unknowable, yet it speaks of parinirvāṇa existing"). It manifests Māras and the deeds of Māras. (The Tang translation says: "Furthermore, there currently exist Māras and...")
Due to the retribution for the karma of Māra and evil deeds—such as the cases of the Māna-son Ciñcā and the woman Sundarī—the Tathāgata emerged with an empty bowl.
Thus, the obstructions of evil karma manifested. How could it be said that the Tathāgata has attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) yet remains not free from faults? [The Tang translation states:
"Furthermore, there were other retributions, namely the Brahmin woman Ciñcā, the heretical woman Sundarī, and returning with an empty bowl."]
Regarding such matters: since the Blessed One possesses such karmic obstructions, how could he have attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
And once he has already attained the knowledge of all modes, why would he not be free from such faults?
The Commentary states: There are ten doubts in total; some are explained in this very sutra, while others are explained in other sutras.

However, by consulting the Tang dynasty translation, the sections will become clear of themselves. Regarding "Māra": when the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), the armies of Māra came to disturb him.
Regarding "the deeds of Māra" (mārakarma): when the Buddha was in the royal palace, he fully experienced the pleasures of the five desires for ten years.
Furthermore, Cincā Māṇavikā was a Brahmin woman who tied wooden fish to her belly and slandered the Buddha, claiming he had sexual relations with her.
Sundarī was a woman of a non-Buddhist sect whose body was murdered and buried at the Buddha’s dwelling; she slandered the Buddha, claiming he had killed her.
His emerging with an empty bowl was the incident that occurred in the village of Kharjūrika. The term "and so forth" includes [the episodes of] the golden spear and the horse-barley.
These refer to matters such as headaches and backaches. △ Second, the granting of permission to teach.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: “Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon this well. I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: “Excellent, World-Honored One! So be it; we shall receive your instruction.”
III. The Correct Exposition has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. △ Now, the first part. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is for the sake of *nirvāṇa* without remainder that I speak thus, in order to induce and encourage those who practice the bodhisattva path" (the Tang translation says:
"I do so for the sake of the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, secretly exhorting them to cultivate the bodhisattva practices"). This and other [teachings] in the world...

For those bodhisattva practitioners who abide in the realms and delight in the nirvāṇa of the Śrāvaka vehicle, in order to cause them to abandon the Śrāvaka vehicle and advance toward the Mahāyāna, the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha bestows predictions upon the śrāvakas;

it is not the *dharmatābuddha* who does so. (The Tang translation states: "Furthermore, it is the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha who bestows predictions upon emanated śrāvakas, and not the *dharmatābuddha* who bestows predictions upon śrāvakas; this is a secret teaching. O Mahāmati, because of this...

For this reason, it is recorded that the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are not different. Mahāmati, "not different" means that for the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddha-tathāgatas, the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are severed, and their liberation is of a single taste;
it is not that the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed. Mahāmati, as for the cognitive hindrance, it is the superior purity of seeing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
As for the afflictive hindrance, it is first practiced through the vision of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), and then severed.
The seven consciousnesses cease. (The Tang translation says: "When one perceives the non-self of persons, the mental consciousness is relinquished; at this time, the first severance occurs.

One attains liberation from the hindrances to phenomena (*dharmāvaraṇa*), and the habitual tendencies of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are extinguished, reaching ultimate purity. (The Tang translation says: "Only when the habitual tendencies of the storehouse consciousness are extinguished and one is liberated from the hindrances to phenomena does one attain eternal purity.")
The Commentary states: This answers the first doubt regarding whether Arhats can attain Bodhi.

Since this has not yet undergone the revelation and clarification of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is merely a secret prediction within the two *Prajñāpāramitā* (the "Milk") sutras; therefore, it is called a "secret teaching.

A transformation Buddha bestows a prediction upon a transformed śrāvaka in order to cause the śrāvakas of true practice to turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna. As for these śrāvakas of true practice...

Because they have not yet seen the Buddha of the Dharma (*dharmabuddha*). If, upon reaching the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, their three faculties (*indriya*) have matured, then the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) constitutes the attainment of the Buddha of the Dharma.

Next, regarding the discrimination of the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*): this is the same for both the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas. However, they differ from the Bodhisattvas in that they have not yet severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Only by severing the cognitive hindrances does one truly become a Buddha; this simultaneously explains the second "non-" [in the context of the non-arising of dharmas].
This is the doubt regarding the nature of attaining Buddhahood.

Because of the dharma of primordial abiding (*pūrvasthita-dharma*), the preceding and succeeding [states] are not of a different nature. This is because of the inexhaustible original vow (the Tang translation states:

"I rely on the dharma of primordial abiding to speak these esoteric words; they are not different from the Buddhas of the past, for there shall be no further teaching hereafter, as all such syllables were already complete from the beginning").
The Commentary states: This answers the third doubt concerning the non-speaking of a single word.
The Tathāgata expounds the Dharma without deliberation or investigation, because he is transformed by right wisdom and because his mindfulness is not deluded.

He is without deliberation or investigation (the Tang translation reads: "The Tathāgata’s right wisdom is free from deluded thoughts; he does not wait for thought and reflection before preaching the Dharma").
Because the habit-energies of the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance-dwelling are severed, the two types of afflictions are abandoned;
one is freed from the two kinds of death, realizes the selflessness of persons and phenomena, and severs the two obstacles.
The Commentary states: This answers the fourth doubt regarding permanent meditative concentration and the fifth doubt regarding transformation Buddhas.

Mahāmati, the seven—mind, intellect, mentation, and the visual consciousnesses and so forth—are the causes of momentary habitual tendencies; they are excluded from the category of wholesome, untainted [dharmas].

They no longer undergo cyclic existence. (The Tang translation states: "The seven habit-energies—namely, the mental consciousness, the manas-consciousness, the eye-consciousness, and so forth—act as causes.

They are of a momentary nature; apart from untainted goodness, they are not dharmas that flow [toward liberation]. Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and of suffering and happiness.
It cannot be realized by foolish ordinary people whose wisdom is distracted by emptiness. (The Tang translation states: "The Tathāgatagarbha...")
The causes of the cycle of birth and death as well as of nirvāṇa, and of suffering and joy, are not known by the ignorant and foolish, who falsely cling to emptiness.
The Commentary states: This answers the doubt concerning the sixth moment. The seventh consciousness has no independent substance; its entire substance is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Because its whole substance follows conditions, it is said to be momentary (*kṣaṇika*). When one thoroughly understands that while following conditions it remains unchanging, then...
This belongs to the category of wholesome, untainted qualities. This Tathāgatagarbha is not only unrecognized by ordinary beings;
it is also not realized by the confused wisdom regarding emptiness of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).

Because the two vehicles possess only the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, they perceive only emptiness, yet there still remains the transformation-death and the constant flow of the true and eternal, which is like a rapid stream appearing to be still.
The current flows so swiftly that it cannot be seen; it is not that there is no current. Therefore, it is called "disturbed mind.
Mahāmati, those who are followed and protected by the Vajrapāṇi are merely transformation Buddhas (nirmāṇa-buddha), not the true Tathāgata. Mahāmati.
The True Tathāgata is free from all faculties and measures (*indriya-pramāṇa*).

All the faculties and measures of ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists are entirely extinguished (the Tang translation says: "that which cannot be known by those of the Two Vehicles or non-Buddhists").

Because he has attained the patience regarding the knowledge of the uninterrupted Dharma (*anantara-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and dwells in the bliss of the present life (the Tang translation says: "dwelling in the bliss of the present life, he accomplishes wisdom and patience"), he is not [known] by the Vajrapāṇis.
"Protected. The commentary states: This answers the seventh doubt regarding constant attendance and protection.

All transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) are not born of karma. A transformation-buddha is not [identical to] a Buddha, yet is not separate from a Buddha. (The Tang translation says: "not identical to...")
This is the Buddha, yet it is also not non-Buddha; he teaches the Dharma by means of signs produced by sentient beings, such as a potter’s wheel.

(The Tang translation states: "For example, just as a potter produces something through the combination of various factors, so too does the Transformation Buddha preach the Dharma, fully endowed with all marks.
This is not spoken from the realm of self-realization accessible only to oneself.
The Commentary says: This is a transcendent response to the ninth doubt concerning the manifestation of Māras and māra-activities, as well as the retribution of evil karma.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, fools give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the seven consciousness-bodies (the Chinese translation says: "seeing the cessation of the six consciousnesses").

Because they do not realize the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the view of permanence. Because of their own false conceptualization, they do not know the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).

[The Tang translation says: "One's own mental discrimination is its original limit; therefore, it cannot be apprehended. When the wisdom of one's own false conceptualization is extinguished, there is liberation. [The Tang translation says:]...
"By departing from this discrimination, one immediately attains liberation.
The Commentary states: This is a retrospective answer to the eighth doubt concerning the "limit of manifestation" (*prajñapti-mūla-koṭi*).

When one perceives the cessation of the six consciousnesses, one erroneously identifies the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) as *nirvāṇa*. When one perceives that a portion of the ego-clinging within the seventh [consciousness] has been suppressed and severed...
Consequently, they mistakenly identify the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles as the ultimate state,
unaware that these will eventually arise again and are not a state of total extinction. Upon hearing of the existence of the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*),

they give rise to the view of eternalism, failing to realize that it receives perfuming and maintains seeds, revolving perpetually like a flowing stream— acting as the fruit in relation to what precedes it, and acting as the cause in relation to what follows.
It appears to be permanent and appears to be unitary, yet it is neither unitary nor permanent. Since false conceptualization has no intrinsic nature, how could there be a primordial limit?
By realizing its lack of intrinsic nature, one attains liberation; therefore it is said: "The prior limit is unknowable, yet parinirvāṇa is spoken of."
"Because the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the four stages of abiding and the stage of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) are severed, all faults are severed.
The Commentary states: "This concludes the response to the tenth doubt regarding the non-separation from various faults. The long prose section is finished.
II. Verse Summary."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The three vehicles are also not vehicles;
the Tathāgata does not perish" (in the Tang translation: "there is no nirvāṇa for a Buddha"). This is what all Buddhas have prophesied, teaching the departure from all faults and evils.
It is for the sake of all uninterrupted wisdom (which the Tang translation calls "the attainment of ultimate wisdom") and for nirvana without remainder.
To entice and advance those of inferior capacity, it is therefore taught through concealment (which the Tang translation calls "spoken according to this intentional meaning").

The wisdom arising from all Buddhas is precisely the analytical teaching of the path (which the Tang translation calls "proclaiming such a path"). The various vehicles are not [true] vehicles; they are not [true] nirvana.
"Parinirvāṇa. (In the Tang language: "Only this, and nothing else; therefore, for them there is no nirvāṇa. Desire, form, existence, and views—these are said to be the four grounds of abiding.

They arise from the mental consciousness; consciousness is the dwelling, and the mind (*manas*) is that which dwells therein. (In the Tang language: "The storehouse-consciousness and the mind are also within it.

The mind and the visual consciousness, etc., are described as being subject to cessation and impermanence. (In the Tang language: "Because one sees that the mind, the visual consciousness, and so forth, are impermanent...")

They may speak of severance, or form a view of nirvāṇa; yet for them it is taught as being eternally abiding (the Tang translation says: "The deluded manas gives rise to the notion of permanence, and false wisdom calls this 'nirvāṇa'").
The Commentary states: This verse summarizes only the first and eighth points; the remaining doubts may be resolved accordingly.
Of the [total] three initial verses, the first summarizes the first point, and the latter two summarize the eighth point.

Regarding "the dwelling of consciousness," the eighth consciousness serves as the cave-dwelling for the preceding seven. Regarding "that upon which the mind resides," the seventh consciousness serves as the immediate support for the sixth.
Furthermore, the first seven consciousnesses are said to be impermanent because they arise and perish moment by moment.

Even if they are temporarily extinguished, this is still not *nirvāṇa*, because the seeds flowing within the *ālayavijñāna* have not been permanently severed. When one transforms and abandons the *ālayavijñāna* to realize the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), one then realizes the primordially abiding Dharma.
Not a single word is spoken; the mind is always in meditative concentration, and it is not a phenomenon of momentary flux.
He assumes the guise of an attendant and is able to perform various transformative deeds, forever free from all faults.

He even guides those of the three vehicles and the icchantikas, so that they shall ultimately and equally realize entry [into enlightenment]. The thirty-eighth section, "The Gate of Resolving the Doubts of the Assembly," concludes.
Section Thirty-Nine: The Chapter on Prohibiting the Consumption of Meat. (In the Wei translation, this is titled "Chapter Sixteen: Prohibiting the Consumption of Meat";
in the Tang translation, it is "Chapter Eight: Prohibiting the Consumption of Meat. The text is divided into three parts: first, the inquiry; second, the granting of permission to teach;
third, the formal exposition. △ Now, the first part.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati asked in verse: “Regarding those bodhisattvas who are resolute in seeking the Buddha-way, how should they regard alcohol, meat, and onions—should they be consumed or not?
I pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One, out of compassion, will explain this for us.
These things to which fools are greedily attached are foul-smelling, impure, and bring ill repute; they are [the food] of tigers, wolves, and [other beasts].”

"Delighting in sweets—how can these be eaten? Eating gives rise to various faults; not eating is meritorious and wholesome. I pray that you will explain for me the transgressions and blessings of eating and not eating.
After the Bodhisattva Mahāmati had spoken this verse of inquiry, he further addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the merits and faults, the virtues and evils, of eating and not eating meat, both for myself and for all other Bodhisattvas.'"

In the present and the future, you shall preach the Dharma in various ways for those beings who desire to eat meat, causing those beings to direct their hearts toward one another with loving-kindness.
Having attained this loving-kindness, each shall clearly understand their own stage of abiding and swiftly attain ultimate, unsurpassed Bodhi.
Furthermore, having brought rest to their respective stages as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they too shall quickly achieve success.

Even for those followers of external paths who pursue the teachings of evil and heterodox doctrines—those with false views who are inverted in their attachments to the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism—there are still prohibitions that do not permit the eating of meat.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, the protector of the world, who has perfected the True Dharma?
"And yet you eat meat?
The commentary states: "To eat meat is to lack compassion; it is despised by the world and is unsuitable for one who cultivates the Way.
If one abstains from eating meat, oneself and others will be at peace, and compassion will be nurtured. Furthermore, Mount Laṅkā is the dwelling place of yakṣas."
Although one may hear the True Dharma, if one has not yet ceased eating meat, and if one does not cease eating meat, one will not enter the path of correct practice;

therefore, I specifically submit this inquiry as a vital gateway for true cultivation and practical realization, much like the meaning of the three gradual stages of practice in the *Mahāvaipulya Śrī-māyā-viśva-vimokṣa-sūtra*.
△ Second, the granting of the teaching.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "So be it; we shall receive your instruction."
III. The Correct Exposition has two parts: first, the long prose; second, the verse summary. △ Now, the first part. The Buddha addressed Mahāmati:
"There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat. Nevertheless, I shall now briefly explain them for you.
That is to say, all sentient beings, from the very beginning, have been related through successive causes and conditions, having frequently been one’s own six kinds of kin. Because they were kin..."

(1) Because it involves mental conceptualization, one should not eat meat. (2) Because the flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, and other such creatures is sold mixed together by butchers, one should not eat meat.
(3) Because it grows from impure elements and vapors, one should not eat meat.
(4) When sentient beings smell its odor, they all become terrified, just as dogs do upon seeing outcasts such as Caṇḍālas or Taṃbas.

(4) Because it causes revulsion and because one is terrified by the howling of packs of dogs, one should not eat meat. (5) Furthermore, because it prevents the arising of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in the practitioner, one should not eat meat.
(6) Because it is what the ignorant and foolish crave, being foul-smelling, filthy, and impure, and because it brings no good reputation, one should not eat meat.
One should not eat meat. (6) Because it causes various incantations and spells to fail to achieve their results. One should not eat meat.

(7) Because those who kill living beings perceive the form and give rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor. (The Tang translation says: "Upon seeing its color and form, one already gives rise to a mind that craves its taste.
How can a Bodhisattva, who regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were his own body, see them and then make them into food?)
(8) One should not eat meat, for those who eat meat are abandoned by the devas; therefore, one should not eat meat. (9) One should not eat meat, for it causes the breath to smell foul;
therefore, one should not eat meat. (10) One should not eat meat, for it causes many evil dreams; therefore, one should not eat meat.

(11) One should not eat meat, for tigers and wolves will catch its scent in secluded forests; therefore, one should not eat meat. (12) It causes one’s consumption of food and drink to lack moderation.
Therefore, one should not eat meat. (13) Because it causes practitioners to fail to develop revulsion [for cyclic existence], one should not eat meat.
(14) I have previously stated that regarding whatever food and drink one consumes, one should conceive of it as the flesh of one's own child and as the taking of medicine.
One should not eat meat. (15) There is no basis for the claim that eating meat is permitted.
The Commentary states: *Caṇḍāla* is translated here as "butcher"; *Tānava* is translated here as "hunter.

If one must regard even leftover food as being like the flesh of one's own child and is forbidden from indulging in it with craving, how much more so regarding the flesh of sentient beings—how could such eating ever be permitted? The rest is self-evident.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasaudāsa (translated into Chinese as "Born of Lions").
He ate various kinds of meat until he eventually came to eat human flesh. His ministers and subjects could no longer endure this, so they plotted a rebellion and cut off his stipends.
Because those who eat meat have such faults as these, one should not eat meat.
The Commentary says: This further cites past failures as a solemn warning for the present.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, whenever there are those who kill for the sake of profit, slaughtering and selling living beings, those foolish sentient beings who eat meat use money as a net to catch various meats. As for those who kill, if they do so with wealth and goods...
If one uses hooks and nets to capture those beings that move through the air, on water, or on land, and slaughters them in various ways for profit from butchering and trade—
O Mahāmati, there is no fish or meat that does not involve instruction, seeking, and conceptualization. For this reason, one should not eat meat.

The Commentary says: Although one does not kill oneself, nor does one command another to kill, yet by merely ordering that money be used to purchase meat already prepared, the seller will only sell the meat for the sake of that money;
thus, it is still the buyer who causes the killing. Were there no one to buy it...
As for those who purchase ready-made meat, it is still due to their mental construction of seeking it that they do so.
Mahāmati, at times I have spoken of prohibiting five kinds of meat, or restricted ten kinds;
however, in this sutra, through skillful means, I have excluded all exceptions at all times, and thus all [meat-eating] is entirely forbidden.

The Commentary says: "There are times when five types [of meat] are prohibited; that is to say, one must not eat meat that has been seen to be killed, heard to have been killed, suspected to have been killed, not naturally deceased, or not scavenged by birds.
Alternatively, ten types are restricted; namely, humans, snakes, elephants, horses, dragons, and foxes."
Pigs, dogs, lions, and monkeys—these ten kinds of impure meat must not be eaten. These were all provisional and gradual methods employed when there was no other choice;
therefore, in this present sutra, they are all completely prohibited, which alone constitutes the true meaning.
"Mahāmati, even the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have no food to eat, much less the eating of fish and meat. (The Tang translation says:
'Even my noble disciples do not consume the coarse, material food of ordinary beings, much less the impure food of flesh and blood.
Mahāmati, even Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas subsist solely on the food of Dharma; how much more so the Tathāgata?"
Wisdom: The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not a body sustained by various foods; furthermore, because he is preceded by great compassion, he regards all sentient beings as his only child.
For this reason, he does not permit the eating of one's own child's flesh.
The Commentary states: "Those who obtain the food of dharma-joy and the delight of dhyāna no longer rely on solid food; how much less would they consume the foul flavors of flesh and blood?
"Great compassion as the precursor" means that great compassion is the foremost. This concludes the initial long prose section.
△ Second, the verses in praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Once all were our own kin;
they are base, filthy, and impure. Born from what is impure, their very scent causes terror upon being smelled. All meats and onions, as well as various..."
"Various types of intoxicants, such as garlic and the like, should always be avoided by those who practice [the path].
The commentary states: "Because the consumption of meat was prohibited, the five pungent plants (*pañca-garaka*) and alcohol were also prohibited.

As for the five pungent plants: first, scallions; second, leeks; third, garlic; fourth, chives (the term 'and so forth' includes this); and fifth, *hingukṣā* (also known as *qiázi*; in the region south of the Yangtze River...").
It is found in many places; it may be used for those who speak falsely in the assembly. Great error! Great error! ○ *Khang-kyu* (hing-chü):

This is not found in this region. "Fang" means unrestrained indulgence; "yi" means transgression and excess. Drinking various kinds of wine can cause the mind and will to become unrestrainedly indulgent.

This transgresses and exceeds the rites and laws. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: a single moment of negligence is called drinking the wine of the three poisons.
One should also always avoid sesame oil and beds with perforated slats, for those tiny insects within them are utterly terrified.

The Commentary states: In the Western lands, sesame oil is first soaked to extract the insects and only then pressed; therefore, it is unfit for consumption. Food and drink give rise to negligence (*pramāda*);
negligence gives rise to various perceptions (*vitarka*)—the Chinese translation says "perverted perceptions. From these perceptions, craving arises. For this reason, one should not eat it.
Because eating gives rise to craving, and craving causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated; this delusion and intoxication lengthen the thirst of desire, giving rise to [further suffering].
One will not be liberated from death.
The commentary states: This reveals that food and drink serve as the predominant and superior conditions for birth and death; therefore, one should not indulge in them with craving.
To kill sentient beings for profit, or to purchase various meats with wealth—both are evil karmas; after death, one falls into the Raurava (Crying) Hell.
If there is no conceptual seeking (*vijñapti-saṃjñā*), then the three kinds of pure meat do not exist. These do not arise without a cause;
therefore, one should not eat them. The Commentary says: People know the evil of the killer, yet they do not know the evil of the buyer.
If I do not buy it, why would he kill? Although it is said that one has not seen the killing, nor heard of the killing, nor suspects it was killed for oneself, in reality...
Thus, they buy meat because of me; there must be something that causes them to conceive such thoughts and seek it out. How could it exist without a cause?
Because of this, all those practitioners completely distance themselves from it, and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, reprove them.
Passing from one state to another, they devour one another; upon death, they fall among the species of tigers and wolves. Foul and loathsome, they are born constantly ignorant and dull-witted.
They are mostly born as Caṇḍālas, hunters, or Taṃbas; or they are born as Dāyinīs, or among those whose nature is to eat flesh.
"Rākṣasas, cats, raccoons, and the like are born everywhere within this [realm].
The commentary states: "This reveals the evil retribution for eating meat. *Tāyanī*—in the Wei translation, she is rendered as a "rākṣasī."
In the *Baddhagaja-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, and this *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, I have prohibited the eating of meat in all instances.
The Commentary states: Regarding the *Baddhagaja*, both translations render it as *Gajapārśva* (Elephant’s Armpit), which is likewise a title of a sūtra.

In the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and within this present sūtra, the consumption of meat is entirely forbidden; there is no teaching therein that permits it as a provisional concession.
Rebuked by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas, those who eat meat without shame or remorse will be perpetually ignorant and deluded in every birth.

Having previously declared that one must abstain from all meat regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected, yet they fail to realize this through their false imaginings; thus they are born into places where meat is eaten.
(The Tang translation states: "Because of their evil habits, the foolish engage in false discrimination.")
The Commentary states: When the three kinds of pure meat were first established, all meat was already prohibited.
This is because, apart from those meats for which there is no suspicion of having been seen, heard, or doubted, no other meat that has not been killed can possibly exist.
To then engage in deluded conceptualization and claim that there actually exists pure meat fit for consumption—how foolish this is!
Just as those faults of sensual desire obstruct noble liberation, so too do wine, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic all serve as obstacles to the Noble Path.
In future ages, sentient beings will speak out of delusion regarding meat, saying: "This is pure and without fault; the Buddha permitted us to eat it."
The Commentary states: All sentient beings are born depending upon sexual desire and survive depending upon food and drink;
therefore, craving for desire, as well as meat, wine, and the like, are all capable of obstructing the holy path and liberation.
To claim that pure meat may be eaten is merely the teaching of the ignorant in the final age; how could it ever be permitted by the Buddha’s teachings?

One should regard food as if taking medicine, or like eating the flesh of one's own child. (The Tang translation says: "Even pure food should be regarded as medicine, and one should maintain the thought that it is like the flesh of a child.

One who gives rise to contentment and renunciation, practicing the alms-round and dwelling securely in a mind of loving-kindness—I say that such a person is always disenchanted [with worldly things] and may constantly dwell together with tigers, wolves, and all manner of evil beasts. If one eats various kinds of flesh and blood, sentient beings will all...

It is terrifying. Therefore, the practitioner does not eat meat with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). One who eats meat lacks compassion and wisdom, and is forever turned away from true liberation (*samyag-vimukti*) and contrary to the outward marks of the noble ones (*ārya-liṅga*).
For this reason, one should not eat it. One will be born into the lineage of Brahmins, in various places of practice, and into families of wisdom and prosperity;
all this results from not eating meat. (The Tang translation says: "If, regarding wine, meat, and so forth, even one... [text fragment])
If one refrains from eating all [forbidden food], one will surely be born among the worthy and holy (ārya), possessing abundant wealth and complete wisdom).
The commentary states: This concludes by revealing the faults of eating and the merits of not eating.
A *brāhmaṇa* is also called a *brahmacārin*. The Buddha once said of himself: "I am truly a śramaṇa; I am truly a brāhmaṇa. Therefore, he was born as a brahmacārin.
"Seed" refers to the seed of Buddhahood. "Wisdom" refers to the virtue of *prajñā*. "Nobility, honor, and abundant wealth" refer to the virtue of liberation.
"Seed of Buddhahood" refers to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. By being able to refrain from eating meat, one will perfectly realize the secret treasury of these three virtues.
What are these merits like? The section on the Main Teaching (Zhengzongfen) concludes above.
III. The Section on Dissemination (Liutongfen). The Song translation does not transmit this;
it is the Dhāraṇī Chapter (in the Wei translation, the seventeenth; in the Tang translation, the ninth).
Chapter XVIII: General Summary (Wei); Chapter X: Verses in Praise (Tang). The Commentary states:

The *Dhāraṇī-parivarta* concerns the protection and circulation [of the teaching] through mantras; the *General Verses in Praise* (*Saṃgraha-gāthā-parivarta*) is a reiteration of the preceding meanings for the sake of circulation.
According to both sutras, there are praises of Sukhāvatī as well as the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon Nāgārjuna.
This text is now transcribed according to the Tang dynasty translation.

Within all the buddha-lands of the ten directions, among sentient beings and bodhisattvas, there exist all the Dharma-body Buddhas, Reward-body Buddhas, Transformation-body Buddhas, and Emanation-body Buddhas.
All have come from Amitāyus, emerging from the realm of Sukhāvatī.
O Mahāmati, you should know that after the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata, there will be those in future ages who uphold my Dharma.

In the land of South India, there was a bhikṣu of great fame and virtue named Nāgārjuna. He was able to demolish the doctrines of existence and non-existence and manifest within the world my unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma.
Having attained the first stage, the Stage of Joy, he was reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
The Commentary states: Nāgārjuna is the patriarch of both the Chan and Tiantai schools; the Buddha had already previously bestowed upon him the prediction of rebirth in the Pure Land.
The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is the ultimate destination of all Buddhas and patriarchs. Most perfect and most sudden, it allows one to perceive the Buddha-mind within the ordinary mind.
Apart from this, how could there be any other matter that transcends it? I pray that those with wisdom will have deep faith.
May firm vows guide all practices, and together may we contemplate Amitābha Buddha so that his vow for perfect enlightenment is fulfilled.
*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Fascicle Four, Exegesis Part Two (Jǔ) Postscript Written After Setting Down the Pen.

I still recall that when I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I immediately applied myself to the Chan school. After several years, I had also engaged with the Vinaya and the doctrinal teachings, producing a considerable amount of writing.
As for this *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, I intended to annotate it only after completing my reading of the entire Tripitaka.

However, during the summer retreat at Seong-gi Hermitage in the year of Renchen (1692), there was no place to borrow the canon; thus, on the third day of the sixth month, I took up my pen, continuing until the eleventh day of the eighth month.
I set down my brush at the Cold Fragrance Hall in the southern suburbs of Changshui.

In barely seventy days, there was hardly a single day that was not occupied by Buddhist affairs, demonic hindrances, physical ailments, or external obstacles. Only after moving through three locations did the manuscript finally emerge from its draft. Alas, alas! The Brahmajāla Sūtra.

The commentaries on the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Samantabhadra-caryā-nirdeśa-vidhi*, and the various Vinaya texts—how harmonious and easy they are!

How much more so the single commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra*—how contrary and difficult it is! Is it not because this work, by means of the Dharma-gate of Self-Awakened Noble Wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna*), directly refutes the prevailing corruptions of the degenerate age, thereby provoking the wrath of Pāpīyas?
Yet, Pāpīyas was able to cause me no sooner had I settled upon my mat than he drove me away. And yet...
It could not disturb my aspirations, nor could it obstruct my array of brushes. Thus, I must surely transform that Pāpīyas into a fellow practitioner of the Buddha-way.
Is it not true, as Vimalakīrti said, that "demons and heretics are all my attendants"? How could I not believe this?
Yet, I am ashamed to have been misled by empty fame, thereby violating the prediction of Bodhidharma that one who clarifies the Way but does not practice it will fall into error. Nevertheless...

This is still better than merely speaking of the Way without clarifying its principles. If the worthy and accomplished can enter into the meaning through these words, as a lamp illuminates forms, they will perhaps not fail my sincere efforts to sacrifice myself for the benefit of others.

From this day forward, relying on the power of the Triple Gem, I shall further complete the *Zangzhi zhijin* (A Guide to the Treasury of Scriptures), the *Fahai guanlan* (Gazing upon the Waves of the Dharma Ocean), as well as the commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*.
If one brings the causal practices of the Lotus to perfection, then this life will be without regret. Written by Ouyi Xu at Ouhua Zhou as a postscript.

All the words of the Buddhas clarify one's own mind; yet when the First Patriarch came from the West, he specifically pointed to the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as that which could serve as a seal for the mind.

Is this not because the *Laṅkāvatāra* elucidates both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and proclaims both the essence of the school (*zong*) and its expositions (*shuo*), making it particularly sufficient as a guide for leading in others?
However, this sutra has difficult phrasing and profound meaning; those who read it are unable to fathom its ultimate purport. It is, for example, like...
Traveling by night, one encounters strange mountains and monstrous rocks; how could one possibly set foot upon them?
Thus, although these scriptures have been transmitted to the present day, those who recognize their true value are as few as those who can identify a gem within the rough jade of Mount Jing.

The Elder of Lingfeng alone felt a profound concern for this, and so he convened the three translations, cross-referencing and elucidating them to compose this *Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning). In the summer of the Jiawu year, he dispatched [Ling] Sheng along with his elder brother Jian to...

In the capital city, funds were solicited for the carving of woodblocks, and an order was issued to print and circulate [this work], so that the lamp of the Dharma language might illuminate the entire dharma-realm.
Thereupon, the calculation for carving and printing required a total of over one hundred gold pieces; likewise, various monastics and laypeople of like mind all contributed according to their means.

After three months, both the carving and printing were completed. Now, the names of those who provided the financial support are recorded and listed in detail at the end of this volume. I prostrate myself...

May those who provide assistance and those who solicit [this work], as well as all sentient beings throughout the dharma realm, together open the noble wisdom of self-awakening and collectively realize the ultimate mind (*paramārthacitta*).
May they perpetuate the life-force of wisdom for eternal flourishing, and brighten the lamp of truth so that it remains inexhaustible.
Respectfully inscribed by the junior disciple of Lingfeng, Lingsheng Canghui.
